pages.title: Welcome
pages.content:
# Welcome Welcome to the Yet Another Mechanism System (YAMS) documentation. YAMS fuses simulation and real control as closely as possible to real life. You can debug and program your robot without the actual robot. You can also program your robot before it is built. YAMS targets WPILib 2027 (`2027_alpha7`) and the SystemCore. Upgrading a 2026 project? See [Upgrading from 2026 to 2027](/documentation/upgrading-from-2026-to-2027.md). ### Installation YAMS ships as two vendordeps, one per WPILib command framework. Install **only one** of them; they conflict with each other. | Command framework | Vendordep | Online URL | | ------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------- | | Commands v2 (`org.wpilib.command2`, Java and C++) | Yet Another Mechanism System (Commands v2) | `https://cdn.yassrobotics.com/yams_commands2.json` | | Commands v3 (`org.wpilib.command3`, Java only) | Yet Another Mechanism System (Commands v3) | `https://cdn.yassrobotics.com/yams_commands3.json` | If you are not sure which one you need, use Commands v2. The [tutorials](/documentation/tutorials/project-setup.md) have a tab for Java with Commands v2, Java with Commands v3, and C++. {% tabs %} {% tab title="Online" %} 1. In VS Code, open the command palette with Ctrl+Shift+P (Cmd+Shift+P on macOS). 2. Run **WPILib: Manage Vendor Libraries**, then **Install new libraries (online)**. 3. Paste the vendordep URL for your command framework from the table above and press Enter. {% endtab %} {% tab title="Offline" %} 1. Install WPILib 2027 (`2027_alpha7`) first, which creates the `2027_alpha7` WPILib home folder. 2. Download `-YAMS-Offline.zip` from the [YAMS GitHub releases](https://github.com/Yet-Another-Software-Suite/YAMS/releases). 3. Extract it into the WPILib home folder, so its `maven` and `vendordeps` folders merge with the existing ones: * **Windows:** `C:\Users\Public\wpilib\2027_alpha7` * **macOS and Linux:** `~/wpilib/2027_alpha7` 4. In VS Code, run **WPILib: Manage Vendor Libraries**, then **Install new libraries (offline)**, and pick **Yet Another Mechanism System (Commands v2)** or **Yet Another Mechanism System (Commands v3)**. {% endtab %} {% endtabs %} YAMS maven artifacts are served from `https://cdn.yassrobotics.com/`. ### Get started with YAMG The quickest way to get started is [YAMG](https://yamg.yassrobotics.com/), the Yet Another Mechanisms Generator. Fill in a form about your mechanism and it writes the code for you, ready to copy into your project. 1. Pick your WPILib version with the toggle at the top right: 2027, or 2026 for a 2026 project. 2. Turn on **Use YAMS**. Without it, YAMG writes code that uses only WPILib and the motor controller's vendor library. 3. Name your subsystem and pick the mechanism type: an elevator, an arm, a pivot or a flywheel. 4. Pick the command framework that matches the vendordep you installed: Commands v2 or Commands v3. 5. Fill in your motor controller, motor, gearing, limits and gains. 6. Copy each generated file into your project, or press **Download All**. Along with the mechanism, YAMG writes `Robot.java` and, for Commands v2, `RobotContainer.java` with controller bindings, or, for Commands v3, a teleop op mode. **Copy Link** puts the whole form into a link, so you can share the mechanism with your team or come back to it later. The tutorials below build the same mechanisms step by step and explain each part. ### Jump right in

:bolt:

Create an ArmCreate your first Arm.Arm

:leaf:

Create an ElevatorCreate your first elevator.Elevator
:crosshairs:Create a shooterCreate your first shooter.Shooter/FlyWheels

pages.title: Why YAMS?
pages.content:
# Why YAMS?

## The problem with rolling your own subsystem

Writing a motor subsystem from scratch is repetitive and error-prone. A production-quality subsystem requires:

* Motor controller configuration (PID, feedforward, gearing, current limits, zero power mode, ramp rates…)
* A physics simulation that actually matches your hardware
* Periodic telemetry publishing so you can see what's happening
* `Mechanism2d` visualizations for AdvantageScope
* Command factories that respect WPILib's requirement system
* Soft limits, hard limits
* Separate sim-only tuning paths
* Invisible simulation from standard classes.

Teams routinely spend days getting a single mechanism working in simulation, only to discover the real robot behaves differently because the sim wasn't accurate enough to tune against. YAMS eliminates that cycle.

## What YAMS replaces

A typical hand-rolled Arm subsystem is 150-300 lines of code: config, sim state, periodic updates, command factories, limit enforcement, and telemetry. The YAMS equivalent is roughly 15 lines, one `SmartMotorControllerConfig`, one `ArmConfig`, one `Arm`, and a couple of command wrappers.

```java
// Everything below replaces ~200 lines of boilerplate
SmartMotorControllerConfig motorConfig = new SmartMotorControllerConfig(this)
    .withControlMode(ControlMode.CLOSED_LOOP)
    .withClosedLoopController(4, 0, 0)
    .withTrapezoidalProfile(DegreesPerSecond.of(180), DegreesPerSecondPerSecond.of(90))
    .withFeedforward(new ArmFeedforward(0, 0, 0, 0))
    .withGearing(new MechanismGearing(GearBox.fromReductionStages(3, 4)))
    .withZeroPower(MotorMode.BRAKE)
    .withStatorCurrentLimit(Amps.of(40))
    .withTelemetry("ArmMotor", TelemetryVerbosity.HIGH);

SmartMotorController smc = new SparkWrapper(new SparkMax(CANPort.CAN_S0, 1, MotorType.kBrushless), DCMotor.getNEO(1), motorConfig);

ArmConfig armConfig = new ArmConfig()
    .withLength(Feet.of(2))
    .withHardLimits(Degrees.of(-10), Degrees.of(120));

Arm arm = new Arm(armConfig, smc);
```

That's it. Simulation, telemetry, hard limits, and a physics-backed `Mechanism2d` all come for free.

## Physics simulation out of the box

Every YAMS mechanism type ships with a physics model:

* **Arm / Pivot**, `SingleJointedArmSim`, gravity compensation included
* **Elevator**, `ElevatorSim` with configurable carriage weight and angle
* **FlyWheel**, `FlywheelSim` with configurable moment of inertia

YAMS runs the simulation automatically when `RobotBase.isSimulation()` is true. Call `arm.simIterate()` in `simulationPeriodic()` and you're done, no additional sim wiring needed.

Because the simulation uses accurate physics, the PID and feedforward gains you tune in sim are a reliable starting point for real hardware. You may still need minor adjustments, but you won't be starting from zero on the field.

## TunerX in simulation (CTRE hardware)

For CTRE TalonFX and TalonFXS motors, YAMS feeds its physics results directly back through Phoenix's vendorsim layer via `getSimState()`. This means:

1. Run your robot code in simulation as normal
2. Open Phoenix Tuner X and connect to the simulation
3. Every TalonFX signal, position, velocity, voltage, current, reads exactly as it would from real hardware

You can watch closed-loop error, plot signal graphs, and verify your gains in TunerX's familiar interface without touching a physical robot. The same workflow you use to diagnose real hardware works identically in simulation. See [TunerX in simulation](/documentation/understanding/live-tuning/tunerx-in-simulation.md) for the steps.

## Live tuning without reflashing

`TelemetryVerbosity.HIGH` publishes all PID gains, feedforward constants, motion profile constraints, soft limits, and current limits as writable NetworkTable entries. At `HIGH` verbosity YAMS also registers a `Live Tuning` command for each motor (call `setupLiveTuning()` on the config to register it in other cases). The command (visible in Elastic or any NT-aware dashboard) applies those values to the running motor controller in real time.

Changing `kP` from 4 to 6 and seeing the mechanism respond takes seconds, not the minutes a redeploy would cost. See the [Live Tuning](/documentation/understanding/live-tuning.md) page for a full field-by-field reference.

## Loop overruns

Heavy subsystems with hand-rolled telemetry, simulation, and visualization code can push the 20 ms robot loop toward or past its budget, especially when multiple mechanisms run simultaneously. YAMS's telemetry and simulation paths are tightly optimized and only run the work that the verbosity level requires; `LOW` publishes only the fields you actually need for competition, keeping loop time predictable.

The SystemCore, which YAMS 2027 runs on, has plenty of processing headroom, so running `TelemetryVerbosity.HIGH` with multiple mechanisms active is not a practical loop time concern.

## Safety by default

YAMS enforces mechanism safety automatically:

* **Hard limits** are enforced in simulation as physical stops, the mechanism cannot travel past them
* **Soft limits** are pushed to the motor controller so the closed-loop controller respects them independent of your command logic
* **Temperature cutoff** stops the motor if the controller overheats
* Custom exceptions are thrown at construction time if limits are misconfigured (e.g., lower limit greater than upper limit), so misconfigurations surface immediately in testing rather than during a match

## AdvantageKit integration

YAMS publishes telemetry in a layout that works naturally with AdvantageKit's IO layer. See the [AdvantageKit Integration](/documentation/understanding/advantagekit-integration.md) page for patterns that combine YAMS's simulation fidelity with AdvantageKit's logging replay.

pages.title: Upgrading from 2026 to 2027
pages.content:
# Upgrading from 2026 to 2027

YAMS 2027 is built on WPILib 2027 (`2027_alpha7`) and runs on the SystemCore. Upgrading a 2026 robot project touches four areas:

1. [WPILib 2027 itself](#wpilib-2027-and-the-systemcore): new `org.wpilib.*` packages, Java 25 and the 2027 vendor libraries.
2. [The YAMS vendordep](#install-the-2027-yams-vendordep): there are now two of them (Commands v2 and Commands v3), served from `cdn.yassrobotics.com`.
3. [The YAMS Java packages](#yams-java-package-split): YAMS is split into `yams.core`, `yams.commands2` and `yams.commands3`.
4. [YAMS API changes](#renamed-and-changed-apis): mechanism constructors, mechanism configs, Trigger factories, live tuning, encoder getters and swerve gyro handling.

{% hint style="warning" %}
These are breaking changes. Code written against 2026 YAMS will fail to compile until it's updated using the patterns below. The [Quick checklist](#quick-checklist) at the end of this page lists every step.
{% endhint %}

## WPILib 2027 and the SystemCore

Install the WPILib 2027 (`2027_alpha7`) release and create or import your project with it. The parts that affect YAMS code are:

* **Java packages are now `org.wpilib.*`.** `edu.wpi.first.*` imports no longer exist. For example:

  | 2026 import                                                | 2027 import                                       |
  | ---------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
  | `edu.wpi.first.units.Units`                                | `org.wpilib.units.Units`                          |
  | `edu.wpi.first.units.measure.Angle`                        | `org.wpilib.units.measure.Angle`                  |
  | `edu.wpi.first.math.system.plant.DCMotor`                  | `org.wpilib.math.system.DCMotor`                  |
  | `edu.wpi.first.math.controller.ArmFeedforward`             | `org.wpilib.math.controller.ArmFeedforward`       |
  | `edu.wpi.first.math.geometry.Pose2d`                       | `org.wpilib.math.geometry.Pose2d`                 |
  | `edu.wpi.first.math.kinematics.ChassisSpeeds`              | `org.wpilib.math.kinematics.ChassisVelocities`    |
  | `edu.wpi.first.math.kinematics.SwerveModuleState`          | `org.wpilib.math.kinematics.SwerveModuleVelocity` |
  | `edu.wpi.first.wpilibj2.command.Command` / `SubsystemBase` | `org.wpilib.command2.Command` / `SubsystemBase`   |
  | `edu.wpi.first.wpilibj2.command.button.Trigger`            | `org.wpilib.command2.button.Trigger`              |
  | (new) Commands v3                                          | `org.wpilib.command3.*`                           |
* **New projects use the `first.robot` package**, with `first/Main.java` starting `first.robot.Robot`. The examples in these docs use `first.robot` too.
* **Java 25** is required (it ships with the WPILib 2027 installer).
* **Vendor libraries:** use the 2027 builds of the vendor libraries YAMS is built against: Phoenix 6 `26.70` alpha, REVLib 2027 and ThriftyLib 2027. Some vendor constructors now take a CAN bus, for example `new TalonFX(1, new CANBus(CANPort.CAN_S0))` and `new SparkMax(CANPorts.fromBusId(1), 2, MotorType.kBrushless)`.
* **C++:** WPILib 2027 uses `wpi::` namespaces (for example `wpi::units::turn_t`, `wpi::math::Rotation2d`, `wpi::cmd::Trigger`) instead of `frc::`, `frc2::` and `units::`. YAMS C++ include paths (`yams/mechanisms/positional/Arm.hpp`, `yams/motorcontrollers/local/SparkWrapper.hpp`, ...) and the `yams::` namespaces did not change.

## Install the 2027 YAMS vendordep

The 2026 vendordep (`https://yet-another-software-suite.github.io/YAMS/yams.json`) does not work with WPILib 2027. Remove it from your project's `vendordeps` folder, then install **exactly one** of the 2027 vendordeps, matching the command framework your robot uses:

| Command framework                   | Vendordep name                             | Vendordep URL                                      |
| ----------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------- |
| Commands v2 (`org.wpilib.command2`) | Yet Another Mechanism System (Commands v2) | `https://cdn.yassrobotics.com/yams_commands2.json` |
| Commands v3 (`org.wpilib.command3`) | Yet Another Mechanism System (Commands v3) | `https://cdn.yassrobotics.com/yams_commands3.json` |

The two vendordeps conflict with each other, so a project can only have one of them. The Commands v3 vendordep is Java only, because WPILib has no C++ Commands v3; C++ projects use the Commands v2 vendordep. See [Installation](/documentation/readme.md#installation) for the online and offline install steps.

YAMS maven artifacts are served from `https://cdn.yassrobotics.com/`. If your `build.gradle` or a vendordep JSON still points at the old `yet-another-software-suite.github.io` maven URL, replace it.

## YAMS Java package split

YAMS's Java API is now split into three package trees:

* **`yams.core`**: mechanism and motor controller state, physics simulation, telemetry, configs, wrappers, gearing, math, units and exceptions. It has no dependency on a command framework.
* **`yams.commands2`**: the classes that bind to WPILib Commands v2 (`Subsystem`, `Command`, `Trigger`). Shipped in the Commands v2 vendordep.
* **`yams.commands3`**: the same classes bound to WPILib Commands v3 (`Mechanism`, `Command`, `Trigger` from `org.wpilib.command3`). Shipped in the Commands v3 vendordep.

Robot code imports the mechanisms, `SmartMotorControllerConfig`, `SwerveDriveConfig`, `SwerveDrive` and `SwerveInputStream` from `yams.commands2` (or `yams.commands3`). Everything else comes from `yams.core`. Do not construct the `yams.core` versions of the command-bound classes directly.

| Old package (2026)                                                                                                | New package for robot code                                                                   |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `yams.mechanisms.positional.Arm`                                                                                  | `yams.commands2.mechanisms.Arm`                                                              |
| `yams.mechanisms.positional.Elevator`                                                                             | `yams.commands2.mechanisms.Elevator`                                                         |
| `yams.mechanisms.positional.Pivot`                                                                                | `yams.commands2.mechanisms.Pivot`                                                            |
| `yams.mechanisms.positional.DifferentialMechanism`                                                                | `yams.commands2.mechanisms.DifferentialMechanism`                                            |
| `yams.mechanisms.positional.DoubleJointedArm`                                                                     | `yams.commands2.mechanisms.DoubleJointedArm`                                                 |
| `yams.mechanisms.velocity.FlyWheel`                                                                               | `yams.commands2.mechanisms.FlyWheel`                                                         |
| `yams.mechanisms.swerve.SwerveDrive`                                                                              | `yams.commands2.swerve.SwerveDrive`                                                          |
| `yams.mechanisms.swerve.utility.SwerveInputStream`                                                                | `yams.commands2.swerve.SwerveInputStream`                                                    |
| `yams.motorcontrollers.SmartMotorControllerConfig`                                                                | `yams.commands2.config.SmartMotorControllerConfig`                                           |
| `yams.mechanisms.config.SwerveDriveConfig`                                                                        | `yams.commands2.config.SwerveDriveConfig`                                                    |
| `yams.mechanisms.config.ArmConfig`, `ElevatorConfig`, `PivotConfig`, `FlyWheelConfig`, `SwerveModuleConfig`, etc. | unchanged, now under `yams.core.mechanisms.config`                                           |
| `yams.mechanisms.swerve.SwerveModule`, `yams.mechanisms.SmartMechanism`                                           | `yams.core.mechanisms.swerve.SwerveModule`, `yams.core.mechanisms.SmartMechanism`            |
| `yams.motorcontrollers.SmartMotorController`                                                                      | `yams.core.motorcontrollers.SmartMotorController`                                            |
| `yams.motorcontrollers.local.SparkWrapper`, `yams.motorcontrollers.remote.TalonFX*Wrapper`                        | unchanged, now under `yams.core.motorcontrollers.*`                                          |
| `SmartMotorControllerConfig.ControlMode`, `SmartMotorControllerConfig.MotorMode`                                  | `yams.core.motorcontrollers.enums.ControlMode`, `yams.core.motorcontrollers.enums.MotorMode` |
| `SmartMotorControllerConfig.TelemetryVerbosity`                                                                   | `yams.core.telemetry.enums.TelemetryVerbosity`                                               |
| `yams.exceptions.*`, `yams.gearing.*`, `yams.math.*`, `yams.units.*`, `yams.telemetry.*`                          | unchanged, now under `yams.core.*`                                                           |

For Commands v3, use the same class names under `yams.commands3` (for example `yams.commands3.mechanisms.Arm` and `yams.commands3.config.SmartMotorControllerConfig`).

For most robot code, migration is an import change:

```java
// Before (2026)
import edu.wpi.first.wpilibj2.command.SubsystemBase;
import yams.mechanisms.config.ArmConfig;
import yams.mechanisms.positional.Arm;
import yams.motorcontrollers.SmartMotorController;
import yams.motorcontrollers.SmartMotorControllerConfig;
import yams.motorcontrollers.SmartMotorControllerConfig.TelemetryVerbosity;
import yams.motorcontrollers.local.SparkWrapper;
```

```java
// After (2027, Commands v2)
import org.wpilib.command2.SubsystemBase;
import yams.commands2.config.SmartMotorControllerConfig;
import yams.commands2.mechanisms.Arm;
import yams.core.mechanisms.config.ArmConfig;
import yams.core.motorcontrollers.SmartMotorController;
import yams.core.motorcontrollers.local.SparkWrapper;
import yams.core.telemetry.enums.TelemetryVerbosity;
```

Method names, constructor argument order and config builder methods are the same in `yams.commands2` and `yams.commands3`. With Commands v3, the class that owns the mechanism implements `org.wpilib.command3.Mechanism` instead of extending `SubsystemBase`, and passes itself to `new SmartMotorControllerConfig(this)` the same way. See `examples/commands3/simple_robot-2027` in the YAMS repository for a complete Commands v3 robot.

## Renamed and changed APIs

### Mechanism constructors now take the `SmartMotorController` directly

Every positional/velocity mechanism (`Arm`, `Elevator`, `Pivot`, `FlyWheel`, ...) used to take a single-argument constructor, with the `SmartMotorController` attached to the config via `.withSmartMotorController(...)`. That setter is gone. Pass the `SmartMotorController` as a second constructor argument instead.

```java
// Before (2026)
SmartMotorController smc = new TalonFXWrapper(new TalonFX(1), DCMotor.getKrakenX60(1), motorConfig);
FlyWheelConfig config = new FlyWheelConfig()
    .withDiameter(Inches.of(4))
    .withSmartMotorController(smc);
FlyWheel flywheel = new FlyWheel(config);
```

```java
// After (2027)
SmartMotorController smc = new TalonFXWrapper(new TalonFX(1, new CANBus(CANPort.CAN_S0)), DCMotor.getKrakenX60(1), motorConfig);
FlyWheelConfig config = new FlyWheelConfig()
    .withDiameter(Inches.of(4));
FlyWheel flywheel = new FlyWheel(config, smc);
```

This applies identically to `Arm`, `Elevator`, and `Pivot`: swap `new Mechanism(config.withSmartMotorController(smc))` for `new Mechanism(config, smc)` everywhere.

### Moment of inertia moved to `SmartMotorControllerConfig`

`withMass(Mass)` was removed from `ArmConfig`, `ElevatorConfig`, and `FlyWheelConfig`. Configure the simulated moment of inertia on the `SmartMotorControllerConfig` instead, either from a length + mass estimate (the same `SingleJointedArmSim.estimateMOI(...)` calculation used previously) or a known MOI value straight from CAD.

```java
// Before (2026)
FlyWheelConfig config = new FlyWheelConfig()
    .withDiameter(Inches.of(4))
    .withMass(Pounds.of(2));
```

```java
// After (2027)
SmartMotorControllerConfig motorConfig = new SmartMotorControllerConfig(this)
    // ...
    .withMomentOfInertia(Inches.of(4), Pounds.of(2)); // length, weight: same estimateMOI() as before

FlyWheelConfig config = new FlyWheelConfig()
    .withDiameter(Inches.of(4));
```

For an `Arm`, use the arm's length in place of diameter: `.withMomentOfInertia(Inches.of(30), Pounds.of(8))`. If you already know the MOI (e.g. from CAD), skip the estimate entirely with `.withMomentOfInertia(MomentOfInertia)`.

### Starting position moved to `SmartMotorControllerConfig`

`withStartingPosition(Angle)` (and the `Distance` overload on `ElevatorConfig`) was removed from the mechanism configs. Set it on `SmartMotorControllerConfig` instead:

```java
// Before (2026)
ArmConfig config = new ArmConfig()
    .withHardLimits(Degrees.of(-180), Degrees.of(180))
    .withStartingPosition(Degrees.of(-180));
```

```java
// After (2027)
SmartMotorControllerConfig motorConfig = new SmartMotorControllerConfig(this)
    // ...
    .withStartingPosition(Degrees.of(-180));

ArmConfig config = new ArmConfig()
    .withHardLimits(Degrees.of(-180), Degrees.of(180));
```

### `isNear(...)` Trigger factory renamed to `near(...)`

In Java, the Trigger factory `isNear(...)` was renamed to `near(...)`, matching the other Trigger factories (`gte()`, `lte()`, `between()`, `max()`, `min()`). The boolean check with the same arguments (for use outside a `Command`/`Trigger`, for example in a sensor supplier) is still called `isNear(...)`.

```java
// Before (2026)
arm.isNear(Degrees.of(80), Degrees.of(2)).onTrue(indexer.run());

// After (2027)
arm.near(Degrees.of(80), Degrees.of(2)).onTrue(indexer.run());

// Unchanged: boolean check
boolean atTarget = arm.isNear(Degrees.of(80), Degrees.of(2));
```

The C++ API still names the Trigger factory `IsNear(...)`.

### Live tuning registration

The "Live Tuning" command is registered automatically against the config's `Subsystem` (or Commands v3 `Mechanism`) when the motor controller sets up its telemetry with `TelemetryVerbosity.HIGH`, which YAMS mechanisms do for you. If you set up telemetry yourself with `setupTelemetry(NetworkTable, NetworkTable)`, call `setupLiveTuning()` on the config afterwards. Before the telemetry is set up the call does nothing:

```java
SmartMotorControllerConfig motorConfig = new SmartMotorControllerConfig(this)
    .withTelemetry("ArmMotor", TelemetryVerbosity.HIGH);
SmartMotorController motor = new TalonFXWrapper(armMotor, DCMotor.getKrakenX60(1), motorConfig);

motor.setupTelemetry(telemetryTable, tuningTable);
motorConfig.setupLiveTuning();
```

Tunable fields are in degrees and RPM (meters and meters per second for linear mechanisms), while the read-only fields next to them are in rotations and rotations per second.

See [Live tuning](/documentation/understanding/live-tuning.md) for how to use it.

### `withIdleMode` renamed to `withZeroPower`

`SmartMotorControllerConfig.withIdleMode(MotorMode)` is now `withZeroPower(MotorMode)` (`WithZeroPower` in C++). `MotorMode` itself moved to `yams.core.motorcontrollers.enums.MotorMode`.

```java
// Before (2026)
.withIdleMode(MotorMode.BRAKE)

// After (2027)
.withZeroPower(MotorMode.BRAKE)
```

### External encoder zero offset getter renamed

The setter `withExternalEncoderZeroOffset(...)` is unchanged. Its getter `SmartMotorControllerConfig.getZeroOffset()` was renamed to `getExternalEncoderZeroOffset()` (`GetExternalEncoderZeroOffset()` in C++). The TalonFX wrapper no longer applies this offset to the rotor (internal) encoder; it only applies to the external encoder.

### Encoder getters on `SmartMotorController`

The external encoder getters were renamed, and new getters read only the motor's relative (internal) encoder:

| 2026                           | 2027 (Java)                             | 2027 (C++)                              |
| ------------------------------ | --------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| `getExternalEncoderPosition()` | `getExternalEncoderMechanismPosition()` | `GetExternalEncoderMechanismPosition()` |
| `getExternalEncoderVelocity()` | `getExternalEncoderMechanismVelocity()` | `GetExternalEncoderMechanismVelocity()` |
| (new)                          | `getRelativeMechanismPosition()`        | `GetRelativeMechanismPosition()`        |
| (new)                          | `getRelativeMechanismVelocity()`        | `GetRelativeMechanismVelocity()`        |

`getMechanismPosition()` and `getMechanismVelocity()` are unchanged: they read the external encoder when `withUseExternalFeedbackEncoder(true)` is set, otherwise the relative encoder. The external encoder getters return an empty `Optional` when no external encoder is attached.

### EasyCRT

`EasyCRTConfig` is gone. `EasyCRT` now takes the three tooth counts and the two readings, and works out its own tolerance:

```java
// Before (2026)
EasyCRTConfig config = new EasyCRTConfig(encoderA::get, encoderB::get)
    .withCommonDriveGear(1.0, 100, 19, 21)
    .withAbsoluteEncoderOffsets(offsetA, offsetB)
    .withMechanismRange(Rotations.of(-1.5), Rotations.of(1.5))
    .withMatchTolerance(Rotations.of(0.006));
Optional<Angle> angle = new EasyCRT(config).getAngleOptional();

// After (2027)
Optional<Angle> angle = new EasyCRT(100, 19, 21).solve(encoderA.get(), encoderB.get());
```

* Offsets and inversion are no longer EasyCRT settings. Set them on the encoders, or adjust the readings before passing them in. The old offsets were added to the raw reading.
* `solve(a, b)` assumes travel centered on zero. Use `solve(a, b, min, max)` otherwise.
* The solved angle is the angle of the gear both pinions mesh with. If the mechanism is geared to that gear (the old `commonRatio`), divide the result by the ratio.
* The status, error and iteration getters and the gear recommender are removed. The [EasyCRT](/documentation/understanding/easycrt.md) page shows how to choose gears and check your margin yourself.
* C++ changed the same way: `EasyCRT{100, 19, 21}.Solve(a, b)`.

### Swerve drive (Java)

* `SwerveDriveConfig.withGyro(...)` now takes a `Supplier<Rotation3d>` (the robot's attitude) instead of a `Supplier<Angle>`. Pass the gyro's full rotation, for example `.withGyro(pigeon::getRotation3d)`.
* `getGyroAngle()` was removed from `SwerveDriveConfig` and `SwerveDrive`. Use `getGyroRotation3d()` and take the heading from it, for example `drive.getGyroRotation3d().toRotation2d()`. The heading wraps at +/-180 degrees.
* If the gyro is mounted so the robot turning shows up as its roll or pitch, set `.withGyroHeadingAxis(GyroAxis.ROLL)` or `.withGyroHeadingAxis(GyroAxis.PITCH)` (`yams.core.mechanisms.config.enums.GyroAxis`, default `YAW`).
* Swerve APIs use WPILib 2027's `ChassisVelocities` and `SwerveModuleVelocity` instead of `ChassisSpeeds` and `SwerveModuleState`, for example `drive.setRobotRelativeChassisSpeeds(ChassisVelocities)`.
* `lockPose()` now turns every module toward the robot center (the X pattern) and holds it there.
* `SwerveInputStream` can publish telemetry and live tuning values with `.withTelemetry(name, verbosity)`. See [Swerve Input Stream](/documentation/understanding/swerve-drive/swerve-input-stream.md).

The C++ swerve API still uses `GetGyroAngle()` and has no `GyroAxis` yet.

## Quick checklist

* [ ] Install WPILib 2027 (`2027_alpha7`) and the 2027 builds of your vendor libraries (Phoenix 6, REVLib, ThriftyLib).
* [ ] Replace every `edu.wpi.first.*` import with its `org.wpilib.*` equivalent, and `ChassisSpeeds`/`SwerveModuleState` with `ChassisVelocities`/`SwerveModuleVelocity`.
* [ ] Remove the 2026 `yams.json` vendordep and install exactly one of `https://cdn.yassrobotics.com/yams_commands2.json` or `https://cdn.yassrobotics.com/yams_commands3.json`.
* [ ] Update YAMS imports: mechanisms, `SmartMotorControllerConfig`, `SwerveDriveConfig`, `SwerveDrive` and `SwerveInputStream` from `yams.commands2` (or `yams.commands3`), everything else from `yams.core`.
* [ ] Import `ControlMode`/`MotorMode` from `yams.core.motorcontrollers.enums` and `TelemetryVerbosity` from `yams.core.telemetry.enums`.
* [ ] Replace `config.withSmartMotorController(smc)` + `new Mechanism(config)` with `new Mechanism(config, smc)`.
* [ ] Move every `.withMass(Mass)` call from a mechanism config to `.withMomentOfInertia(Distance, Mass)` (or `.withMomentOfInertia(MomentOfInertia)`) on that mechanism's `SmartMotorControllerConfig`.
* [ ] Move every `.withStartingPosition(...)` call from a mechanism config to the corresponding `SmartMotorControllerConfig`.
* [ ] Rename Trigger factory calls `isNear(...)` to `near(...)` (Java). Keep `isNear(...)` where you need a `boolean`.
* [ ] Rename `withIdleMode(...)` to `withZeroPower(...)`.
* [ ] Rename `getZeroOffset()` to `getExternalEncoderZeroOffset()`, and `getExternalEncoderPosition()`/`getExternalEncoderVelocity()` to `getExternalEncoderMechanismPosition()`/`getExternalEncoderMechanismVelocity()`.
* [ ] If you set up motor controller telemetry yourself, call `config.setupLiveTuning()` after `setupTelemetry(...)` to get the "Live Tuning" command.
* [ ] Replace `EasyCRTConfig` with `new EasyCRT(sharedGearTeeth, encoderATeeth, encoderBTeeth)` and `solve(encoderA, encoderB)`, and move offsets and inversion onto the encoders.
* [ ] Swerve (Java): pass a `Supplier<Rotation3d>` to `withGyro(...)`, replace `getGyroAngle()` with `getGyroRotation3d()`, and add `withGyroHeadingAxis(...)` if your gyro is not mounted flat.
* [ ] Double-check any hard-limit setter names: `withHardLimits(...)` (plural) is correct on `ArmConfig`/`ElevatorConfig`/`PivotConfig`; there has never been a singular `withHardLimit(...)`.

pages.content: # Arm Learn how to program an Arm. {% hint style="info" %} Two motors on one shaft or gearbox? Add the second as a follower with `withFollowers`. Two motors that aren't on the same shaft or gearbox, such as one on each side of the mechanism? pages.title: Step 3: Commands and buttons
pages.content_preview: # Step 3: Commands and buttons Make commands from the Arm and bind them to controller buttons. The `Arm` makes commands for you. Your class hands them out, and the buttons schedule them.

pages.title: Step 4: Simulate it
pages.content: # Step 4: Simulate it Run the arm in simulation and drive it with a controller. The code from the first three steps runs on your computer exactly as it will on the robot. YAMS simulates the motor, the gearing and the arm, so the closed loop, the limits and the commands all behave the way they will on the real mechanism. ## Start the simulation {% tabs %} {% tab title="Java, Commands v2" %} Open the command palette with Ctrl+Shift+P and run **WPILib: Simulate Robot Code**. If you are asked which extensions to run, tick **Sim GUI**. {% endtab %} {% tab title="Java, Commands v3" %} Open the command palette with Ctrl+Shift+P and run **WPILib: Simulate Robot Code**. If you are asked which extensions to run, tick **Sim GUI**. The buttons are bound in the `ExampleTeleop` op mode, so that is the op mode to run when you enable. If the simulated mechanism never moves, check that `Robot.java` has a `simulationInit()` that calls `startSimulation(...)` for the mechanism. {% endtab %} {% tab title="C++" %} Open the command palette with Ctrl+Shift+P and run **WPILib: Simulate Robot Code**. If you are asked which extensions to run, tick **Sim GUI**. The first C++ build compiles the whole project, so it takes a few minutes. Later builds are much faster. {% endtab %} {% endtabs %} ## Drive it 1. Connect a controller to your computer, then drag it from **System Joysticks** to **Joystick\[0]**. 2. Open the simulated mechanism with **NetworkTables -> SmartDashboard -> Arm -> mechanism**. 3. Resize **Arm/mechanism** to your liking. 4. Press **Teleoperated** in **Robot State**. The controller now drives the simulated arm just as it would the real one. Congratulations on programming your Arm! :tada::tada: ## Where to go next * Tune the gains while the simulation runs: [Live tuning](/documentation/understanding/live-tuning.md) * See everything the mechanism can do: [Arms](/documentation/understanding/arms.md) and [ArmConfig](/documentation/understanding/arms/arm-config.md) * Look at what the mechanism publishes: [Telemetry](/documentation/understanding/telemetry.md) * Keep your configs tidy as the robot grows: [Organizing configs in constants](/documentation/understanding/config-organization.md)

pages.title: Double FlyWheel
pages.content: # Double FlyWheel We will learn how to program a Double FlyWheel shooter! {% hint style="danger" %} Mechanism classes are meant to be used with "tightly coupled" mechanisms where the Mechanism has 1 or more motor controlling it on a connected shaft, gearbox, or other linkage. {% endhint %} ## Intro At the end of this tutorial you will have a **Double FlyWheel** shooter with two independently controlled flywheels that works in both real life and simulation with the same code! Double flywheels are used where the spin on the game piece matters: running one wheel faster than the other adds backspin or topspin to a shot. ## What is a Double FlyWheel? A double flywheel is a shooter with two separate flywheels, one on each side of the game piece: * **Upper FlyWheel**: drives the top surface of the game piece * **Lower FlyWheel**: drives the bottom surface of the game piece By running them at different speeds, you can: * Add **backspin** (lower faster than upper) * Add **topspin** (upper faster than lower) * Shoot with **no spin** (equal speeds) ## Details This double flywheel uses the following hardware and controls: * Two `TalonFX` (Kraken X60), one for each flywheel * A `3:1` gearbox on each flywheel * 4 inch diameter, 1 pound flywheels * Pressing the bottom face button (`A` on an Xbox controller) sets both flywheels to 3000 RPM (no spin) * Pressing the right face button (`B` on an Xbox controller) sets the upper to 2500 RPM and the lower to 3500 RPM (backspin) * Pressing the left face button (`X` on an Xbox controller) sets the upper to 3500 RPM and the lower to 2500 RPM (topspin) * Pressing the top face button (`Y` on an Xbox controller) stops both flywheels ## The steps Every step has a tab for **Java with Commands v2**, **Java with Commands v3** and **C++**. | Step | What you do | | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | | [Before you start](/documentation/tutorials/project-setup.md) | Create a WPILib project and install YAMS and Phoenix 6. Skip this if you already have a project. | | [Step 1: Two motor controllers](/documentation/tutorials/double-flywheel/motor-controllers.md) | One config and one `SmartMotorController` for each flywheel. | | [Step 2: Commands and buttons](/documentation/tutorials/double-flywheel/commands.md) | One command that sets both speeds, presets for each kind of shot, and the buttons. | | [Step 3: Spin control and followers](/documentation/tutorials/double-flywheel/spin-and-followers.md) | A spin ratio between the wheels, and loosely coupled followers. | {% hint style="info" %} A subsystem should hold at most one YAMS mechanism class, so that live tuning keeps working. Both flywheels here are driven together by one subsystem, so this tutorial controls the two `SmartMotorController`s directly instead of creating two `FlyWheel` mechanisms. This is the same approach as the `DoubleFlyWheelSubsystem` in the YAMS examples. If you would rather have a `FlyWheel` mechanism (with its `Mechanism2d` and Trigger factories) for each wheel, give each wheel its own subsystem and follow the [Shooter/FlyWheels](/documentation/tutorials/shooter-flywheels.md) tutorial for both. {% endhint %} ## Complete Example The following files from the YAMS `simple_robot-2027` Commands v2 example show a complete double flywheel subsystem with two independent flywheels, and a hood pivot in its own subsystem. {% @github-files/github-code-block url="" %} {% @github-files/github-code-block url="" %} The same subsystem in the other two flavors: * **Java, Commands v3:** [`DoubleFlyWheelMechanism.java`](https://github.com/Yet-Another-Software-Suite/YAMS/blob/master/examples/commands3/simple_robot-2027/src/main/java/first/robot/mechanisms/doubleflywheel/DoubleFlyWheelMechanism.java) in `examples/commands3/simple_robot-2027` * **C++:** [`DoubleFlyWheelSubsystem.h`](https://github.com/Yet-Another-Software-Suite/YAMS/blob/master/examples/cpptest/src/main/include/subsystems/doubleflywheel/DoubleFlyWheelSubsystem.h) and [`DoubleFlyWheelSubsystem.cpp`](https://github.com/Yet-Another-Software-Suite/YAMS/blob/master/examples/cpptest/src/main/cpp/subsystems/doubleflywheel/DoubleFlyWheelSubsystem.cpp) in `examples/cpptest`

pages.title: Swerve Drive
pages.content: # Swerve Drive Learn how to program a Swerve Drive. {% hint style="danger" %} Swerve drive requires more hardware configuration than a tank drive. Make sure you have installed YAMS, REVLib (for the `SparkMax` motor controllers) and Phoenix 6 (for the `CANcoder`s and the `Pigeon2`) before starting. [Create a project and install YAMS](/documentation/tutorials/project-setup.md) walks through it. {% endhint %} ## Intro This tutorial builds a swerve drive that works in real life and simulation with the same code. ## Details This swerve drive uses the following hardware and controls: * 4x `SparkMax` (NEO) drive motors, CAN IDs 1, 4, 7, 10 * 4x `SparkMax` (NEO) azimuth motors, CAN IDs 2, 5, 8, 11 * 4x `CANcoder` absolute encoders, CAN IDs 3, 6, 9, 12 * `Pigeon2` gyro, CAN ID 14 * Drive gear ratio `12.75:1`, azimuth gear ratio `6.75:1`, 4 inch wheels * The left stick translates, and the right stick's X axis rotates * Holding the left bumper drives to a pose on the field {% hint style="warning" %} **Simulation Processing Requirements**: YAMS simulates **each motor individually**. With 4 modules containing 2 motors each, that is 8 `SmartMotorController` instances running physics simulation simultaneously. This provides highly accurate simulation but requires more processing power than simplified kinematic-only simulations. {% endhint %} ## The steps Every step has a tab for **Java with Commands v2**, **Java with Commands v3** and **C++**. | Step | What you do | | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | [Before you start](/documentation/tutorials/project-setup.md) | Create a WPILib project and install YAMS, REVLib and Phoenix 6. Skip this if you already have a project. | | [Step 1: The module motors](/documentation/tutorials/swerve-drive/module-motors.md) | A config for the drive motors and a config for the azimuth motors. | | [Step 2: The modules and the drive](/documentation/tutorials/swerve-drive/modules-and-drive.md) | Build four `SwerveModule`s, add the gyro, and create the `SwerveDrive`. | | [Step 3: Driving](/documentation/tutorials/swerve-drive/driving.md) | Drive commands, a `SwerveInputStream` for the sticks, and the bindings. | ## Complete example The following files from the YAMS `simple_robot-2027` Commands v2 example show a complete swerve drive implementation matching the hardware described in this tutorial. {% @github-files/github-code-block url="" %} {% @github-files/github-code-block url="" %} The same drive in the other two flavors: * **Java, Commands v3:** [`SwerveMechanism.java`](https://github.com/Yet-Another-Software-Suite/YAMS/blob/master/examples/commands3/simple_robot-2027/src/main/java/first/robot/mechanisms/SwerveMechanism.java) in `examples/commands3/simple_robot-2027` * **C++:** [`SwerveSubsystem.h`](https://github.com/Yet-Another-Software-Suite/YAMS/blob/master/examples/cpptest/src/main/include/subsystems/SwerveSubsystem.h) and [`SwerveSubsystem.cpp`](https://github.com/Yet-Another-Software-Suite/YAMS/blob/master/examples/cpptest/src/main/cpp/subsystems/SwerveSubsystem.cpp) in `examples/cpptest` ## Next steps * Learn about [AdvantageKit Integration](/documentation/understanding/advantagekit-integration.md) for swerve * See [Organizing Configs in Constants](/documentation/understanding/config-organization.md) for cleaner code * Record this drive's telemetry to a file and review it after a match, see [How do I view my DataLog in AdvantageScope?](/documentation/how-to-simulation-and-logging/how-do-i-view-my-datalog-in-advantagescope.md)

pages.title: How do I shoot on the move?
pages.content: # How do I shoot on the move? Where to learn shooting on the move, and how the ideas in those sources apply to YAMS. Shooting on the move means scoring while the robot is still driving, instead of stopping to line up first. We covered this in a YASS Weekly Workshop, **How To Program Target Tracking And Shooting On The Fly for FRC**. Watch it first: {% embed url="" %} This page does not try to teach it. People in the FRC community have already explained it well, and their work is where you should learn it. What this page adds is the YAMS side: which YAMS call supplies each thing those sources ask for, what the [Swerve Input Stream](/documentation/understanding/swerve-drive/swerve-input-stream.md) does for you and what it does not, and a [complete example](#a-complete-example) that goes from an empty project to a robot that shoots on the move. ## Read these first | Source | Read it for | | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | [Shooting on the Fly](https://blog.eeshwark.com/robotblog/shooting-on-the-fly) and [Shooting on the Fly, Part 2: The LUT Approach](https://blog.eeshwark.com/robotblog/shooting-on-the-fly-pt2), by Eeshwar | The best place to start. Part 1 explains the idea as plain vector math, then covers what goes wrong on a real robot: latency, a flywheel that slows and slips, spin and drag, lobbed shots, and a shooter that is itself moving. Part 2 is the practical side: building the lookup table, getting the shot's speed from the time of flight, shooters with a hood, and tuning the latency. | | WPILib's [Fire Control](https://frc-docs--3242.org.readthedocs.build/en/3242/docs/software/advanced-controls/fire-control/index.html) pages: [Static Shooting via Look-Up Table](https://frc-docs--3242.org.readthedocs.build/en/3242/docs/software/advanced-controls/fire-control/static-shooting.html), [Dynamic Shooting via Time-of-Flight Recursion](https://frc-docs--3242.org.readthedocs.build/en/3242/docs/software/advanced-controls/fire-control/dynamic-shooting.html), [Newton's Method for Dynamic Shooting](https://frc-docs--3242.org.readthedocs.build/en/3242/docs/software/advanced-controls/fire-control/newton-shooting.html) and [Linear Drag (First-Order Air Friction)](https://frc-docs--3242.org.readthedocs.build/en/3242/docs/software/advanced-controls/fire-control/linear-drag.html) | Three firing strategies and a drag correction, with interactive simulations that show where each one converges and where it does not. | | [Shoot on the move from the code perspective](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/shoot-on-the-move-from-the-code-perspective/511815) (Chief Delphi) | A short explanation of the virtual target, with links to much of the rest. | | [Time of Flight Determination](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/time-of-flight-determination/512542) (Chief Delphi) | The different ways teams measure or calculate the time of flight. | | [Shoot While Move Code (1706)](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/shoot-while-move-code-1706/410494) (Chief Delphi) | Team 1706 walking through its 2022 code. | | [Orbit 1690 Online Software Sessions](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/orbit-1690-online-software-sessions/467221) (Chief Delphi) | Recorded sessions from Team 1690 on their swerve and system control software. | | [Mechanical Advantage 6328's `LaunchCalculator.java`](https://github.com/Mechanical-Advantage/RobotCode2026Public/blob/main/src/main/java/org/littletonrobotics/frc2026/subsystems/launcher/LaunchCalculator.java) | A complete launch calculator from a 2026 robot. | | [Hammerheads 5000's `TurretCalculator.java`](https://github.com/hammerheads5000/2026Rebuilt/blob/main/src/main/java/frc/robot/subsystems/turret/TurretCalculator.java), with a [build thread post](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/frc-5000-hammerheads-2026-build-thread-open-alliance/507502/129) that walks through it | A complete shot calculator for a turret from a 2026 robot. | {% hint style="info" %} The WPILib fire control pages are a work in progress in [wpilib-docs #3242](https://github.com/wpilibsuite/wpilib-docs/pull/3242). They have not been merged, so the links go to the pull request's preview and may move. {% endhint %} ## The idea in one picture A game piece keeps the robot's velocity when it leaves the shooter, so a robot that aims straight at the target while driving sideways misses. The sources above all solve the same problem: work out a **lead** that cancels the robot's motion. ## A primer: vector subtraction **Read:** Eeshwar's [Shooting on the Fly](https://blog.eeshwark.com/robotblog/shooting-on-the-fly) and [Shooting on the Fly, Part 2: The LUT Approach](https://blog.eeshwark.com/robotblog/shooting-on-the-fly-pt2). Before you pick a firing strategy, it helps to see the lead as one subtraction, which is how Eeshwar's posts explain it: 1. The time of flight in your lookup table gives the horizontal speed of the standing shot: the distance divided by the time. 2. Point a velocity of that speed at the target. This is the velocity the game piece needs over the ground. 3. Subtract the robot's velocity. What is left is the velocity the shooter has to give the game piece. 4. The direction of that vector is where to aim, and its length is the speed the shot needs. Two things follow from this, and every firing strategy below has to deal with both. The **aim** changes when the robot moves, and so does the **speed** of the shot: drive toward the target and the shooter needs less, drive away and it needs more. The strategies below are different ways of working out that same lead from the time of flight in your table. ## How the sources' ideas apply to YAMS Each row is a concept from the sources, where to read about it, and the YAMS piece that does that job. | Concept | Read about it in | In YAMS | | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | The robot's position and field velocity | Eeshwar's [part 1](https://blog.eeshwark.com/robotblog/shooting-on-the-fly), "Prerequisites" | `drive.getPose()` and `drive.getFieldRelativeSpeed()` on the [Swerve Drive](/documentation/understanding/swerve-drive.md) | | A lookup table of shots that score, measured standing still | [Static Shooting via Look-Up Table](https://frc-docs--3242.org.readthedocs.build/en/3242/docs/software/advanced-controls/fire-control/static-shooting.html), and Eeshwar's [part 2](https://blog.eeshwark.com/robotblog/shooting-on-the-fly-pt2) | WPILib's [`InterpolatingDoubleTreeMap`](https://github.wpilib.org/allwpilib/docs/release/java/edu/wpi/first/math/interpolation/InterpolatingDoubleTreeMap.html), with the result sent to a [FlyWheel](/documentation/understanding/shooters.md) | | A flywheel speed that changes every loop | Eeshwar's [part 1](https://blog.eeshwark.com/robotblog/shooting-on-the-fly), "Wait, The Shooter Speed Changed?" | `FlyWheel.run(Supplier)`, which reads the supplier every loop | | Turning to face a point while the driver keeps driving | Every source | [`withAim`](/documentation/understanding/swerve-drive/swerve-input-stream.md#aim-at-a-target), which takes a supplier so the point can move every loop | | A time of flight lead, as a virtual target | [Dynamic Shooting via Time-of-Flight Recursion](https://frc-docs--3242.org.readthedocs.build/en/3242/docs/software/advanced-controls/fire-control/dynamic-shooting.html), and [Shoot on the move from the code perspective](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/shoot-on-the-move-from-the-code-perspective/511815) | You calculate it. Give the result to `withAim` | | A time of flight lead, as a shot vector with the robot's velocity subtracted | Eeshwar's [part 1](https://blog.eeshwark.com/robotblog/shooting-on-the-fly), "The Math Implementation", and [part 2](https://blog.eeshwark.com/robotblog/shooting-on-the-fly-pt2), "Getting Horizontal Velocity from ToF" | You calculate it. Give its direction to `withAim`, [`withHeading`](/documentation/understanding/swerve-drive/swerve-input-stream.md#heading-snap-control) or a turret, and its speed to the flywheel | | Latency compensation: aim from where the robot will be | Eeshwar's [part 1](https://blog.eeshwark.com/robotblog/shooting-on-the-fly), "Latency Compensation", and [part 2](https://blog.eeshwark.com/robotblog/shooting-on-the-fly-pt2), "The Latency Constant" | [`withAimLookahead`](/documentation/understanding/swerve-drive/swerve-input-stream.md#aim-lookahead) | | A heading that keeps up with a moving aim point | Specific to turning the whole robot. The sources mostly aim a turret | [`withAimFeedforward`](/documentation/understanding/swerve-drive/swerve-input-stream.md#aim-feedforward), and the rotation controller in [`SwerveDriveConfig`](/documentation/understanding/swerve-drive/swerve-drive-config.md) | | A shooter that does not point out of the front, or a small aim correction for spin | Eeshwar's [part 1](https://blog.eeshwark.com/robotblog/shooting-on-the-fly), "The Magnus Effect and Air Resistance" | [`withAimHeadingOffset`](/documentation/understanding/swerve-drive/swerve-input-stream.md#aim-heading-offset) | | Only shooting when the shot is trustworthy | [Dynamic Shooting via Time-of-Flight Recursion](https://frc-docs--3242.org.readthedocs.build/en/3242/docs/software/advanced-controls/fire-control/dynamic-shooting.html), "Shot Quality in Practice", and Eeshwar's [part 1](https://blog.eeshwark.com/robotblog/shooting-on-the-fly), "Shooter Wheel Dynamics" | [`aimLock`](/documentation/understanding/swerve-drive/swerve-input-stream.md#aim-lock) for the heading, and the flywheel's `near` trigger for the speed: see [How do I shoot with a shooter?](/documentation/how-to-mechanisms/how-to-shoot-with-a-shooter.md) | | A hood, or a turret | Eeshwar's [part 2](https://blog.eeshwark.com/robotblog/shooting-on-the-fly-pt2), the hood variants, and the two team calculators | An [Arm](/documentation/understanding/arms.md) or a [Pivot](/documentation/understanding/turrets-wrists.md), each in its own subsystem | ## What `SwerveInputStream` does, and what it leaves to you The stream's aim mode uses the simplest method there is, **point at the pose**. [`withAim`](/documentation/understanding/swerve-drive/swerve-input-stream.md#aim-at-a-target) takes a target pose, works out the direction from the robot to it, and lets the drive's rotation PID controller turn the front of the robot that way while the left stick keeps translating. Four options refine it: [`withAimLookahead`](/documentation/understanding/swerve-drive/swerve-input-stream.md#aim-lookahead), [`withAimFeedforward`](/documentation/understanding/swerve-drive/swerve-input-stream.md#aim-feedforward), [`withAimHeadingOffset`](/documentation/understanding/swerve-drive/swerve-input-stream.md#aim-heading-offset) and [`aimLock`](/documentation/understanding/swerve-drive/swerve-input-stream.md#aim-lock). The [Swerve Input Stream](/documentation/understanding/swerve-drive/swerve-input-stream.md#aim-at-a-target) page explains each one. Even with all four, the stream on its own does **not** shoot on the move the way you might expect: * **The lookahead is one fixed time.** Aiming from where the robot will be in 0.3 seconds is the same as leading the target by 0.3 seconds of travel. That is only the right lead when the time of flight is 0.3 seconds, which is true at one distance. Use the lookahead for what the sources call latency: the short, constant delay before the game piece leaves the robot. * **It only turns the robot.** A lead changes the distance of the shot as well as its direction. The stream knows nothing about your flywheel, your hood or your tables, so it cannot change the shot to match. * **It assumes a straight line.** The lookahead takes the robot's velocity right now and assumes it stays the same. * **Without a feedforward, the rotation lags.** The PID controller only reacts to error, so while the robot drives past the target it trails a little behind. So let the stream do the turning, and give it the right thing to turn to. The lead itself comes from one of the methods in the sources, which is the part you write. ## A complete example This goes from an empty project to a robot that aims, sets its shooter speed and feeds only when the shot is ready. It repeats the code of the [Swerve Drive](/documentation/tutorials/swerve-drive.md) and [Shooter](/documentation/tutorials/shooter-flywheels.md) tutorials so that everything is in one place. Read the source named in a step before you copy its code: the code is short because the explanation lives there. {% hint style="info" %} The code is shown for Java with Commands v2 and Commands v3. The C++ `SwerveInputStream` has the same options, so the same approach works there. Every file compiles against YAMS, but none of it has been run on a robot: the numbers in the tables are placeholders for your own measurements. {% endhint %} {% stepper %} {% step %} ### Create the project Make a new WPILib project from the **Command v2 Robot** or **Command v3 Robot** template, and install the matching YAMS vendordep. [Create a project and install YAMS](/documentation/tutorials/project-setup.md) walks through it with screenshots. {% tabs %} {% tab title="Java, Commands v2" %} Use the Java **Command v2 Robot** template, and install **Yet Another Mechanism System (Commands v2)**. Your classes go in the `subsystems` folder. {% endtab %} {% tab title="Java, Commands v3" %} Use the Java **Command v3 Robot** template, and install **Yet Another Mechanism System (Commands v3)**. Your classes go in the `mechanisms` folder. {% endtab %} {% endtabs %} {% endstep %} {% step %} ### Create the swerve drive The drive supplies the two things every calculation starts from: where the robot is, and how fast it is moving on the field. This is the drive from the [Swerve Drive](/documentation/tutorials/swerve-drive.md) tutorial with `getPose()` and `getFieldVelocity()` added near the end. The tutorial explains every part of it. {% tabs %} {% tab title="Java, Commands v2" %} {% code title="subsystems/SwerveSubsystem.java" lineNumbers="true" %} ```java package first.robot.subsystems; import static org.wpilib.units.Units.Amps; import static org.wpilib.units.Units.DegreesPerSecond; import static org.wpilib.units.Units.Inches; import static org.wpilib.units.Units.Meters; import static org.wpilib.units.Units.MetersPerSecond; import com.ctre.phoenix6.CANBus; import com.ctre.phoenix6.hardware.CANcoder; import com.ctre.phoenix6.hardware.Pigeon2; import com.revrobotics.spark.SparkLowLevel.MotorType; import com.revrobotics.spark.SparkMax; import java.util.function.DoubleSupplier; import java.util.function.Supplier; import org.wpilib.command2.Command; import org.wpilib.command2.SubsystemBase; import org.wpilib.hardware.bus.CANPort; import org.wpilib.math.controller.PIDController; import org.wpilib.math.controller.SimpleMotorFeedforward; import org.wpilib.math.geometry.Pose2d; import org.wpilib.math.geometry.Rotation2d; import org.wpilib.math.geometry.Translation2d; import org.wpilib.math.kinematics.ChassisVelocities; import org.wpilib.math.system.DCMotor; import yams.commands2.config.SmartMotorControllerConfig; import yams.commands2.config.SwerveDriveConfig; import yams.commands2.swerve.SwerveDrive; import yams.commands2.swerve.SwerveInputStream; import yams.core.gearing.MechanismGearing; import yams.core.mechanisms.config.SwerveModuleConfig; import yams.core.mechanisms.swerve.SwerveModule; import yams.core.motorcontrollers.SmartMotorController; import yams.core.motorcontrollers.local.SparkWrapper; import yams.core.telemetry.enums.TelemetryVerbosity; public class SwerveSubsystem extends SubsystemBase { private final SwerveDrive drive; // The gyro: a Pigeon2 with CAN ID 14. private final Pigeon2 gyro = new Pigeon2(14, new CANBus(CANPort.CAN_S0)); /** The config of one drive motor. Drive motors are velocity controlled. */ private SmartMotorControllerConfig buildDriveCfg() { return new SmartMotorControllerConfig(this) // The wheel diameter turns wheel rotations into distance driven. .withWheelDiameter(Inches.of(4)) // kP trims the velocity error that is left after the feedforward. .withClosedLoopController(0.3, 0, 0) // Gearing from the motor rotor to the wheel. .withGearing(new MechanismGearing(12.75)) // kV does most of the work of holding a speed. .withFeedforward(new SimpleMotorFeedforward(0, 12.0 / (MetersPerSecond.of(1).in(MetersPerSecond) / Inches.of(4).in(Meters)), 0.01)) .withStatorCurrentLimit(Amps.of(40)) .withTelemetry("driveMotor", TelemetryVerbosity.HIGH); } /** The config of one azimuth (steering) motor. Azimuth motors are position controlled. */ private SmartMotorControllerConfig buildAzimuthCfg() { return new SmartMotorControllerConfig(this) .withClosedLoopController(1, 0, 0) .withFeedforward(new SimpleMotorFeedforward(0, 1)) // Gearing from the motor rotor to the module's steering axis. .withGearing(new MechanismGearing(6.75)) // The azimuth motor rarely works hard, so it gets a lower limit. .withStatorCurrentLimit(Amps.of(20)) .withTelemetry("angleMotor", TelemetryVerbosity.HIGH); } /** All four modules share their gearing and gains, so one method builds each of them. */ private SwerveModule createModule(SparkMax drive, SparkMax azimuth, CANcoder absoluteEncoder, String moduleName, Translation2d location) { SmartMotorController driveMotor = new SparkWrapper(drive, DCMotor.getNEO(1), buildDriveCfg()); SmartMotorController azimuthMotor = new SparkWrapper(azimuth, DCMotor.getNEO(1), buildAzimuthCfg()); return new SwerveModule(new SwerveModuleConfig(driveMotor, azimuthMotor) // The CANcoder tells the module which way it points when the robot turns on. .withAbsoluteEncoder(absoluteEncoder.getAbsolutePosition().asSupplier()) .withTelemetry(moduleName, TelemetryVerbosity.HIGH) // Where the module is on the robot: +X is forward, +Y is left. .withLocation(location) // Turn the module at most 90 degrees, reversing the wheel instead of turning further. .withOptimization(true)); } public SwerveSubsystem() { // Each module is 24 inches forward or back and 24 inches left or right of the robot center. // CAN IDs are grouped by module: drive, azimuth, CANcoder. var frontLeft = createModule(new SparkMax(CANPort.CAN_S0, 1, MotorType.kBrushless), new SparkMax(CANPort.CAN_S0, 2, MotorType.kBrushless), new CANcoder(3, new CANBus(CANPort.CAN_S0)), "frontleft", new Translation2d(Inches.of(24), Inches.of(24))); var frontRight = createModule(new SparkMax(CANPort.CAN_S0, 4, MotorType.kBrushless), new SparkMax(CANPort.CAN_S0, 5, MotorType.kBrushless), new CANcoder(6, new CANBus(CANPort.CAN_S0)), "frontright", new Translation2d(Inches.of(24), Inches.of(-24))); var backLeft = createModule(new SparkMax(CANPort.CAN_S0, 7, MotorType.kBrushless), new SparkMax(CANPort.CAN_S0, 8, MotorType.kBrushless), new CANcoder(9, new CANBus(CANPort.CAN_S0)), "backleft", new Translation2d(Inches.of(-24), Inches.of(24))); var backRight = createModule(new SparkMax(CANPort.CAN_S0, 10, MotorType.kBrushless), new SparkMax(CANPort.CAN_S0, 11, MotorType.kBrushless), new CANcoder(12, new CANBus(CANPort.CAN_S0)), "backright", new Translation2d(Inches.of(-24), Inches.of(-24))); SwerveDriveConfig config = new SwerveDriveConfig(this, frontLeft, frontRight, backLeft, backRight) // The gyro's attitude. Its yaw is the heading used for field relative driving. .withGyro(gyro::getRotation3d) .withStartingPose(new Pose2d(0, 0, Rotation2d.fromDegrees(0))) // Used by driveToPose(). A kP of 1 is a careful place to start. .withTranslationController(new PIDController(1, 0, 0)) .withRotationController(new PIDController(1, 0, 0)); drive = new SwerveDrive(config); } /** Drive with field relative chassis speeds. */ public Command drive(Supplier speedsSupplier) { return run(() -> drive.setFieldRelativeChassisSpeeds(speedsSupplier.get())) .withName("Field Oriented Drive"); } /** Drive to a pose on the field. */ public Command driveToPose(Pose2d pose) { return drive.driveToPose(pose); } /** Turn the wheels into an X, which resists being pushed. */ public Command lock() { return run(drive::lockPose);
