WPILib's [`InterpolatingDoubleTreeMap`](https://github.wpilib.org/allwpilib/docs/release/java/edu/wpi/first/math/interpolation/InterpolatingDoubleTreeMap.html) fills in the distances in between. `inRange` says whether the robot is at a distance you measured, which the last step uses. {% code title="ShotCalculator.java" %} ```java package first.robot; import static org.wpilib.units.Units.RPM; import org.wpilib.math.geometry.Pose2d; import org.wpilib.math.geometry.Rotation2d; import org.wpilib.math.geometry.Translation2d; import org.wpilib.math.interpolation.InterpolatingDoubleTreeMap; import org.wpilib.math.kinematics.ChassisVelocities; import org.wpilib.units.measure.AngularVelocity; /** Works out where to aim and how fast to spin the flywheel. */ public final class ShotCalculator { /** Where to aim, and the flywheel speed that reaches it. */ public record Shot(Pose2d target, AngularVelocity flywheelSpeed) {} // Where the real target is on the field, in meters. private static final Translation2d TARGET = new Translation2d(4.6, 4.0); // Distance to the target in meters, to flywheel speed in RPM. private static final InterpolatingDoubleTreeMap FLYWHEEL_RPM = new InterpolatingDoubleTreeMap(); // Distance to the target in meters, to how long the shot is in the air in seconds. private static final InterpolatingDoubleTreeMap TIME_OF_FLIGHT = new InterpolatingDoubleTreeMap(); static { // Measure these on your own robot, standing still. FLYWHEEL_RPM.put(1.5, 2400.0); FLYWHEEL_RPM.put(3.0, 3000.0); FLYWHEEL_RPM.put(4.5, 3700.0); TIME_OF_FLIGHT.put(1.5, 0.45); TIME_OF_FLIGHT.put(3.0, 0.70); TIME_OF_FLIGHT.put(4.5, 0.95); } private ShotCalculator() {} /** Whether the robot is at a distance the tables cover. Outside it they only repeat their last entry. */ public static boolean inRange(Pose2d robotPose) { double distance = robotPose.getTranslation().getDistance(TARGET); return distance >= 1.5 && distance <= 4.5; } /** The shot that reaches a point on the field from where the robot is. */ private static Shot shotAt(Pose2d robotPose, Translation2d aimPoint) { double distance = robotPose.getTranslation().getDistance(aimPoint); return new Shot(new Pose2d(aimPoint, new Rotation2d()), RPM.of(FLYWHEEL_RPM.get(distance))); } } ``` {% endcode %} **For your robot:** set `TARGET`, fill both tables with your own measurements, change the two distances in `inRange` to match, and flip the target for the red alliance. {% endstep %} {% step %} ### Pick a firing strategy Each tab is one method to add to `ShotCalculator`. They are the three strategies of the WPILib fire control pages, written against the tables above. The two for a moving robot are **time of flight** methods: they get the lead from the time of flight you measured. {% tabs %} {% tab title="Standing still" %} **Read first:** [Static Shooting via Look-Up Table](https://frc-docs--3242.org.readthedocs.build/en/3242/docs/software/advanced-controls/fire-control/static-shooting.html). Aim at the real target, and read the flywheel speed for the distance. Only right while the robot is not moving. {% code title="ShotCalculator.java" %} ```java /** Aim at the real target. Only right while the robot is standing still. */ public static Shot standing(Pose2d robotPose) { return shotAt(robotPose, TARGET); } ``` {% endcode %} {% endtab %} {% tab title="Time of flight recursion" %} **Read first:** [Dynamic Shooting via Time-of-Flight Recursion](https://frc-docs--3242.org.readthedocs.build/en/3242/docs/software/advanced-controls/fire-control/dynamic-shooting.html). A time of flight method. It moves the target against the robot's velocity by the time of flight, which changes the distance and so the time of flight, and repeats until the time stops changing. This is the virtual target that most teams use. {% code title="ShotCalculator.java" %} ```java /** Lead the target by the time of flight, and repeat until the time settles. */ public static Shot recursive(Pose2d robotPose, ChassisVelocities fieldVelocity) { Translation2d virtualTarget = TARGET; // Each pass uses the distance from the pass before, so the answer settles after a few. for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) { double distance = robotPose.getTranslation().getDistance(virtualTarget); double timeOfFlight = TIME_OF_FLIGHT.get(distance); // The shot drifts by the robot's velocity times the time of flight, so aim that far the other way. virtualTarget = TARGET.minus( new Translation2d(fieldVelocity.vx * timeOfFlight, fieldVelocity.vy * timeOfFlight)); } return shotAt(robotPose, virtualTarget); } ``` {% endcode %} {% endtab %} {% tab title="Newton's method" %} **Read first:** [Newton's Method for Dynamic Shooting](https://frc-docs--3242.org.readthedocs.build/en/3242/docs/software/advanced-controls/fire-control/newton-shooting.html). A time of flight method. It finds the same time of flight as the recursion in fewer passes, which helps when driving fast toward or away from the target. {% code title="ShotCalculator.java" %} ```java /** Find the same time of flight with Newton's method, which needs fewer passes. */ public static Shot newton(Pose2d robotPose, ChassisVelocities fieldVelocity) { Translation2d toTarget = TARGET.minus(robotPose.getTranslation()); double distance = toTarget.getNorm(); // How fast the game piece covers ground, from the standing shot at this distance. double projectileSpeed = distance / TIME_OF_FLIGHT.get(distance); // How fast the robot is closing on the target. Negative while it drives away. double closingSpeed = (toTarget.getX() * fieldVelocity.vx + toTarget.getY() * fieldVelocity.vy) / distance; // A first guess that already allows for the robot's motion toward or away from the target. double timeOfFlight = distance / (projectileSpeed + closingSpeed); for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) { // The virtual target for this guess. double dx = toTarget.getX() - fieldVelocity.vx * timeOfFlight; double dy = toTarget.getY() - fieldVelocity.vy * timeOfFlight; double virtualDistance = Math.hypot(dx, dy); // How far the guess is from what the table says for that distance. double error = timeOfFlight - TIME_OF_FLIGHT.get(virtualDistance); // How fast that error changes as the guess changes. double slope = 1 + (dx * fieldVelocity.vx + dy * fieldVelocity.vy) / (projectileSpeed * virtualDistance); timeOfFlight -= error / slope; } Translation2d virtualTarget = TARGET.minus( new Translation2d(fieldVelocity.vx * timeOfFlight, fieldVelocity.vy * timeOfFlight)); return shotAt(robotPose, virtualTarget); } ``` {% endcode %} {% endtab %} {% endtabs %} {% endstep %} {% step %} ### Aim, set the shooter speed, and shoot safely This is where it comes together. Replace the template's file with this one. `shot()` calls the strategy you picked: it uses the recursion here, and swapping strategies only changes that one line. {% tabs %} {% tab title="Java, Commands v2" %} {% code title="RobotContainer.java" lineNumbers="true" %} ```java package first.robot; import static org.wpilib.units.Units.Degrees; import static org.wpilib.units.Units.Seconds; import first.robot.Constants.OperatorConstants; import first.robot.subsystems.FeederSubsystem; import first.robot.subsystems.ShooterSubsystem; import first.robot.subsystems.SwerveSubsystem; import org.wpilib.command2.Command; import org.wpilib.command2.Commands; import org.wpilib.command2.button.CommandGamepad; import org.wpilib.command2.button.Trigger; import yams.commands2.swerve.SwerveInputStream; public class RobotContainer { private final SwerveSubsystem drive = new SwerveSubsystem(); private final ShooterSubsystem shooter = new ShooterSubsystem(); private final FeederSubsystem feeder = new FeederSubsystem(); private final CommandGamepad driverController = new CommandGamepad(OperatorConstants.DRIVER_CONTROLLER_PORT); /** The shot for where the robot is, and how it is moving, right now. */ private ShotCalculator.Shot shot() { return ShotCalculator.recursive(drive.getPose(), drive.getFieldVelocity()); } public RobotContainer() { // The left stick translates and the right stick's X axis rotates. // Pushing a stick forward or left reads negative, so negate each axis to match // WPILib's convention: +X forward, +Y left, counterclockwise positive. SwerveInputStream input = drive.getChassisSpeedsSupplier( () -> -driverController.getLeftY(), () -> -driverController.getLeftX(), () -> -driverController.getRightX()) // While the right bumper is held, face the shot's target instead of // turning with the right stick. The left stick keeps driving. .withAim(() -> shot().target(), driverController.rightBumper()) // Aim from where the robot will be when the game piece leaves it. .withAimLookahead(Seconds.of(0.1)); drive.setDefaultCommand(drive.drive(input)); // With no button held, the flywheel coasts and the feeder is stopped. shooter.setDefaultCommand(shooter.set(0)); feeder.setDefaultCommand(feeder.set(0)); // While the right bumper is held, keep the flywheel at the speed the shot needs. driverController.rightBumper().whileTrue(shooter.track(() -> shot().flywheelSpeed())); // The shot is ready when the robot faces the aim heading, the flywheel is at the shot's // speed, and the robot is at a distance the tables cover. All three must hold for a tenth // of a second, so that one lucky loop does not fire a shot. Trigger ready = input.aimLock(Degrees.of(2)) .and(shooter.atSpeed(() -> shot().flywheelSpeed())) .and(() -> ShotCalculator.inRange(drive.getPose())) .debounce(0.1); // Feed only while the shot is ready. The moment it is not, the feeder stops. ready.whileTrue(feeder.set(0.8)); } public Command getAutonomousCommand() { return Commands.none(); } } ``` {% endcode %} {% endtab %} {% tab title="Java, Commands v3" %} {% code title="Robot.java" lineNumbers="true" %} ```java package first.robot; import first.robot.constants.DriverConstants; import first.robot.mechanisms.ExampleMechanism; import first.robot.mechanisms.FeederMechanism; import first.robot.mechanisms.ShooterMechanism; import first.robot.mechanisms.SwerveMechanism; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import org.wpilib.command3.Scheduler; import org.wpilib.command3.button.CommandGamepad; import org.wpilib.framework.OpModeRobot; import org.wpilib.system.Notifier; import org.wpilib.telemetry.Telemetry; public class Robot extends OpModeRobot { // The template's ExampleAuto still uses this one. final ExampleMechanism exampleMechanism = new ExampleMechanism(); final SwerveMechanism drive = new SwerveMechanism(); final ShooterMechanism shooter = new ShooterMechanism(); final FeederMechanism feeder = new FeederMechanism(); final CommandGamepad exampleController = new CommandGamepad(DriverConstants.DRIVER_CONTROLLER_PORT); // The scheduler that runs every command. private final Scheduler scheduler = Scheduler.getDefault(); // Each mechanism's simulation Notifier, kept so that it is not garbage collected. private final List simulationNotifiers = new ArrayList<>(); /** The shot for where the robot is, and how it is moving, right now. */ ShotCalculator.Shot shot() { return ShotCalculator.recursive(drive.getPose(), drive.getFieldVelocity()); } public Robot() { // With no button held, the flywheel coasts and the feeder is stopped. shooter.setDefaultCommand(shooter.idle()); feeder.setDefaultCommand(feeder.idle()); } @Override public void robotPeriodic() { // Runs every loop, on the robot and in simulation. // Update every mechanism before the scheduler runs its commands. drive.periodic(); shooter.periodic(); feeder.periodic(); scheduler.run(); // Publish the scheduler, so that a dashboard shows which commands are running. Telemetry.log("Scheduler", scheduler, Scheduler.proto); } @Override public void simulationInit() { // Runs once, when the simulation starts. // Run each mechanism's simulation in its own Notifier, every robot loop. startSimulation("Drive", drive::simulationPeriodic); startSimulation("Shooter", shooter::simulationPeriodic); startSimulation("Feeder", feeder::simulationPeriodic); } /** Runs a mechanism's simulation in its own Notifier, every robot loop period. */ private void startSimulation(String name, Runnable simulationPeriodic) { Notifier notifier = new Notifier(simulationPeriodic); notifier.setName(name + " Simulation"); notifier.startPeriodic(getPeriod()); simulationNotifiers.add(notifier); } } ``` {% endcode %} {% code title="ExampleTeleop.java" lineNumbers="true" %} ```java package first.robot; import static org.wpilib.units.Units.Degrees; import static org.wpilib.units.Units.Seconds; import org.wpilib.command3.Trigger; import org.wpilib.opmode.OpMode; import org.wpilib.opmode.Teleop; import yams.commands3.swerve.SwerveInputStream; @Teleop public class ExampleTeleop implements OpMode { public ExampleTeleop(Robot robot) { // The left stick translates and the right stick's X axis rotates. // Pushing a stick forward or left reads negative, so negate each axis to match // WPILib's convention: +X forward, +Y left, counterclockwise positive. SwerveInputStream input = robot.drive.getChassisSpeedsSupplier( () -> -robot.exampleController.getLeftY(), () -> -robot.exampleController.getLeftX(), () -> -robot.exampleController.getRightX()) // While the right bumper is held, face the shot's target instead of // turning with the right stick. The left stick keeps driving. .withAim(() -> robot.shot().target(), robot.exampleController.rightBumper()) // Aim from where the robot will be when the game piece leaves it. .withAimLookahead(Seconds.of(0.1)); robot.drive.setDefaultCommand(robot.drive.drive(input)); // While the right bumper is held, keep the flywheel at the speed the shot needs. robot.exampleController.rightBumper() .whileTrue(robot.shooter.track(() -> robot.shot().flywheelSpeed())); // The shot is ready when the robot faces the aim heading, the flywheel is at the shot's // speed, and the robot is at a distance the tables cover. All three must hold for a tenth // of a second, so that one lucky loop does not fire a shot. Trigger ready = input.aimLock(Degrees.of(2)) .and(robot.shooter.atSpeed(() -> robot.shot().flywheelSpeed())) .and(() -> ShotCalculator.inRange(robot.drive.getPose())) .debounce(Seconds.of(0.1)); // Feed only while the shot is ready. The moment it is not, the feeder stops. ready.whileTrue(robot.feeder.set(0.8)); } } ``` {% endcode %} {% endtab %} {% endtabs %} Holding the right bumper does three things at once: 1. **Aims.** [`withAim`](/documentation/understanding/swerve-drive/swerve-input-stream.md#aim-at-a-target) turns the robot to face the shot's target while the left stick keeps driving, and [`withAimLookahead`](/documentation/understanding/swerve-drive/swerve-input-stream.md#aim-lookahead) covers the short delay before the game piece leaves. 2. **Sets the shooter speed.** `shooter.track(...)` keeps the flywheel at the speed the shot needs, which changes as the robot moves. 3. **Shoots, but only when it is safe to.** The feeder runs only while `ready` is true. `ready` is what makes the shot safe. It is true only when all of these hold, and have held for a tenth of a second: | Check | Why | | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | [`aimLock`](/documentation/understanding/swerve-drive/swerve-input-stream.md#aim-lock): the robot is aiming and within 2 degrees of the aim heading | A shot fired while the robot is still turning goes wide. It is also false whenever the bumper is not held, so nothing feeds by accident. | | `shooter.atSpeed(...)`: the flywheel is within 50 RPM of the shot's speed | A flywheel that is still spinning up, or still recovering from the last shot, throws short. | | `ShotCalculator.inRange(...)`: the robot is at a distance you measured | Outside the tables, the lookup just repeats its last entry and the shot misses. | | `debounce(0.1)` | One loop where everything happens to line up is not a ready shot. | Releasing the bumper ends the aim and the flywheel command. `ready` goes false, the feeder stops, and the default commands let the flywheel coast. **For your robot:** tune the lookahead, the 2 degree and 50 RPM tolerances, and the debounce. Tighter is more accurate and slower to fire. If your shooter does not point out of the front of the robot, add [`withAimHeadingOffset`](/documentation/understanding/swerve-drive/swerve-input-stream.md#aim-heading-offset). {% endstep %} {% step %} ### Try it in simulation Run **WPILib: Simulate Robot Code**, connect a controller, and enable teleop. Hold the right bumper and drive: the robot keeps facing the shot's target, and the flywheel's setpoint follows the shot. Watch the feeder in telemetry to see when `ready` lets it run. The simulation does not model the game piece, so it shows that the logic works, and not whether shots land. {% endstep %} {% endstepper %} ## Tuning the YAMS side The sources cover how to tune the shot itself. These are the YAMS settings that go with their advice: | Their advice | The YAMS setting | | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Get the standing shot consistent before anything else (Eeshwar's [part 1](https://blog.eeshwark.com/robotblog/shooting-on-the-fly), "Prerequisites") | The flywheel's gains: see WPILib's [Tuning a Flywheel Velocity Controller](https://docs.wpilib.org/en/stable/docs/software/advanced-controls/introduction/tuning-flywheel.html) and [How do I shoot with a shooter?](/documentation/how-to-mechanisms/how-to-shoot-with-a-shooter.md) | | Tune the latency constant by driving straight across the front of the target (Eeshwar's [part 2](https://blog.eeshwark.com/robotblog/shooting-on-the-fly-pt2), "The Latency Constant") | The time you give [`withAimLookahead`](/documentation/understanding/swerve-drive/swerve-input-stream.md#aim-lookahead). Start at 0.1 seconds | | A moving shot is only as good as the pose it starts from | Vision measurements into the drive's pose estimate: see WPILib's [Pose Estimators](https://docs.wpilib.org/en/stable/docs/software/advanced-controls/state-space/state-space-pose-estimators.html) | | Watch whether the heading keeps up as you drive past | The rotation controller in [`SwerveDriveConfig`](/documentation/understanding/swerve-drive/swerve-drive-config.md), then [`withAimFeedforward`](/documentation/understanding/swerve-drive/swerve-input-stream.md#aim-feedforward) | | Hold fire when the shot is not trustworthy ([Dynamic Shooting via Time-of-Flight Recursion](https://frc-docs--3242.org.readthedocs.build/en/3242/docs/software/advanced-controls/fire-control/dynamic-shooting.html), "Shot Quality in Practice") | The tolerance you give [`aimLock`](/documentation/understanding/swerve-drive/swerve-input-stream.md#aim-lock), and the flywheel's `near` tolerance | ## WPILib building blocks The released WPILib documentation covers the classes the example uses. These pages are written for WPILib 2026. The ideas are the same in 2027, though some classes were renamed: `ChassisSpeeds`, for example, is `ChassisVelocities`. | Page | Why it matters here | | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | | [Coordinate System](https://docs.wpilib.org/en/stable/docs/software/basic-programming/coordinate-system.html) | Which way X, Y and a positive rotation point. | | [Translation, Rotation, and Pose](https://docs.wpilib.org/en/stable/docs/software/advanced-controls/geometry/pose.html) | The classes that the distance and direction to the target are calculated with. | | [Transformations](https://docs.wpilib.org/en/stable/docs/software/advanced-controls/geometry/transformations.html) | Getting from the center of the robot to where the shooter really is. | | [Introduction to Kinematics and The ChassisSpeeds Class](https://docs.wpilib.org/en/stable/docs/software/kinematics-and-odometry/intro-and-chassis-speeds.html) | Robot relative and field relative velocity. |

pages.title: How do I use absolute encoders on my arm?
pages.content: # How do I use absolute encoders on my arm? Relative encoders (built into most NEOs and Falcons) lose their zero reference on every power cycle, so an arm must be homed before closed-loop control is accurate. Absolute encoders retain their position across power cycles and eliminate the homing step entirely, which is especially important for arms that park at a non-zero angle. YAMS accepts an absolute encoder offset that maps the encoder's native range to your arm's coordinate system. Absolute encoders report the physical position of a mechanism within a single rotation and retain that reading across power cycles and reboots. On an Arm (or Pivot) mechanism this means the robot always knows where the arm is the moment it powers on, no homing routine, no encoder drift from brownouts or e-stops. ## Supported encoder types Each `SmartMotorController` wrapper only accepts the encoders from its own vendor ecosystem. `SparkWrapper` and `NovaWrapper` throw an `IllegalArgumentException` when given an encoder type they do not support. | Wrapper | Supported absolute encoders | | ------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `SparkWrapper` (SparkMax / SparkFlex) | `SparkAbsoluteEncoder` (`armMotor.getAbsoluteEncoder()`), `DetachedEncoder` | | `TalonFXWrapper` (TalonFX / Kraken) | `CANcoder`, `CANdi` | | `TalonFXSWrapper` (TalonFXS / Minion) | `CANcoder`, `CANdi` | | `NovaWrapper` (Thrifty Nova) | `FeedbackSensorType.ABS` (absolute encoder on the Nova's data port), Thrifty `CanEncoder` | ## Check your inversion Using the vendor hardware client (REV Hardware Client or Phoenix Tuner X), apply positive power to the motor and graph the absolute encoder position. The position should **increase** as the motor turns in the positive direction. If it decreases, invert the encoder reading: ```java .withExternalEncoderInverted(true) ``` ## Check your gear ratio and mount The absolute encoder must complete **at most one full rotation** across the entire range of motion of the arm. Confirm this in the hardware client by moving the arm through its full travel and watching the encoder position, it must never wrap from 1 rotation back to 0 more than once. Use `.withExternalEncoderGearing(1.0)` if the encoder is mounted directly on the mechanism shaft. If the encoder is driven through a reduction, pass the encoder-to-mechanism ratio. {% hint style="warning" %} If the gear ratio causes the encoder to exceed 1 rotation during the arm's range of motion, the encoder position will wrap unpredictably and **cannot** be used as the primary PID feedback device. Either remount the encoder closer to the mechanism output shaft or change the reduction so the encoder never exceeds 1 rotation. {% endhint %} ## Set the discontinuity point An absolute encoder wraps at its **discontinuity point**, the angle at which the reading jumps from its maximum value back to zero (or vice versa). There are two supported ranges: * `Rotations.of(1.0)`, range is **\[0, 1]**; the encoder wraps at 1 rotation back to 0 * `Rotations.of(0.5)`, range is **\[-0.5, 0.5]**; the encoder wraps at ±0.5 rotations ```java .withExternalEncoderDiscontinuityPoint(Rotations.of(1.0)) // [0, 1] range // or .withExternalEncoderDiscontinuityPoint(Rotations.of(0.5)) // [-0.5, 0.5] range ``` {% hint style="info" %} If you don't set a discontinuity point, `SparkWrapper` and `NovaWrapper` use `Rotations.of(1.0)` (the **\[0, 1]** range). Setting it explicitly is recommended for clarity on every wrapper. On a `SparkWrapper`, setting both `.withExternalEncoderGearing(...)` and a discontinuity point raises an alert, because the discontinuity point is not scaled by the gearing. {% endhint %} {% hint style="warning" %} If the arm's physical range of motion crosses the discontinuity point, the position will jump mid-travel and break closed-loop control. If this happens, remove the encoder, rotate the bearing so the discontinuity point falls outside the arm's travel range, and remount. {% endhint %} ## Find your zero offset Move the arm to exactly horizontal (0° from horizontal, parallel to the ground). Read the raw encoder position in the hardware client, that value is your zero offset. ```java .withExternalEncoderZeroOffset(Degrees.of(33.25)) // replace with your measured value ``` Negative offsets are automatically converted to their positive equivalent (1 rotation is added internally). The offset is applied to the absolute encoder itself (for example the CANcoder's magnet offset or the SPARK's absolute encoder zero offset). `TalonFXWrapper` and `TalonFXSWrapper` no longer set a separate rotor offset on the motor. To check the result, read the encoder back through the `SmartMotorController`: `getExternalEncoderMechanismPosition()` returns the absolute encoder's position in mechanism units (empty if there is no external encoder), and `getRelativeMechanismPosition()` returns the motor's built-in relative encoder position. With the offset set correctly, both should read about 0° with the arm horizontal. ## Configure the simulation starting position Simulation has no physical encoder, so the absolute encoder reading is unavailable in sim. Use `.withSimStartingPosition()` to tell the simulator where the arm starts. On a real robot this value is ignored, the true encoder reading is always used. ```java .withSimStartingPosition(Degrees.of(0)) // arm starts horizontal in sim ``` *** ## Complete examples ### SparkMax + SparkAbsoluteEncoder ```java private final SparkMax armMotor = new SparkMax(CANPort.CAN_S0, 1, MotorType.kBrushless); private final SmartMotorControllerConfig motorConfig = new SmartMotorControllerConfig(this) .withControlMode(ControlMode.CLOSED_LOOP) .withClosedLoopController(4, 0, 0) .withTrapezoidalProfile(DegreesPerSecond.of(180), DegreesPerSecondPerSecond.of(90)) .withFeedforward(new ArmFeedforward(0, 0, 0, 0)) .withSoftLimits(Degrees.of(-30), Degrees.of(100)) .withGearing(new MechanismGearing(GearBox.fromReductionStages(3, 4))) .withZeroPower(MotorMode.BRAKE) .withTelemetry("ArmMotor", TelemetryVerbosity.HIGH) .withStatorCurrentLimit(Amps.of(40)) .withExternalEncoder(armMotor.getAbsoluteEncoder()) .withExternalEncoderInverted(false) .withExternalEncoderGearing(1.0) .withExternalEncoderZeroOffset(Degrees.of(33.25)) .withExternalEncoderDiscontinuityPoint(Rotations.of(1.0)) // [0, 1] range .withUseExternalFeedbackEncoder(true) .withSimStartingPosition(Degrees.of(0)); private final SmartMotorController smc = new SparkWrapper(armMotor, DCMotor.getNEO(1), motorConfig); ``` ### TalonFX + CANcoder ```java private final TalonFX armMotor = new TalonFX(1, new CANBus(CANPort.CAN_S0)); private final CANcoder cancoder = new CANcoder(2, new CANBus(CANPort.CAN_S0)); private final SmartMotorControllerConfig motorConfig = new SmartMotorControllerConfig(this) .withControlMode(ControlMode.CLOSED_LOOP) .withClosedLoopController(4, 0, 0) .withTrapezoidalProfile(DegreesPerSecond.of(180), DegreesPerSecondPerSecond.of(90)) .withFeedforward(new ArmFeedforward(0, 0, 0, 0)) .withSoftLimits(Degrees.of(-30), Degrees.of(100)) .withGearing(new MechanismGearing(GearBox.fromReductionStages(3, 4))) .withZeroPower(MotorMode.BRAKE) .withTelemetry("ArmMotor", TelemetryVerbosity.HIGH) .withStatorCurrentLimit(Amps.of(40)) .withExternalEncoder(cancoder) .withExternalEncoderInverted(false) .withExternalEncoderGearing(1.0) .withExternalEncoderZeroOffset(Degrees.of(33.25)) .withExternalEncoderDiscontinuityPoint(Rotations.of(0.5)) // [-0.5, 0.5] range .withUseExternalFeedbackEncoder(true) .withSimStartingPosition(Degrees.of(0)); private final SmartMotorController smc = new TalonFXWrapper(armMotor, DCMotor.getKrakenX60(1), motorConfig); ``` ### TalonFXS + CANdi The `CANdi` connects to the TalonFXS via its PWM port and is treated the same as a CANcoder for configuration purposes. A `CANdi` has two PWM inputs, so tell the Talon which one the encoder is on with a vendor config. Without it, YAMS throws a `SmartMotorControllerConfigurationException` because no PWM input is selected. Use `SyncCANdiPWM1` for the PWM1 input or `SyncCANdiPWM2` for PWM2. YAMS sets the matching input on the `CANdi` from the other options here. ```java private final TalonFXS armMotor = new TalonFXS(1, new CANBus(CANPort.CAN_S0)); private final CANdi candi = new CANdi(2, new CANBus(CANPort.CAN_S0)); private final SmartMotorControllerConfig motorConfig = new SmartMotorControllerConfig(this) .withControlMode(ControlMode.CLOSED_LOOP) .withClosedLoopController(4, 0, 0) .withTrapezoidalProfile(DegreesPerSecond.of(180), DegreesPerSecondPerSecond.of(90)) .withFeedforward(new ArmFeedforward(0, 0, 0, 0)) .withSoftLimits(Degrees.of(-30), Degrees.of(100)) .withGearing(new MechanismGearing(GearBox.fromReductionStages(3, 4))) .withZeroPower(MotorMode.BRAKE) .withTelemetry("ArmMotor", TelemetryVerbosity.HIGH) .withStatorCurrentLimit(Amps.of(40)) // The encoder is on the CANdi's PWM1 input. .withVendorConfig(new TalonFXSConfiguration() .withExternalFeedback(new ExternalFeedbackConfigs() .withExternalFeedbackSensorSource(ExternalFeedbackSensorSourceValue.SyncCANdiPWM1))) .withExternalEncoder(candi) .withExternalEncoderInverted(false) .withExternalEncoderGearing(1.0) .withExternalEncoderZeroOffset(Degrees.of(33.25)) .withUseExternalFeedbackEncoder(true) .withSimStartingPosition(Degrees.of(0)); private final SmartMotorController smc = new TalonFXSWrapper(armMotor, DCMotor.getKrakenX60(1), motorConfig); ``` On a TalonFX the feedback source is in `Feedback` instead: ```java .withVendorConfig(new TalonFXConfiguration() .withFeedback(new FeedbackConfigs() .withFeedbackSensorSource(FeedbackSensorSourceValue.SyncCANdiPWM1))) ``` The CTRE types come from Phoenix 6: `com.ctre.phoenix6.configs.TalonFXSConfiguration`, `ExternalFeedbackConfigs`, `TalonFXConfiguration` and `FeedbackConfigs`, and `com.ctre.phoenix6.signals.ExternalFeedbackSensorSourceValue` and `FeedbackSensorSourceValue`. ### Thrifty Nova + absolute encoder on the data port Pass `FeedbackSensorType.ABS` as the external encoder and tell the Nova which encoder is wired to its data port through the vendor config. A Thrifty `CanEncoder` on the same CAN bus works too: pass the `CanEncoder` object to `.withExternalEncoder(...)` instead. ```java private final Nova armMotor = new Nova(0, 1, MotorType.NEO); private final SmartMotorControllerConfig motorConfig = new SmartMotorControllerConfig(this) .withControlMode(ControlMode.CLOSED_LOOP) .withClosedLoopController(4, 0, 0) .withTrapezoidalProfile(DegreesPerSecond.of(180), DegreesPerSecondPerSecond.of(90)) .withFeedforward(new ArmFeedforward(0, 0, 0, 0)) .withSoftLimits(Degrees.of(-30), Degrees.of(100)) .withGearing(new MechanismGearing(GearBox.fromReductionStages(3, 4))) .withZeroPower(MotorMode.BRAKE) .withTelemetry("ArmMotor", TelemetryVerbosity.HIGH) .withStatorCurrentLimit(Amps.of(40)) .withVendorConfig(NovaConfig.absoluteEncoderType(AbsoluteEncoderType.REV_ENCODER)) .withExternalEncoder(FeedbackSensorType.ABS) .withExternalEncoderInverted(false) .withExternalEncoderGearing(1.0) .withExternalEncoderZeroOffset(Degrees.of(33.25)) .withExternalEncoderDiscontinuityPoint(Rotations.of(1.0)) // [0, 1] range .withUseExternalFeedbackEncoder(true) .withSimStartingPosition(Degrees.of(0)); private final SmartMotorController smc = new NovaWrapper(armMotor, DCMotor.getNEO(1), motorConfig); ``` The Nova types come from ThriftyLib: `com.thrifty.nova.Nova`, `com.thrifty.nova.NovaConfig`, `com.thrifty.core.Motor.MotorType`, `com.thrifty.core.Motor.FeedbackSensorType` and `com.thrifty.core.Motor.AbsoluteEncoderType`. The [motor controller feature matrix](/documentation/understanding/editor/feature-matrix.md) lists what the Nova supports. {% hint style="info" %} Imports for these examples: `SmartMotorControllerConfig` comes from `yams.commands2.config` (or `yams.commands3.config` for Commands v3). `SmartMotorController`, the wrappers (`yams.core.motorcontrollers.local.SparkWrapper`, `yams.core.motorcontrollers.local.NovaWrapper`, `yams.core.motorcontrollers.remote.TalonFXWrapper`, `yams.core.motorcontrollers.remote.TalonFXSWrapper`), `yams.core.motorcontrollers.enums.ControlMode`/`MotorMode`, `yams.core.gearing.*` and `yams.core.telemetry.enums.TelemetryVerbosity` all come from `yams.core`. CTRE devices take a `com.ctre.phoenix6.CANBus`, built here from WPILib's `org.wpilib.hardware.bus.CANPort`. {% endhint %} *** ## Using absolute encoders on a Pivot The exact same external encoder setup described above works identically for `Pivot` mechanisms (turrets, wrists, and any other single-axis rotational mechanism). The configuration API and all five setup steps are unchanged, just substitute your `PivotConfig` and the appropriate wrapper. ## Code reference The arm example demonstrates configuring an arm with a CANcoder as its external feedback encoder: {% @github-files/github-code-block url="" %}

pages.title: How do I control a mechanism that carries a game piece?
pages.content:
# How do I control a mechanism that carries a game piece?

A game piece makes a mechanism heavier, and can move its center of mass, which changes the feedforward and feedback gains it needs.

Gains tuned on an empty mechanism are tuned for that mechanism. Pick up a game piece and the elevator is heavier, and the arm is heavier and has its center of mass further out. An empty arm that holds its angle perfectly can sag below it with a game piece, or overshoot and oscillate when it moves.

How much changes depends on the mechanism: how heavy the game piece is next to the mechanism, and where it is held.

## What changes, and what doesn't

| Gain           | Depends on                                                   | With a game piece                                                         |
| -------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `kS`           | Friction in the gearbox and bearings                         | Barely changes                                                            |
| `kV`           | The motor and the gearing                                    | **Does not change.** It is the voltage the motor needs to spin at a speed |
| `kG`           | The weight, and for an arm how far out the center of mass is | **Goes up**, often a lot                                                  |
| `kA`           | The mass, or for an arm the moment of inertia                | Goes up                                                                   |
| `kP`, `kD`     | The mass or inertia they have to move                        | The same gains move a heavier mechanism more slowly, with more overshoot  |
| Profile limits | How fast the motors can accelerate the mechanism             | A heavier mechanism may not keep up with the profile                      |

`kG` is usually the one that matters. It holds the mechanism up, so a `kG` that is too small makes the mechanism sit below its setpoint, with `kP` pushing against the difference.

## How much it changes, by mechanism

### Elevator

`kG` is in proportion to the weight the elevator lifts:

```
kG with the game piece = kG empty × (carriage weight + game piece weight) / carriage weight
```

A 1 kg game piece on a 4 kg carriage needs 25% more `kG`. A spring or counterweight that holds up part of the carriage takes a fixed amount off `kG`, so the change is the same in volts but a larger share of what is left.

A **continuous** or **cascade** elevator's stages are lifted in turn as it rises, so `kG` steps up as each stage is picked up, with or without a game piece. If the elevator sags at some heights and not others, this is a likely reason.

### Arm

`kG` is in proportion to the arm's weight times how far its center of mass is from the pivot, and the game piece adds its own:

```
kG with the game piece = kG empty × (arm weight × arm's center of mass distance
                                     + game piece weight × game piece distance)
                                   / (arm weight × arm's center of mass distance)
```

A game piece at the end of an arm adds far more than its weight suggests. A 1 kg game piece 0.6 m out, on a 3 kg arm whose center of mass is 0.3 m out, needs 67% more `kG`.

A game piece held off to one side of the arm, rather than along it, also moves the angle at which gravity pulls hardest. `ArmFeedforward` assumes the center of mass is on the line from the pivot, at the angle the arm reads. If the game piece is far off that line, the arm holds well at some angles and sags at others. A larger `kG` helps most where the arm is close to level.

### Arm on an elevator, or a telescoping arm

The elevator lifts the arm and the game piece, so the elevator's `kG` goes up with the game piece, but does not depend on the arm's angle.

A **telescoping arm**, or an arm with a wrist, moves its center of mass as it extends or bends. Its `kG` changes all the time, not only with the game piece.

### Shooter flywheel

A game piece passes through the flywheel rather than staying on it. Its `kV` does not change. The flywheel slows as it shoots, and `kP` and the flywheel's own inertia bring it back up. See [How do I shoot with a shooter?](/documentation/how-to-mechanisms/how-to-shoot-with-a-shooter.md).

## Measure the gains with the game piece

Measure the loaded gains on the robot, as you measured the empty ones, with [live tuning](/documentation/understanding/live-tuning.md):

1. Load a game piece, and hold the mechanism where gravity pulls hardest: an arm level, or an elevator anywhere.
2. Raise the voltage until the mechanism just starts to move up, and note it. Lower it until the mechanism just starts to move down, and note that.
3. `kG` is halfway between the two voltages. `kS` is half the difference between them.
4. With that `kG`, check the mechanism reaches its setpoints with the game piece, and raise `kP` (and `kD`) if it is slow.

The formulas above give a starting point, and tell you whether a game piece changes the gains enough to matter. A change of a few percent may not be worth a second set of gains.

## Switch gains when the mechanism picks up a game piece

A motor controller holds up to four [slots](/documentation/understanding/editor/config/closed-loop-control.md#slots) of gains, each with its own [feedforward](/documentation/understanding/editor/config/feedforward.md#slots). Put the empty gains in one slot and the loaded gains in another, and switch slots when the mechanism picks up or lets go of a game piece. Switching is quick: it only changes which slot the motor controller uses.

{% tabs %}
{% tab title="Commands v2" %}

```java
import org.wpilib.command2.Commands;
import org.wpilib.command2.button.Trigger;
import org.wpilib.math.controller.ArmFeedforward;
import yams.core.motorcontrollers.SmartMotorController.ClosedLoopControllerSlot;

private final SmartMotorControllerConfig smcConfig = new SmartMotorControllerConfig(this)
    // Empty.
    .withClosedLoopController(40, 0, 0, ClosedLoopControllerSlot.SLOT_0)
    .withFeedforward(new ArmFeedforward(0.1, 0.35, 1.2), ClosedLoopControllerSlot.SLOT_0)
    // Holding a game piece: more kG to hold it up, and more kP to move the extra weight.
    .withClosedLoopController(55, 0, 0, ClosedLoopControllerSlot.SLOT_1)
    .withFeedforward(new ArmFeedforward(0.1, 0.60, 1.2), ClosedLoopControllerSlot.SLOT_1)
    // ... the rest of the config
    ;

public ArmSubsystem() {
  // Switch gains as the intake picks up and lets go of a game piece. The commands require
  // nothing, so they do not interrupt the command moving the arm.
  new Trigger(this::hasGamePiece)
      .onTrue(Commands.runOnce(() -> motor.setClosedLoopSlot(ClosedLoopControllerSlot.SLOT_1)))
      .onFalse(Commands.runOnce(() -> motor.setClosedLoopSlot(ClosedLoopControllerSlot.SLOT_0)));
}
```

{% endtab %}

{% tab title="Commands v3" %}

```java
import org.wpilib.command3.Command;
import org.wpilib.command3.Trigger;
import org.wpilib.math.controller.ArmFeedforward;
import yams.core.motorcontrollers.SmartMotorController.ClosedLoopControllerSlot;

private final SmartMotorControllerConfig smcConfig = new SmartMotorControllerConfig(this)
    // Empty.
    .withClosedLoopController(40, 0, 0, ClosedLoopControllerSlot.SLOT_0)
    .withFeedforward(new ArmFeedforward(0.1, 0.35, 1.2), ClosedLoopControllerSlot.SLOT_0)
    // Holding a game piece: more kG to hold it up, and more kP to move the extra weight.
    .withClosedLoopController(55, 0, 0, ClosedLoopControllerSlot.SLOT_1)
    .withFeedforward(new ArmFeedforward(0.1, 0.60, 1.2), ClosedLoopControllerSlot.SLOT_1)
    // ... the rest of the config
    ;

public ArmMechanism() {
  // Switch gains as the intake picks up and lets go of a game piece. The commands require
  // nothing, so they do not interrupt the command moving the arm.
  new Trigger(this::hasGamePiece)
      .onTrue(Command.noRequirements(coroutine -> motor.setClosedLoopSlot(ClosedLoopControllerSlot.SLOT_1))
          .named("Arm Loaded Gains"))
      .onFalse(Command.noRequirements(coroutine -> motor.setClosedLoopSlot(ClosedLoopControllerSlot.SLOT_0))
          .named("Arm Empty Gains"));
}
```

{% endtab %}
{% endtabs %}

`hasGamePiece()` is whatever tells you the mechanism has a game piece: a beam break, a distance sensor, or the intake's current, as in [How do I sense activity from the motor current?](/documentation/how-to-motor-controllers-and-sensors/how-do-i-sense-activity-based-off-of-the-current.md). The slot takes effect with the next setpoint, and a mechanism's commands send a setpoint every loop.

[Loosely coupled followers](/documentation/understanding/editor/config/followers.md#withlooselycoupledfollowers) are switched to the same slot. Give each follower the same slots in its own config.

## A mechanism whose gains change as it moves

A telescoping arm, an arm with a wrist, or an elevator picking up its stages needs a different `kG` as it moves, not only with a game piece. Two ways to handle it:

* **Slots for ranges.** Up to four sets of gains, such as retracted, extended, and each with a game piece. Switch with triggers on the position, as above. This is the simplest, and the gains in each slot can be tuned on their own.
* **Change `kG` as it moves**, with `motor.setKg(kG)`, worked out from the extension or angle. Only do this when `kG` has changed enough to matter, not every loop: on a Talon or a SPARK, `setKg` writes the motor controller's configuration, which takes time. On a Nova, or any mechanism whose [closed loop runs on the SystemCore](/documentation/understanding/editor/config/closed-loop-control.md#where-the-loop-runs), it only changes a number.

## Common pitfalls

### Only `kP` was raised

A heavier mechanism that sags looks like it needs more `kP`. Raising `kP` pushes it closer to the setpoint, but it still sits below it, and a `kP` large enough to hide the sag makes the empty mechanism oscillate. Raise `kG` first, and `kP` only if the mechanism is still slow.

### The slot switches on a flickering sensor

A sensor that flickers as a game piece passes switches the gains back and forth. Debounce the trigger, such as `new Trigger(this::hasGamePiece).debounce(0.1)`, so it only switches once the sensor has settled.

### Slot 3 on a Talon

A TalonFX and a TalonFXS have three slots, `SLOT_0` to `SLOT_2`. Selecting `SLOT_3` throws an exception.

### The profile is too fast for the loaded mechanism

The motion profile's limits are the same in every slot. A profile that the empty mechanism keeps up with can be too fast with a game piece, so the mechanism lags behind it and overshoots at the end. Set the profile's limits for the loaded mechanism.

### The simulation is always empty

The simulation uses the mass and moment of inertia in the config, so it never carries the game piece. Gains for the loaded mechanism can be checked in simulation by setting the config's mass to the loaded mass, but tune them on the robot.

pages.title: How do I control a mechanism without a mechanism class?
pages.content_preview: # How do I control a mechanism without a mechanism class? Control each SmartMotorController yourself, such as when the motors of one mechanism need different setpoints. YAMS mechanism classes (`Arm`, `Elevator`, `FlyWheel`, etc.) drive one motor, along with its followers.

pages.title: How do I use a vendor hardware config?
pages.content: # How do I use a vendor hardware config? Some motor controllers ship with on-board configurations stored in flash, and vendor APIs expose options that YAMS does not surface directly, things like CANivore bus selection, custom status frame rates, or audio feedback settings. YAMS integrates with these through a hardware config layer: you pre-build a vendor config object and hand it to `SmartMotorControllerConfig.withVendorConfig()`, and YAMS merges its own settings on top without discarding the rest. Understanding when to use a vendor hardware config (versus configuring purely through YAMS) helps you avoid conflicting settings between the vendor's stored config and YAMS's runtime config. YAMS configures your motor controller automatically based on your `SmartMotorControllerConfig`. But sometimes you need to reach features that YAMS doesn't expose directly, custom voltage limits, CANivore bus names, status frame rates, or device-specific options only available through the vendor's own configuration object. `SmartMotorControllerConfig.withVendorConfig(Object config)` lets you supply a pre-built vendor config as a baseline. YAMS merges its own settings on top of it, so anything you set in `SmartMotorControllerConfig` always wins, but everything else you configured in the vendor object is preserved. ## CTRE TalonFX Pass a `TalonFXConfiguration` object: ```java TalonFXConfiguration talonConfig = new TalonFXConfiguration() .withAudio(new AudioConfigs().withBeepOnBoot(false).withBeepOnConfig(false)) .withVoltage(new VoltageConfigs().withPeakReverseVoltage(-10).withPeakForwardVoltage(10)); SmartMotorControllerConfig motorConfig = new SmartMotorControllerConfig(this) .withVendorConfig(talonConfig) .withControlMode(ControlMode.CLOSED_LOOP) .withClosedLoopController(4, 0, 0) .withGearing(new MechanismGearing(GearBox.fromReductionStages(3, 4))) .withZeroPower(MotorMode.BRAKE); TalonFX talonFX = new TalonFX(1, new CANBus(CANPort.CAN_S0)); SmartMotorController smc = new TalonFXWrapper(talonFX, DCMotor.getKrakenX60(1), motorConfig); ``` ## CTRE TalonFXS Pass a `TalonFXSConfiguration` object: ```java TalonFXSConfiguration talonConfig = new TalonFXSConfiguration() .withMotorOutput(new MotorOutputConfigs().withNeutralMode(NeutralModeValue.Brake)) .withCommutation(new CommutationConfigs().withMotorArrangement(MotorArrangementValue.Minion_JST)); SmartMotorControllerConfig motorConfig = new SmartMotorControllerConfig(this) .withVendorConfig(talonConfig) .withControlMode(ControlMode.CLOSED_LOOP) .withClosedLoopController(4, 0, 0) .withGearing(new MechanismGearing(GearBox.fromReductionStages(3, 4))); TalonFXS talonFXS = new TalonFXS(1, new CANBus(CANPort.CAN_S0)); SmartMotorController smc = new TalonFXSWrapper(talonFXS, DCMotor.getKrakenX60(1), motorConfig); ``` ## REV SparkMax Pass a `SparkMaxConfig` object: ```java SparkMaxConfig sparkConfig = new SparkMaxConfig(); sparkConfig.signals .primaryEncoderPositionPeriodMs(10) .primaryEncoderVelocityPeriodMs(20); SmartMotorControllerConfig motorConfig = new SmartMotorControllerConfig(this) .withVendorConfig(sparkConfig) .withControlMode(ControlMode.CLOSED_LOOP) .withClosedLoopController(4, 0, 0) .withGearing(new MechanismGearing(GearBox.fromReductionStages(3, 4))) .withZeroPower(MotorMode.BRAKE); SparkMax spark = new SparkMax(CANPort.CAN_S0, 1, MotorType.kBrushless); SmartMotorController smc = new SparkWrapper(spark, DCMotor.getNEO(1), motorConfig); ``` ## REV SparkFlex Pass a `SparkFlexConfig` object: ```java SparkFlexConfig sparkConfig = new SparkFlexConfig(); sparkConfig.signals .primaryEncoderPositionPeriodMs(10) .primaryEncoderVelocityPeriodMs(20); SmartMotorControllerConfig motorConfig = new SmartMotorControllerConfig(this) .withVendorConfig(sparkConfig) .withControlMode(ControlMode.CLOSED_LOOP) .withClosedLoopController(4, 0, 0) .withGearing(new MechanismGearing(GearBox.fromReductionStages(3, 4))) .withZeroPower(MotorMode.BRAKE); SparkFlex spark = new SparkFlex(CANPort.CAN_S0, 1, MotorType.kBrushless); SmartMotorController smc = new SparkWrapper(spark, DCMotor.getNeoVortex(1), motorConfig); ``` ## Thrifty Nova Pass a ThriftyLib `NovaConfig.Config`, usually a `NovaConfigBatch` holding one or more `NovaConfig` options. The vendor config is applied to the Nova before the YAMS config: ```java SmartMotorControllerConfig motorConfig = new SmartMotorControllerConfig(this) .withVendorConfig(new NovaConfigBatch(NovaConfig.tempThrottleEnable(true))) .withControlMode(ControlMode.CLOSED_LOOP) .withClosedLoopController(4, 0, 0) .withGearing(new MechanismGearing(GearBox.fromReductionStages(3, 4))) .withZeroPower(MotorMode.BRAKE); Nova nova = new Nova(0, 1, MotorType.NEO); // CAN bus 0, CAN ID 1 SmartMotorController smc = new NovaWrapper(nova, DCMotor.getNEO(1), motorConfig); ``` Any other vendor config type throws a `SmartMotorControllerConfigurationException`. ## How precedence works YAMS uses your vendor config as a starting point and then writes its own settings on top of it. This means: * Any field you set in `SmartMotorControllerConfig` (PID gains, gearing, zero power mode, current limits, etc.) **will overwrite** the corresponding field in your vendor config. * Any field you set **only** in the vendor config and that YAMS doesn't touch will be preserved exactly as you set it. If you set the same option in both places, `SmartMotorControllerConfig` wins. Think of the vendor config as the floor, not the ceiling. {% hint style="warning" %} Always verify the final applied configuration on your hardware. Use your vendor's tuning tool (such as Phoenix Tuner X or REV Hardware Client) to confirm that YAMS didn't silently overwrite a setting you intended to keep from your vendor config. {% endhint %}

pages.title: How do I find my mechanism's circumference?
pages.content: # How do I find my mechanism's circumference? YAMS converts between rotational encoder counts and real-world linear distance using a mechanism's circumference. Getting this value right is critical: an incorrect circumference causes every position setpoint to be off by a constant factor, making closed-loop control impossible to tune. Mechanism circumference is used to convert mechanism rotations to measurements. This is primarily useful for Elevators or Linear Slides where the primary unit of control is in `Distance` (usually meters). Your **Mechanism Circumference** is the circumference of your final sprocket/gear which translates directly to Distance. For elevators this is the drum circumference $$c = 2\*\pi \* r$$ OR if driven by a sprocket $$c = pitch\*teeth$$ {% hint style="warning" %} Remember that you measurement ≠ actual height of the mechanism UNLESS you set the elevator starting height to be relative to the floor AND adjust your limits accordingly {% endhint %} ## Set the circumference in YAMS ```java SmartMotorControllerConfig smcConfig = new SmartMotorControllerConfig(this) .withControlMode(ControlMode.CLOSED_LOOP) // Elevator drum radius API: pass the chain pitch and tooth count directly. .withDrumRadius(Inches.of(0.25), 22) .withMechanismCircumference(Inches.of(4).times(Math.PI)) // 4in * PI .withWheelDiameter(Inches.of(4)) // Same as above .withWheelRadius(Inches.of(2)) // Same as above .withStartingPosition(Meters.of(0)); ```
pages.content_preview: # How do I find my mechanism's circumference? YAMS converts between rotational encoder counts and real-world linear distance using a mechanism's circumference.

pages.title: How do I use exponential profiles?
pages.content: # How do I use exponential profiles? An exponential profile plans a move the way a DC motor actually moves: hard acceleration at first, then less as it nears top speed. Every `SmartMotorController` in YAMS supports them. This is the short version: [Exponential profiles](/documentation/understanding/editor/exponential-profiles.md) has the full explanation and the tuning steps. ## Use one Add `withExponentialProfile(...)` instead of `withTrapezoidalProfile(...)`. The helpers on `yams.core.math.ExponentialProfilePIDController` work out starting values from the mechanism: ```java private final Distance chainPitch = Inches.of(0.25); private final int toothCount = 22; private final Mass weight = Pounds.of(16); private final DCMotor motors = DCMotor.getNEO(1); private final MechanismGearing gearing = new MechanismGearing(GearBox.fromReductionStages(3, 4)); private final SmartMotorControllerConfig motorConfig = new SmartMotorControllerConfig(this) .withDrumRadius(chainPitch, toothCount) .withClosedLoopController(30, 0, 0) .withExponentialProfile( ExponentialProfilePIDController.createElevatorConstraints( Volts.of(12), // Maximum voltage during profile motors, // Motors weight, // Carriage weight chainPitch.times(toothCount).div(2 * Math.PI), // Drum radius gearing)) // Gearing ... ``` There are helpers for arms, flywheels and custom limits too: see [creating constraints](/documentation/understanding/editor/exponential-profiles.md#creating-constraints). ## When should I use one? * **Use one** when a trapezoidal profile is hard to tune, or the mechanism falls behind it and then overshoots. * **Keep the trapezoidal profile** if it already works well, or the motor is always current limited. * **It cannot fix an underpowered mechanism.** See [when to use each profile type](/documentation/understanding/editor/exponential-profiles.md#when-to-use-each-profile-type). ## Tune it Start from the helper's values and [refine the profile live](/documentation/understanding/editor/exponential-profiles.md#refining-the-profile-live). The profile only plans the move, so it still needs a feedforward, and the profile's `kV` and `kA` are [not the feedforward's](/documentation/understanding/editor/config/feedforward.md#these-are-not-an-exponential-profiles-kv-and-ka). ## Code reference {% @github-files/github-code-block url="" %}

pages.title: How do I turn off linear closed loop control?
pages.content:
# How do I turn off linear closed loop control? YAMS defaults to closed-loop position or velocity control expressed in linear units (meters and meters per second) for mechanisms that have a wheel diameter or drum radius configured. There are specific situations, open-loop testing, duty-cycle-based control for simple mechanisms, or debugging actuator response, where you want to read linear measurement data without having the closed-loop controller operate in those linear units. Disabling linear closed-loop lets you get `Measurement` values in meters while still supplying angular setpoints, without restructuring your subsystem. ## What is linear closed loop control? Linear closed loop control is when the closed loop controller operate in `meters` and `meters per second` instead of `rotations` and `rotations per second`. This directly affects your PID gains. ## When would I want to disable it? Sometimes you would like to get `Measurement` (like `SmartMotorController.getMeasurementPosition` and `SmartMotorController.getMeasurementVelocity`) data without enabling linear closed loop control. * Measuring shooter speed in `meters per second` for easier shoot on the move calculation * Supplying linear velocity or data which is translated to angle's or angular velocities inside of the `SmartMotorController`. ## How do I disable it? Inside of your `SmartMotorControllerConfig` you would use `withLinearClosedLoopController(false)` 
SmartMotorControllerConfig motorConfig        = new SmartMotorControllerConfig(this)
      .withControlMode(ControlMode.CLOSED_LOOP)
      .withWheelDiameter(Inches.of(4))
      .withZeroPower(MotorMode.COAST)
      .withClosedLoopController(50,0,0)
      .withLinearClosedLoopController(false);
pages.content_preview: # How do I turn off linear closed loop control? YAMS defaults to closed-loop position or velocity control expressed in linear units (meters and meters per second) for mechanisms that have a wheel diameter or drum radius configured.

pages.title: How do I sense activity from the motor current?
pages.content_preview: # How do I sense activity from the motor current? Current sensing lets your robot detect when a mechanism is stalling against a hard stop, for example, an elevator that has fully descended or a claw that has fully closed, without requiring a dedicated limit switch.

pages.title: How do I use a gyro mounted on its side?
pages.content: # How do I use a gyro mounted on its side? A swerve drive needs the robot's heading, which is rotation about the axis pointing up through the robot. A gyro mounted flat reports that as its yaw. If packaging forces you to mount the gyro on its side (for example vertically on a superstructure plate), the robot turning shows up as the gyro's roll or pitch instead, and a `SwerveDrive` reading yaw will see almost no heading change. `SwerveDriveConfig.withGyroHeadingAxis(GyroAxis)` tells YAMS which gyro axis points up, so the heading and tilt are read correctly without any math in your robot code. {% hint style="info" %} This is currently a Java only feature. The C++ `SwerveDriveConfig` takes a heading supplier in `WithGyro(...)`, so in C++ return the correct axis from that supplier yourself. {% endhint %} ## Give the drive the gyro's full attitude `withGyro(...)` takes a `Supplier`: the gyro's full 3D attitude, not just a yaw angle. Most gyros expose this directly, such as `pigeon::getRotation3d`. ## Pick the heading axis `GyroAxis` lives in `yams.core.mechanisms.config.enums` and names the gyro axis that points up through the robot: | `GyroAxis` | Gyro mounting | Robot turning shows up as | | --------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------- | | `YAW` (default) | Flat, the gyro's Z axis points up | The gyro's yaw | | `ROLL` | On its side, the gyro's X axis points up. The gyro's Y axis is taken to point to the robot's left | The gyro's roll | | `PITCH` | On its side, the gyro's Y axis points up. The gyro's X axis is taken to point to the robot's front | The gyro's pitch | ```java import com.ctre.phoenix6.CANBus; import com.ctre.phoenix6.hardware.Pigeon2; import org.wpilib.hardware.bus.CANPort; import yams.commands2.config.SwerveDriveConfig; import yams.commands2.swerve.SwerveDrive; import yams.core.mechanisms.config.enums.GyroAxis; private final Pigeon2 gyro = new Pigeon2(14, new CANBus(CANPort.CAN_S0)); SwerveDriveConfig config = new SwerveDriveConfig(this, fl, fr, bl, br) .withGyro(gyro::getRotation3d) // The gyro is mounted with its X axis pointing up, so the robot's heading is the gyro's roll. .withGyroHeadingAxis(GyroAxis.ROLL) .withStartingPose(new Pose2d(0, 0, Rotation2d.fromDegrees(0))) .withTranslationController(new PIDController(1, 0, 0)) .withRotationController(new PIDController(1, 0, 0)); drive = new SwerveDrive(config); ``` For Commands v3, import `SwerveDriveConfig` and `SwerveDrive` from `yams.commands3` instead. `GyroAxis` is the same class for both. YAMS rotates the gyro's attitude into the robot's frame before anything reads it. After that, the yaw of the result is the robot's heading, and its roll and pitch are the robot's tilt (which anti-tipping uses), whichever way the gyro is mounted. `withGyroInverted(...)` and `withGyroOffset(...)` apply to the resulting heading. ## Read the heading `getGyroAngle()` was removed from `SwerveDrive` and `SwerveDriveConfig`. Use `getGyroRotation3d()`, which returns the robot's attitude with the heading axis already applied: ```java Rotation2d heading = drive.getGyroRotation3d().toRotation2d(); ``` The heading wraps at ±180 degrees. Use `drive.getPose().getRotation()` if you want the odometry heading instead of the raw gyro heading. ## Check it 1. Put the robot on blocks or a cart and open the drive's telemetry. 2. Rotate the robot counterclockwise (viewed from above). The gyro heading should increase. 3. If the heading barely changes, the wrong axis is selected: try the other of `ROLL` and `PITCH`. 4. If it changes in the wrong direction, add `.withGyroInverted(true)`. ## Related pages * [Swerve Drive](/documentation/tutorials/swerve-drive.md)

pages.title: How do I enable battery discharge simulation?
pages.content_preview: # How do I enable battery discharge simulation? By default, `BatterySim` only models instantaneous voltage sag from combined current draw, and the simulated battery itself never changes, so it sags from the same fully-charged 12V/20mΩ baseline whether it's the first cycle of the match or the last.

pages.title: How do I run a high fidelity simulation?
pages.content_preview: # How do I run a high fidelity simulation? Step the simulated physics every millisecond from a Notifier, so a closed loop running on the motor controller sees a fresh measurement on every run.

pages.title: How do I view my DataLog in AdvantageScope?
pages.content_preview: # How do I view my DataLog in AdvantageScope? {% hint style="danger" %} **This is not "Log Replay."** [AdvantageKit's Log Replay](https://docs.advantagekit.org/getting-started/what-is-advantagekit) re-runs your robot code against a recorded log to deterministically reproduce a match in simulation,...

pages.title: How do I show my mechanisms on a 3D robot model?
pages.content_preview: # How do I show my mechanisms on a 3D robot model? Publish each mechanism's Pose3d, so AdvantageScope moves the matching part of your robot's CAD model as the real mechanism moves.

pages.title: Organizing configs in constants
pages.content_preview: # Organizing configs in constants As your robot grows, managing configuration across multiple subsystems can become unwieldy. YAMS supports a clean pattern where you define all your configs in a centralized Constants file, then bind them to subsystems at construction time using `.withSubsystem()`.

pages.title: Battery simulation
pages.content_preview: # Battery simulation YAMS models a single, shared robot battery in simulation instead of letting each mechanism compute its own voltage sag in isolation.

pages.title: Smart motor controllers
pages.content_preview: # Smart motor controllers ## A quick primer on motors and motor controllers {% embed url="<https://youtu.be/0BfR_viZSmQ>" %} {% embed url="<https://youtu.be/pIKvQX5p1PE>" %} The presentation from the video series continues onto PID, feedforward and motion profiles.

pages.title: SmartMotorControllerConfig
pages.content: # SmartMotorControllerConfig A `SmartMotorControllerConfig` describes one motor: how it is geared, how it is controlled, what it must not do and what it reports. You write it once, in the same way for every vendor, and hand it to a wrapper such as `TalonFXWrapper`, `SparkWrapper` or `NovaWrapper`. ## Where to find each option | Page | What it covers | | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | [Motor basics](/documentation/understanding/editor/config/motor-basics.md) | Control mode, inversion, brake or coast, starting from a clean config, vendor configs, telemetry. | | [Gearing and units](/documentation/understanding/editor/config/gearing-and-units.md) | Gear ratios, circumference, wheels and drums, cascading elevator stages. | | [Closed loop control](/documentation/understanding/editor/config/closed-loop-control.md) | PID gains, slots, tolerance, continuous wrapping, output limits, where the loop runs. | | [Feedforward](/documentation/understanding/editor/config/feedforward.md) | Simple, arm and elevator feedforwards and what each gain does. | | [Motion profiles](/documentation/understanding/editor/config/motion-profiles.md) | Trapezoidal, velocity and exponential profiles. | | [Limits and protection](/documentation/understanding/editor/config/limits-and-protection.md) | Soft limits, current limits, ramp rates, voltage compensation, temperature cutoff. | | [Encoders](/documentation/understanding/editor/config/encoders.md) | Starting position, encoder inversion, external encoders and their zero offset. | | [Followers](/documentation/understanding/editor/config/followers.md) | Followers on one shaft, and loosely coupled followers. | | [Simulation](/documentation/understanding/editor/config/simulation.md) | Simulation-only gains, starting position, moment of inertia and step size. | ## How the config is used ```java SmartMotorControllerConfig config = new SmartMotorControllerConfig(this) .withControlMode(ControlMode.CLOSED_LOOP) .withGearing(new MechanismGearing(GearBox.fromReductionStages(3, 4))) .withClosedLoopController(4, 0, 0) .withFeedforward(new ArmFeedforward(0, 0.3, 1.2)) .withTrapezoidalProfile(DegreesPerSecond.of(180), DegreesPerSecondPerSecond.of(360)) .withSoftLimits(Degrees.of(-20), Degrees.of(100)) .withStatorCurrentLimit(Amps.of(40)) .withZeroPower(MotorMode.BRAKE) .withTelemetry("ArmMotor", TelemetryVerbosity.HIGH); SmartMotorController motor = new SparkWrapper(spark, DCMotor.getNEO(1), config); ``` Three things are worth knowing before reading the option pages: * **Every `with...()` method returns the config**, so options chain. A few options depend on an earlier one and say so on their page, for example `withClosedLoopTolerance` needs a PID controller first. * **Options are checked when the wrapper is created.** An option that motor controller cannot do throws an exception, so problems show up at startup and not mid-match. It is usually a `SmartMotorControllerConfigurationException` that names the method to change, and for a few options an `IllegalArgumentException`. Each option says which. * **A mechanism adds to the config for you.** `Arm`, `Elevator`, `Pivot` and `FlyWheel` configs forward options such as `withSoftLimits` to the motor's config, so set those on the mechanism where one exists. ## Not every option works on every motor controller {% hint style="warning" %} Motor controllers differ. Some options only exist on one of them, and some only work in certain situations, for example only when the closed loop runs on the SystemCore. An option a controller cannot do normally throws a `SmartMotorControllerConfigurationException` or an `IllegalArgumentException` at startup, but check the table for each option you rely on. {% endhint %} Every option on the following pages has a table showing where it works. These are the ones that are **not** supported everywhere: | Option | TalonFX | TalonFXS | SPARK MAX / Flex | Thrifty Nova | | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- [`withVendorControlRequest`](/documentation/understanding/editor/config/motor-basics.md#withvendorcontrolrequest) | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ | | [`withSupplyCurrentLimit`](/documentation/understanding/editor/config/limits-and-protection.md#current-limits) | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ✅ | | [`withVoltageCompensation`](/documentation/understanding/editor/config/limits-and-protection.md#withvoltagecompensation) | ❌ | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ | | [`withClosedLoopTolerance`](/documentation/understanding/editor/config/closed-loop-control.md#withclosedlooptolerance) | ❌ | ❌ | ⚠️ not with [LQR](/documentation/understanding/editor/lqr-controllers.md) | ⚠️ not with [LQR](/documentation/understanding/editor/lqr-controllers.md) | | [Closed loop `SLOT_3`](/documentation/understanding/editor/config/closed-loop-control.md#slots) | ❌ | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ | | [`withFeedbackSynchronizationThreshold`](/documentation/understanding/editor/config/encoders.md#withfeedbacksynchronizationthreshold) | ❌ | ❌ | ⚠️ exponential profile or [LQR](/documentation/understanding/editor/lqr-controllers.md) only | ⚠️ closed loop mode only | | [Separate open and closed loop ramp Many of the ⚠️ entries depend on where the closed loop runs, which is explained in [where the loop runs](/documentation/understanding/editor/config/closed-loop-control.md#where-the-loop-runs). The [motor controller feature matrix](/documentation/understanding/editor/feature-matrix.md) has every option, including the ones that work everywhere, in one place. ## Changing a config later Most options can be changed while the robot runs through [live tuning](/documentation/understanding/live-tuning.md), which is the quickest way to find gains and limits. Once you have them, put the numbers back in the config so they survive a restart. ## Code reference * [`SmartMotorControllerConfig`](https://yet-another-software-suite.github.io/YAMS/javadocs/yams/motorcontrollers/SmartMotorControllerConfig.html)

pages.title: Motor basics
pages.content: # Motor basics The options every motor needs, whatever it drives. {% hint style="warning" %} Not every option on this page is supported on every motor controller. Each option has a table showing where it works, and an option a controller cannot do throws a `SmartMotorControllerConfigurationException` or an `IllegalArgumentException` at startup. Each option says which. The [config overview](/documentation/understanding/editor/config.md#not-every-option-works-on-every-motor-controller) lists them all together. {% endhint %} ## `withControlMode` Chooses whether the motor controller runs a closed loop controller. The default is `ControlMode.CLOSED_LOOP`. ```java .withControlMode(ControlMode.OPEN_LOOP) // a roller that only ever gets a voltage .withControlMode(ControlMode.CLOSED_LOOP) // anything that goes to a position or a speed ``` In `OPEN_LOOP` the closed loop options on the other pages have nothing to act on. On SPARKs the [soft limits](/documentation/understanding/editor/config/limits-and-protection.md#withsoftlimits) are only enabled in `CLOSED_LOOP`. **Supported on:** every supported motor controller. ## `withMotorInverted` Chooses which way the motor turns for a positive output. ```java .withMotorInverted(true) ``` Decide it once, with the mechanism free to move and a small voltage, before tuning anything. Encoders have their own inversion: see [Encoders](/documentation/understanding/editor/config/encoders.md#withencoderinverted). **Supported on:** every supported motor controller. ## `withZeroPower` Chooses what the motor does when the output is zero: `MotorMode.BRAKE` or `MotorMode.COAST`. * **`MotorMode.BRAKE`**: a motor that is not powered resists being moved. It stops quickly, and it is hard to turn by hand. * **`MotorMode.COAST`**: a motor that is not powered moves freely. It keeps going until friction stops it, and it turns easily by hand. ```java .withZeroPower(MotorMode.BRAKE) ``` What that looks like on a mechanism once the output is zero: | Mechanism | Not powered in `BRAKE` | Not powered in `COAST` | | ----------------------- | --------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- | | Elevator | Sinks slowly | Falls | | Arm | Sinks slowly | Falls | | Pivot (turret or wrist) | Stops and stays where it is | Keeps turning, and moves when bumped | | Flywheel | Stops quickly | Keeps spinning and slows down on its own | With nothing pulling on it, a mechanism in brake mode does not move while it is not powered, and the same mechanism in coast mode does. Gravity is something pulling on it, so most arms and elevators still sink in brake mode, only slower than they fall in coast mode. An arm or an elevator can stay up in brake mode, but only when it was built to: * **An elevator with a constant force spring** that carries the weight of the carriage has nothing left pulling it down. * **An arm whose motor resists harder than gravity pulls**, through enough gearing or a light enough arm, stays where it stopped. Both are mechanical, decided when the mechanism is designed, and nothing in your code makes them happen. Treat it as something to strive for when you design a mechanism, not something to expect from one. {% hint style="info" %} **Brake mode is an option, not a requirement, and it is not how a mechanism holds its position.** An arm or an elevator does not need brake mode to hold: the closed loop controller and [`kG`](/documentation/understanding/editor/config/feedforward.md) hold it, in either mode, for as long as it is powered. Brake mode only changes what happens when it is not, such as when the robot is disabled. {% endhint %} **Supported on:** every supported motor controller. ## `withResetPreviousConfig` By default YAMS resets the motor controller to factory defaults before applying your config, so settings left over from another robot or a vendor tool cannot surprise you. ```java .withResetPreviousConfig(false) // keep what is already saved on the controller ``` **Supported on:** every supported motor controller. ## `withVendorConfig` Gives YAMS a vendor config to start from, for settings YAMS has no option for. Your `SmartMotorControllerConfig` options are applied on top of it and win where both set the same thing. ```java .withVendorConfig(new TalonFXConfiguration() .withVoltage(new VoltageConfigs().withPeakReverseVoltage(0))) ``` Each wrapper accepts only its own vendor's root config class. The classes and an example for each vendor are in [vendor configuration classes](/documentation/understanding/editor/feature-matrix.md#vendor-configuration-classes), and [How do I use a vendor hardware config?](/documentation/how-to-motor-controllers-and-sensors/how-do-i-use-a-vendor-hardware-config.md) walks through it. **Supported on every motor controller.** Every controller accepts a vendor config, but only its own class. Any other class throws a `SmartMotorControllerConfigurationException`. | TalonFX | TalonFXS | SPARK MAX / Flex | Thrifty Nova | | ------------------------ | ------------------------- | --------------------------------------- | --------------------- | | ✅ `TalonFXConfiguration` | ✅ `TalonFXSConfiguration` | ✅ `SparkMaxConfig` or `SparkFlexConfig` | ✅ `NovaConfig.Config` | ## `withVendorControlRequest` Replaces the control request YAMS would send for position or velocity control with one of the vendor's own. By default YAMS picks the request for you: a plain position or velocity request, or a Motion Magic one when you set a [motion profile](/documentation/understanding/editor/config/motion-profiles.md). This option is for when you want a different one, most often: * **Torque control**, with a `TorqueCurrentFOC` request, so the closed loop commands current instead of voltage. * **Duty cycle output**, with a `DutyCycle` request, instead of YAMS's voltage requests. * **A request with your own settings on it**, such as `withUpdateFreqHz`, `withOverrideBrakeDurNeutral` or the limit switch options. ### How to use it Build the request once and give it to the config. YAMS keeps your object and fills in the setpoint every time it commands the motor, so every other setting on it stays as you made it. The value you construct it with is a placeholder: `0` is fine. {% code title="ArmSubsystem.java" %} ```java import com.ctre.phoenix6.controls.MotionMagicTorqueCurrentFOC; private final SmartMotorControllerConfig motorConfig = new SmartMotorControllerConfig(this) .withControlMode(ControlMode.CLOSED_LOOP) .withClosedLoopController(60, 0, 4) .withTrapezoidalProfile(DegreesPerSecond.of(180), DegreesPerSecondPerSecond.of(90)) .withGearing(new MechanismGearing(GearBox.fromReductionStages(3, 4))) .withZeroPower(MotorMode.BRAKE) .withTelemetry("ArmMotor", TelemetryVerbosity.HIGH) // Motion Magic on torque current instead of voltage. .withVendorControlRequest(new MotionMagicTorqueCurrentFOC(0)); ``` {% endcode %} Nothing else changes. `arm.runTo(Degrees.of(45))` and every other command work as before, and now send your request. ### Rules * **One request per config.** A position request replaces the one used for positions, and a velocity request replaces the one used for velocities. The other kind keeps YAMS's default. * **Match it to your profile.** YAMS only sets up Motion Magic when the config has a motion profile, so use a `MotionMagic` request with a profile and a `Position` or `Velocity` request without one. * **A `TorqueCurrentFOC` request changes what your gains mean.** The closed loop output is current in amps, not volts, so gains tuned for a voltage request do not carry over. Tune them again from the start. * **A `TorqueCurrentFOC` request cannot have FOC switched on or off.** It is always FOC, so the FOC toggles on the wrapper throw a `SmartMotorControllerConfigurationException` with one. ### Supported requests **Not supported everywhere.** Anything that is not on this list throws a `SmartMotorControllerConfigurationException` when the config is applied. | Motor controller | Position requests | Velocity requests | | ----------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | TalonFX, TalonFXS | `PositionVoltage`, `PositionDutyCycle`, `PositionTorqueCurrentFOC`, `MotionMagicVoltage`, `MotionMagicDutyCycle`, `MotionMagicTorqueCurrentFOC`, `MotionMagicExpoVoltage`, `MotionMagicExpoDutyCycle` | `VelocityVoltage`, `VelocityDutyCycle`, `VelocityTorqueCurrentFOC`, `MotionMagicVelocityVoltage`, `MotionMagicVelocityDutyCycle`, `MotionMagicVelocityTorqueCurrentFOC` | | SPARK MAX / Flex | ❌ Throws a `SmartMotorControllerConfigurationException` | ❌ Throws a `SmartMotorControllerConfigurationException` | | Thrifty Nova | ❌ Throws a `SmartMotorControllerConfigurationException` | ❌ Throws a `SmartMotorControllerConfigurationException` | On a SPARK, YAMS chooses the REV `ControlType` itself: MAXMotion when the config has a trapezoidal profile, plain position or velocity otherwise. ## `withTelemetry` Names the motor and chooses how much it publishes. ```java .withTelemetry("ArmMotor", TelemetryVerbosity.HIGH) ``` `HIGH` is what [live tuning](/documentation/understanding/live-tuning.md) needs. [Telemetry](/documentation/understanding/telemetry.md) lists every key and how to choose fields one by one with a `SmartMotorControllerTelemetryConfig`. **Supported on:** every supported motor controller. ## Code reference * [`SmartMotorControllerConfig`](https://yet-another-software-suite.github.io/YAMS/javadocs/yams/motorcontrollers/SmartMotorControllerConfig.html)
