pages.title: Gearing and units
pages.content: # Gearing and units These options tell YAMS how the motor's rotation becomes the mechanism's movement. Every position and velocity YAMS reports depends on them, so get them right before tuning. * **Rotor** is the motor's own shaft. * **Mechanism** is the output after the gearing: an arm's pivot, an elevator's drum, a flywheel's axle. * **Measurement** is the distance the mechanism travels, for mechanisms that move in a line. ## `withGearing` The reduction between the rotor and the mechanism. ```java .withGearing(new MechanismGearing(GearBox.fromReductionStages(3, 4))) // 3:1 then 4:1 .withGearing(12) // the same, as one number ``` A reduction is a number greater than 1: a "3:1" gearbox is `3`, and a "1:2" overdrive is `0.5`. `GearBox.fromReductionStages` and `Sprocket.fromStages` let you write the stages as they are on the robot. **Supported on:** every supported motor controller. ## `withMechanismCircumference` How far the mechanism travels in one rotation of its output. Setting it lets you use distances (`Meters`, `Inches`) anywhere YAMS takes an angle. ```java .withMechanismCircumference(Meters.of(0.25)) .withWheelRadius(Inches.of(2)) // or withWheelDiameter(Inches.of(4)) .withDrumRadius(Inches.of(1)) .withDrumRadius(Inches.of(0.25), 22) // chain pitch and sprocket teeth ``` All of these set the same value. Use whichever matches what you can measure. [How do I find my mechanism's circumference?](/documentation/how-to-motor-controllers-and-sensors/how-to-find-your-mechanism-circumference.md) covers the measuring. Several options need it first and throw a `SmartMotorControllerConfigurationException` without it: distance `withSoftLimits`, distance `withExternalEncoderZeroOffset`, and anything else that takes a `Distance`. **Supported on:** every supported motor controller. ## `withCascadingElevatorStages` Divides the gearing by the number of cascading stages, because each stage adds the same travel again. ```java .withGearing(new MechanismGearing(GearBox.fromReductionStages(5, 4))) .withCascadingElevatorStages(2) ``` Call it after `withGearing`: it changes the gearing that is already set. Continuous elevators, where one belt or rope runs through every stage, do not need it. **Supported on:** every supported motor controller. ## Code reference * [`SmartMotorControllerConfig`](https://yet-another-software-suite.github.io/YAMS/javadocs/yams/motorcontrollers/SmartMotorControllerConfig.html)
pages.content_preview: # Gearing and units These options tell YAMS how the motor's rotation becomes the mechanism's movement. Every position and velocity YAMS reports depends on them, so get them right before tuning.

pages.title: Closed loop control
pages.content: # Closed loop control Closed loop control is what takes a mechanism to a setpoint and holds it there. These options need [`withControlMode(ControlMode.CLOSED_LOOP)`](/documentation/understanding/editor/config/motor-basics.md#withcontrolmode), which is the default. {% hint style="warning" %} Not every option on this page is supported on every motor controller. Each option has a table showing where it works, and an option a controller cannot do throws a `SmartMotorControllerConfigurationException` or an `IllegalArgumentException` at startup. Each option says which. The [config overview](/documentation/understanding/editor/config.md#not-every-option-works-on-every-motor-controller) lists them all together. {% endhint %} For how to find good values, see [live tuning](/documentation/understanding/live-tuning.md). ## `withClosedLoopController` Sets the PID gains. ```java .withClosedLoopController(4, 0, 0.2) // kP, kI, kD .withClosedLoopController(new PIDController(4, 0, 0.2)) ``` The gains work in rotations and volts, or meters and volts for a [distance based controller](#withlinearclosedloopcontroller). YAMS converts them to whatever the motor controller uses, so the same numbers behave the same on every vendor. [How your gains reach the motor controller](#how-your-gains-reach-the-motor-controller) shows how. Passing an `LQRController` instead replaces the PID with an LQR: see [LQR controllers](/documentation/understanding/editor/lqr-controllers.md). **Supported on every motor controller.** Every controller accepts PID gains. An [LQR controller](/documentation/understanding/editor/lqr-controllers.md) always runs on the SystemCore, on every controller. | TalonFX | TalonFXS | SPARK MAX / Flex | Thrifty Nova | | ------- | -------- | ---------------- | ---------------------------- | | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ PID runs on the SystemCore | ### Slots Each call can name a slot, so one motor can hold several sets of gains and switch between them. ```java .withClosedLoopController(4, 0, 0, ClosedLoopControllerSlot.SLOT_0) .withClosedLoopController(6, 0, 0, ClosedLoopControllerSlot.SLOT_1) // later, while running motor.setClosedLoopSlot(ClosedLoopControllerSlot.SLOT_1); ``` **Not supported everywhere.** Selecting `SLOT_3` on a TalonFX or TalonFXS throws an `IllegalArgumentException`, and a feedforward configured for `SLOT_3` on a TalonFX throws a `SmartMotorControllerConfigurationException`. | TalonFX | TalonFXS | SPARK MAX / Flex | Thrifty Nova | | ----------------------- | ----------------------- | ---------------- | ------------ | | ⚠️ `SLOT_0` to `SLOT_2` | ⚠️ `SLOT_0` to `SLOT_2` | ✅ | ✅ | ## `withClosedLoopTolerance` How close to the setpoint counts as being there. ```java .withClosedLoopController(4, 0, 0) .withClosedLoopTolerance(Degrees.of(1)) ``` Call it after `withClosedLoopController`: it is set on the PID controllers that exist at that moment, and throws a `SmartMotorControllerConfigurationException` if there are none. **Not supported everywhere.** It throws a `SmartMotorControllerConfigurationException` on a TalonFX or TalonFXS. | TalonFX | TalonFXS | SPARK MAX / Flex | Thrifty Nova | | ------- | -------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | ❌ | ❌ | ⚠️ not with an [LQR controller](/documentation/understanding/editor/lqr-controllers.md) | ⚠️ not with an [LQR controller](/documentation/understanding/editor/lqr-controllers.md) | ## `withContinuousWrapping` Tells the controller that the two ends of the range are the same place, so it takes the short way round. ```java .withClosedLoopController(50, 0, 0.5) .withContinuousWrapping(Degrees.of(-180), Degrees.of(180)) ``` It needs a closed loop controller first, and cannot be combined with [soft limits](/documentation/understanding/editor/config/limits-and-protection.md#withsoftlimits) or a distance based controller, because a mechanism with ends cannot wrap. **Supported on:** every supported motor controller. ## `withClosedLoopControllerMaximumVoltage` Caps the voltage the closed loop controller may ask for. ```java .withClosedLoopControllerMaximumVoltage(Volts.of(6)) ``` **Not supported everywhere.** On a TalonFX or TalonFXS it is applied as the peak forward and reverse voltage. On a SPARK it throws a `SmartMotorControllerConfigurationException` unless the loop runs on the SystemCore. | TalonFX | TalonFXS | SPARK MAX / Flex | Thrifty Nova | | ------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------ | | ✅ | ✅ | ⚠️ only with an exponential profile or an [LQR controller](/documentation/understanding/editor/lqr-controllers.md) | ✅ | ## Where the loop runs Some combinations run on the motor controller, at 1 kHz, and some on the SystemCore, every 20 ms by default. It matters for a few options, and YAMS raises an alert when the loop is on the SystemCore. ### PID gains do not carry over between the two PID gains tuned with the loop on the motor controller will never be the same as gains tuned with the loop on the SystemCore, even on the same mechanism. The reason is the closed loop control period: * **On the motor controller** the loop runs at 1 kHz, once every millisecond, right next to the motor and its encoder. That is 20 runs for every one run of the SystemCore loop at its default period. This period is fixed by the motor controller and cannot be changed. * **On the SystemCore** the loop runs once every control period, 20 ms by default, and each measurement and each output also has to cross the CAN bus. A slower loop reacts later to every error, so it cannot use gains as high as a fast one before it starts to oscillate. `kD` and `kI` are affected the most, because they depend directly on the time between two runs of the loop. What this means in practice: * **Tune again whenever the loop moves.** On a SPARK that happens when you switch between a trapezoidal profile, which runs on the controller, and an exponential profile or an [LQR controller](/documentation/understanding/editor/lqr-controllers.md), which run on the SystemCore. Moving a mechanism to a different brand of motor controller can move the loop too. * **Tune again after changing** [**`withClosedLoopControlPeriod`**](#withclosedloopcontrolperiod)**.** A different period is a different loop. * **Do not copy gains from another team or another robot** without checking where their loop ran and how fast. ### `withClosedLoopControlPeriod` Changes how often the SystemCore loop runs. The default is 20 ms. It does not change a loop that runs on the motor controller: that period is fixed at 1 ms (1 kHz). ```java .withClosedLoopControlPeriod(Milliseconds.of(10)) ``` **Not supported everywhere.** Where it is not supported it throws an `IllegalArgumentException` on a TalonFX, TalonFXS or Thrifty Nova, and a `SmartMotorControllerConfigurationException` on a SPARK. | TalonFX | TalonFXS | SPARK MAX / Flex | Thrifty Nova | | ------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------- | | ❌ | ❌ | ⚠️ only with an exponential profile or an [LQR controller](/documentation/understanding/editor/lqr-controllers.md) | ⚠️ only in closed loop mode | ## How your gains reach the motor controller You write every gain once, in mechanism units: volts per mechanism rotation, or per meter for a [distance based controller](#withlinearclosedloopcontroller). Every [feedforward](/documentation/understanding/editor/config/feedforward.md) uses the same units, including an `ArmFeedforward`. Each motor controller wants its gains in its own units, so YAMS converts them when it applies the config, and again every time you change a gain while [live tuning](/documentation/understanding/live-tuning.md). ### Dimensional analysis The conversion is dimensional analysis. A gain is a number with units, like 4 V per mechanism rotation. To change its units, multiply it by fractions that are each worth exactly 1, such as 1 mechanism rotation over 12 motor rotations on a 12:1 gearbox. A unit that appears on both the top and the bottom cancels. Once only the units the motor controller wants are left, the number in front is its gain. {% tabs %} {% tab title="SPARK MAX / Flex" %} A SPARK's closed loop works on its own encoder, not on the mechanism. Its PID output is a duty cycle from -1 to 1, not volts. So every PID gain loses the gear ratio and the 12 V, and a velocity gain also changes from rotations per second to RPM. | Gain | YAMS units | SPARK units | YAMS does | | -------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------- | ----------------------- | | `kP`, position | V per mechanism rotation (or meter) | duty cycle per encoder rotation | ÷ (12 V × ratio) | | `kP`, velocity | V per mechanism rotation (or meter) per second | duty cycle per encoder RPM | ÷ (12 V × ratio × 60) | | `kI` | `kP`'s units per second | `kP`'s units per 1 ms loop | × 0.001 s, then as `kP` | | `kD` | `kP`'s units × seconds | `kP`'s units × 1 ms loops | ÷ 0.001 s, then as `kP` | | `kS`, `kG` | V | V | nothing | | `kV` | V per mechanism rotation (or meter) per second | V per encoder RPM | ÷ (ratio × 60) | | `kA` | V per mechanism rotation (or meter) per second² | V per encoder RPM per second | ÷ (ratio × 60) | | Profile velocity | mechanism rotations (or meters) per second | encoder RPM | × ratio × 60 | | Profile acceleration | mechanism rotations (or meters) per second² | encoder RPM per second | × ratio × 60 | * **The ratio** is the gearing between the mechanism and the encoder the SPARK uses: your [gearing](/documentation/understanding/editor/config/gearing-and-units.md), or the [external encoder's gearing](/documentation/understanding/editor/config/encoders.md#withexternalencodergearing) when the SPARK uses an external encoder for feedback. * **The 12 V** is your [voltage compensation](/documentation/understanding/editor/config/limits-and-protection.md#withvoltagecompensation) if you set one, and 12 V if you do not. The SPARK's PID output is a fraction of full output, from -1 to 1, in every closed loop control type YAMS sends: position, velocity and both MAXMotion types. With voltage compensation, full output is the compensation voltage, so the gains are exact. Without it, full output is the battery's voltage, so at 11 V the PID pushes about 8% less than you tuned for. * **The feedforward is in volts**, not a fraction of full output. The SPARK's `kS`, `kV`, `kA`, `kG` and `kCos` are in volts, and YAMS sends its own feedforward with each setpoint in volts (`ArbFFUnits.kVoltage`), so the feedforward does not change with the battery's voltage. * **An elevator, or any distance based controller,** has every gain per meter, as on a Talon: `kP`, `kI`, `kD`, `kV` and `kA`, and the profile's limits. `kS` and `kG` are volts either way. YAMS first divides a gain per meter by the mechanism rotations per meter (multiplies, for a profile limit), then converts the result as in the table. An `ElevatorFeedforward` or [`withLinearClosedLoopController`](#withlinearclosedloopcontroller) makes the controller distance based. * **Position and velocity need different gains.** A SPARK measures position error in rotations and velocity error in RPM, so YAMS writes the position or velocity version of your gains whenever the type of setpoint changes. You still tune only one set. * **An arm's `kG`** goes to the SPARK's `kCos`, with a `kCosRatio` of 1 over the ratio so the SPARK can turn its encoder's rotations into the arm's angle. * **In simulation**, REVLib's SPARK applies `kI` and `kD` per second instead of per loop, so YAMS skips the 0.001 s step there. {% endtab %} {% tab title="TalonFX / TalonFXS" %} YAMS sets the Talon's `SensorToMechanismRatio` to your gear ratio, so the Talon already measures in mechanism rotations and works in volts. An angle based gain goes to the Talon unchanged. Only a [distance based controller](#withlinearclosedloopcontroller) is converted, from meters to mechanism rotations. | Gain | YAMS units | Talon units | YAMS does | | ----------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `kP`, `kI`, `kD` | V per mechanism rotation (or meter) | V per mechanism rotation | ÷ mechanism rotations per meter when distance based | | `kS`, `kG` | V | V | nothing, and sets `GravityType` to `Arm_Cosine` for an arm or `Elevator_Static` for an elevator | | `kV`, `kA` | V per mechanism rotation (or meter) per second (²) | V per mechanism rotation per second (²) | ÷ mechanism rotations per meter when distance based | | Motion Magic velocity, acceleration | mechanism rotations (or meters) per second (²) | mechanism rotations per second (²) | × mechanism rotations per meter when distance based | | Motion Magic Expo `kV`, `kA` | from the [exponential profile](/documentation/understanding/editor/exponential-profiles.md) | V per mechanism rotation per second (²) | ÷ mechanism rotations per meter when distance based | With an [external encoder](/documentation/understanding/editor/config/encoders.md#withexternalencoder), the `SensorToMechanismRatio` is the encoder's gearing and the `RotorToSensorRatio` is the rest of the gearing, so the gains are still per mechanism rotation. {% endtab %} {% tab title="Thrifty Nova" %} The Nova's closed loop [runs on the SystemCore](#where-the-loop-runs) in YAMS units, so nothing is converted. Your gains are used exactly as you wrote them, and the Nova only receives the voltage the loop asks for. {% endtab %} {% endtabs %} {% hint style="info" %} WPILib's `ArmFeedforward` documents its `kV` and `kA` per radian. In YAMS they are per rotation, like every other gain. When the loop runs on the SystemCore, YAMS converts them to radians for WPILib's math. {% endhint %} The units are the same on every controller, but [where the loop runs](#where-the-loop-runs) still matters. A loop on the motor controller runs every millisecond, so gains tuned there are not the best gains for a loop on the SystemCore. ## `withLinearClosedLoopController` Chooses whether the controller works in rotations or in meters. It turns on by itself when you give a distance profile, a distance exponential profile or an `ElevatorFeedforward`, and it only takes effect when a [circumference](/documentation/understanding/editor/config/gearing-and-units.md#withmechanismcircumference) is set. [How do I turn off linear closed loop control?](/documentation/how-to-motor-controllers-and-sensors/how-to-disable-linear-closed-loop-control.md) explains when to turn it off. **Supported on:** every supported motor controller. ## Code reference * [`SmartMotorControllerConfig`](https://yet-another-software-suite.github.io/YAMS/javadocs/yams/motorcontrollers/SmartMotorControllerConfig.html)
pages.content_preview: # Closed loop control Closed loop control is what takes a mechanism to a setpoint and holds it there. These options need [`withControlMode(ControlMode.CLOSED_LOOP)`](/documentation/understanding/editor/config/motor-basics.md#withcontrolmode), which is the default.

pages.title: Feedforward
pages.content: # Feedforward A feedforward predicts the voltage a move needs from what you know about the mechanism, before any error has built up. The PID then only has to fix what the prediction missed. ## `withFeedforward` Takes one of WPILib's three feedforward classes. ```java .withFeedforward(new SimpleMotorFeedforward(0.1, 0.12, 0.01)) // kS, kV, kA .withFeedforward(new ArmFeedforward(0.1, 0.35, 1.2, 0.02)) // kS, kG, kV, kA .withFeedforward(new ElevatorFeedforward(0.1, 0.4, 3.5, 0.1)) // kS, kG, kV, kA ``` | Gain | What it is for | How to find it | | ---- | ----------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `kS` | The voltage that just overcomes friction. | Raise the voltage slowly until the mechanism starts to move. | | `kG` | The voltage that holds the mechanism against gravity. | The voltage at which it neither rises nor falls. For an arm, measure it with the arm level. | | `kV` | The voltage per unit of speed. | Volts above `kS` divided by the steady speed it gives. | | `kA` | The voltage per unit of acceleration. | Usually small. Raise it if the mechanism lags at the start of a move. | `ArmFeedforward` and `SimpleMotorFeedforward` gains are per rotation of the mechanism. `ElevatorFeedforward` gains are per meter, and giving one makes the controller [distance based](/documentation/understanding/editor/config/closed-loop-control.md#withlinearclosedloopcontroller). [Live tuning](/documentation/understanding/live-tuning.md) has the full order for finding these. ### These are not an exponential profile's `kV` and `kA` An [exponential profile](/documentation/understanding/editor/exponential-profiles.md) also has a `kV` and a `kA`. They share the names and the units, but they are separate settings that do different jobs, and changing one pair does not change the other. | | Feedforward `kV` and `kA` | Exponential profile `kV` and `kA` | | ------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Set with | `withFeedforward(...)` | `withExponentialProfile(...)` | | What they do | Turn the velocity and acceleration of the setpoint into volts for the motor. | Shape the plan. The maximum voltage divided by `kV` is the profile's top speed, and divided by `kA` is its maximum acceleration. | | Raising them | Sends the motor more voltage. | Makes the profile slower. No extra voltage is sent. | | Tuned by | Watching how well the mechanism follows the setpoint. | Watching whether the mechanism can keep up with the profile. | A mechanism with an exponential profile needs both pairs: the profile's to plan the move, and the feedforward's to follow it. Do not copy one pair into the other. The profile's values are often set higher than the feedforward's, so the plan asks for less than the motor can give and leaves voltage in reserve. [Measuring kV and kA](/documentation/understanding/editor/exponential-profiles.md#measuring-kv-and-ka-optional) on the exponential profiles page measures the profile's pair, and [refining the profile live](/documentation/understanding/editor/exponential-profiles.md#refining-the-profile-live) tunes them. ### Slots A feedforward can be given a slot, so it switches together with the [PID gains in that slot](/documentation/understanding/editor/config/closed-loop-control.md#slots). ```java .withFeedforward(new ArmFeedforward(0.1, 0.35, 1.2), ClosedLoopControllerSlot.SLOT_0) .withFeedforward(new ArmFeedforward(0.1, 0.60, 1.2), ClosedLoopControllerSlot.SLOT_1) // holding a game piece ``` **Supported on:** every supported motor controller. ## Code reference * [`SmartMotorControllerConfig`](https://yet-another-software-suite.github.io/YAMS/javadocs/yams/motorcontrollers/SmartMotorControllerConfig.html)

pages.title: Motion profiles
pages.content: # Motion profiles A motion profile turns a jump in the goal into a smooth path of setpoints for the closed loop controller to follow. Setting one profile replaces any other. ## `withTrapezoidalProfile` A maximum velocity and a maximum acceleration. ```java .withTrapezoidalProfile(DegreesPerSecond.of(180), DegreesPerSecondPerSecond.of(360)) // arms, pivots .withTrapezoidalProfile(MetersPerSecond.of(1.5), MetersPerSecondPerSecond.of(3)) // elevators ``` The distance version needs a [circumference](/documentation/understanding/editor/config/gearing-and-units.md#withmechanismcircumference) and makes the controller [distance based](/documentation/understanding/editor/config/closed-loop-control.md#withlinearclosedloopcontroller). Choose limits the mechanism can really reach. If the profile asks for more than the motor can give, the mechanism falls behind and the PID fights to catch up: see [when tuning does not help](/documentation/understanding/live-tuning.md#when-tuning-does-not-help). ## A velocity profile For mechanisms that hold a speed, the same method takes a maximum acceleration and a maximum jerk instead. ```java .withTrapezoidalProfile(RotationsPerSecondPerSecond.of(200), RotationsPerSecondPerSecond.per(Second).of(2000)) ``` `withVelocityTrapezoidalProfile(true)` marks an existing trapezoidal profile as a velocity profile. The overload above does that for you. ## `withExponentialProfile` An exponential profile follows what a DC motor can actually do: hard acceleration at first, easing off as it speeds up. ```java .withExponentialProfile(Volts.of(10), DCMotor.getKrakenX60(1), KilogramSquareMeters.of(0.5)) // arm or flywheel .withExponentialProfile(Volts.of(10), DCMotor.getKrakenX60(2), Kilograms.of(8), Inches.of(1)) // elevator .withExponentialProfile(Volts.of(10), RotationsPerSecond.of(2), RotationsPerSecondPerSecond.of(8)) ``` You give it a maximum voltage and either the mechanism (its motor and its moment of inertia, or its mass and drum radius) or a maximum velocity and acceleration. YAMS works out starting values of the profile's kV and kA from those. Tune kV and kA directly from there, as CTRE's Motion Magic Expo documentation describes, and pass your tuned values with `ExponentialProfile.Constraints.fromCharacteristics(maxVoltage, kV, kA)`. [Exponential profiles](/documentation/understanding/editor/exponential-profiles.md) explains when to use one and how to tune it. ## Where each profile runs **Supported on every motor controller.** Every controller accepts both profiles, but they do not run in the same place. | TalonFX | TalonFXS | SPARK MAX / Flex | Thrifty Nova | | ----------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------ | | ✅ on the controller (Motion Magic, Motion Magic Expo) | ✅ on the controller (Motion Magic, Motion Magic Expo) | ✅ trapezoidal on the controller (MAXMotion), exponential on the SystemCore | ✅ both on the SystemCore | Where the profile runs decides which other options are available: see [where the loop runs](/documentation/understanding/editor/config/closed-loop-control.md#where-the-loop-runs). ## Code reference * [`SmartMotorControllerConfig`](https://yet-another-software-suite.github.io/YAMS/javadocs/yams/motorcontrollers/SmartMotorControllerConfig.html)

pages.title: Limits and protection
pages.content: # Limits and protection These options stop a mechanism or a motor from hurting itself or the rest of the robot. {% hint style="warning" %} Not every option on this page is supported on every motor controller. Each option has a table showing where it works, and an option a controller cannot do throws a `SmartMotorControllerConfigurationException` or an `IllegalArgumentException` at startup. Each option says which. The [config overview](/documentation/understanding/editor/config.md#not-every-option-works-on-every-motor-controller) lists them all together. {% endhint %} ## `withSoftLimits` The range the mechanism is allowed to move through. ```java .withSoftLimits(Degrees.of(-20), Degrees.of(100)) .withSoftLimits(Meters.of(0), Meters.of(1.2)) // needs a circumference ``` The lower limit must be below the upper limit. Soft limits cannot be combined with [continuous wrapping](/documentation/understanding/editor/config/closed-loop-control.md#withcontinuouswrapping). Soft limits rely on the encoder being right. If the mechanism does not start where the encoder thinks it does, the limits are in the wrong place: see [starting position](/documentation/understanding/editor/config/encoders.md#withstartingposition). **Not supported everywhere.** | TalonFX | TalonFXS | SPARK MAX / Flex | Thrifty Nova | | ------- | -------- | ------------------------------------ | ------------ | | ✅ | ✅ | ⚠️ only enforced in closed loop mode | ✅ | ## Current limits `withStatorCurrentLimit` limits the current through the motor, which limits its torque and heat. `withSupplyCurrentLimit` limits the current drawn from the battery, which protects the breaker and the battery voltage. ```java .withStatorCurrentLimit(Amps.of(40)) .withSupplyCurrentLimit(Amps.of(30)) ``` [Limiting power consumption](/documentation/understanding/editor/limiting-power-consumption.md#current-limits) explains how to choose them and how to test them against the [battery simulation](/documentation/understanding/battery-simulation.md). **Not supported everywhere.** `withSupplyCurrentLimit` is not available on SPARKs. | TalonFX | TalonFXS | SPARK MAX / Flex | Thrifty Nova | | ------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------ | | ✅ | ✅ | ⚠️ stator limit only: a supply limit throws a `SmartMotorControllerConfigurationException` | ✅ | ## Ramp rates `withOpenLoopRampRate` and `withClosedLoopRampRate` set the shortest time the output may take to go from zero to full. ```java .withOpenLoopRampRate(Seconds.of(0.25)) .withClosedLoopRampRate(Seconds.of(0.1)) ``` A ramp rate is the last thing to reach for. It slows everything the motor does, including the closed loop controller's reactions. To cut a mechanism's power draw, try these first, in order: a [motion profile](/documentation/understanding/editor/config/motion-profiles.md) if one suits the mechanism, then a [supply current limit](#current-limits) where the motor controller has one, then a [stator current limit](#current-limits) where it does not. Use a ramp rate only if none of those is enough. [Limiting power consumption](/documentation/understanding/editor/limiting-power-consumption.md#ramp-rates) explains how they behave. **Not supported everywhere.** | TalonFX | TalonFXS | SPARK MAX / Flex | Thrifty Nova | | ------- | -------- | ---------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ⚠️ one ramp rate for both: two different values throw a `SmartMotorControllerConfigurationException` | ## `withVoltageCompensation` Scales the output so a duty cycle means the same voltage whatever the battery voltage is. ```java .withVoltageCompensation(Volts.of(12)) ``` **Not supported everywhere.** It throws an `IllegalArgumentException` on a TalonFX or TalonFXS. Use a voltage request instead of a duty cycle there. | TalonFX | TalonFXS | SPARK MAX / Flex | Thrifty Nova | | ------- | -------- | ---------------- | ------------ | | ❌ | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ | ## `withTemperatureCutoff` Stops the closed loop controller driving the motor once it reaches a temperature. ```java .withTemperatureCutoff(Celsius.of(80)) ``` While the motor is at or above the cutoff, the closed loop output is zero, so a mechanism that was being held up will drop. Treat it as a last resort and fix the cause with [current limits](/documentation/understanding/editor/limiting-power-consumption.md) or gearing. {% hint style="danger" %} On a SPARK MAX or SPARK Flex with a **trapezoidal** profile, the cutoff does not work: the profile runs on the SPARK, and the cutoff is only checked by the loop on the SystemCore. Use an exponential profile if you rely on the cutoff. {% endhint %} **Not supported everywhere.** The cutoff is enforced by the closed loop running on the SystemCore, so it only works where the loop runs there. An [LQR controller](/documentation/understanding/editor/lqr-controllers.md) always runs there, so the cutoff works with LQR on every motor controller. | TalonFX | TalonFXS | SPARK MAX / Flex | Thrifty Nova | | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------- | | ⚠️ only with an [LQR controller](/documentation/understanding/editor/lqr-controllers.md) | ⚠️ only with an [LQR controller](/documentation/understanding/editor/lqr-controllers.md) | ⚠️ only with an exponential profile or an [LQR controller](/documentation/understanding/editor/lqr-controllers.md) | ⚠️ only in closed loop mode | ## Code reference * [`SmartMotorControllerConfig`](https://yet-another-software-suite.github.io/YAMS/javadocs/yams/motorcontrollers/SmartMotorControllerConfig.html)

pages.title: Encoders
pages.content: # Encoders Every motor has a built in encoder. Many mechanisms add an external one that knows where the mechanism is when the robot turns on. {% hint style="warning" %} Not every option on this page is supported on every motor controller. Each option has a table showing where it works, and an option a controller cannot do throws a `SmartMotorControllerConfigurationException` or an `IllegalArgumentException` at startup. Each option says which. The [config overview](/documentation/understanding/editor/config.md#not-every-option-works-on-every-motor-controller) lists them all together. {% endhint %} ## `withStartingPosition` What the built in encoder is set to when the robot turns on. ```java .withStartingPosition(Degrees.of(90)) .withStartingPosition(Meters.of(0)) // needs a circumference ``` Without it, wherever the mechanism happens to be at startup is called zero. [`withSimStartingPosition`](/documentation/understanding/editor/config/simulation.md#withsimstartingposition) sets a different value for simulation only. ### Why it matters for an arm with `kG` A wrong angle is more than a wrong number on the dashboard. An [`ArmFeedforward`](/documentation/understanding/editor/config/feedforward.md) multiplies `kG` by the cosine of the arm's angle, so it gives the most voltage when the arm is level and none when it is straight up. It uses the angle YAMS thinks the arm is at. If the arm does not start at 0° and you do not say so, that angle is wrong, and a `kG` you tuned carefully is applied in the wrong places. | The arm is really | Needed to hold it | `kG` gives, with no starting position | What happens | | ----------------- | ----------------- | ------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- | | Straight up, 90° | Nothing | All of `kG` | The arm is pushed away from where it should rest | | Level, 0° | All of `kG` | Nothing | The arm sags, and the PID has to make up the whole difference | | Below level, -20° | Most of `kG` | A negative voltage | The arm is pushed down, the wrong way | So set the starting position before you tune `kG`. A `kG` tuned on an arm with the wrong zero only looks right at the one angle it was tuned at. **Supported on:** every supported motor controller. ## `withEncoderInverted` Inverts the built in encoder. Use `withExternalEncoderInverted` for the external one. ```java .withExternalEncoderInverted(true) ``` Most built in encoders are fixed to the rotor and follow [`withMotorInverted`](/documentation/understanding/editor/config/motor-basics.md#withmotorinverted), so they rarely need this. **Not supported everywhere.** `withEncoderInverted` only works on a TalonFXS and throws on every other controller: a `SmartMotorControllerConfigurationException` on a TalonFX, and an `IllegalArgumentException` on a SPARK or Thrifty Nova. `withExternalEncoderInverted` works on every controller that has an external encoder configured. | TalonFX | TalonFXS | SPARK MAX / Flex | Thrifty Nova | | ------- | -------- | ---------------- | ------------ | | ❌ | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ | `withExternalEncoderInverted` throws a `SmartMotorControllerConfigurationException` if no external encoder is configured. ## `withExternalEncoder` Attaches an external encoder. It must be one the motor controller can read directly. ```java .withExternalEncoder(spark.getAbsoluteEncoder()) .withExternalEncoder(new CANcoder(5, new CANBus(CANPort.CAN_S0))) ``` The encoders each wrapper accepts are listed in the [feature matrix](/documentation/understanding/editor/feature-matrix.md#external-encoders). [How do I use absolute encoders on my arm?](/documentation/how-to-mechanisms/how-do-i-use-absolute-encoders-on-my-arm.md) has a complete example for each vendor. ### Keep the discontinuity point outside the travel This applies to **every absolute encoder, whether it is geared or mounted 1:1**. An absolute encoder only knows where it is within one turn of its own shaft. The place where its reading wraps is the **discontinuity point**. It is clearly marked on an absolute encoder, usually as a white line on the casing and another on the bearing: when the two lines line up, the encoder is at its discontinuity point. That is where it is with a discontinuity point of 1 rotation and no zero offset. A discontinuity point of 0.5 rotations moves it to 180° from the line on the casing. The line itself does not move. A zero offset moves it too: see [Zero offsets and the discontinuity point](#zero-offsets-and-the-discontinuity-point). If the encoder passes it anywhere inside the mechanism's travel, two different mechanism positions give the same reading and YAMS cannot tell them apart. An absolute encoder should only be used when careful installation guarantees that it never reaches its discontinuity point anywhere in the range of motion: * **Adequate hard stops.** The mechanism must be physically unable to leave the range. [Soft limits](/documentation/understanding/editor/config/limits-and-protection.md#withsoftlimits) are not enough: they do nothing when the robot is disabled and pushed by hand, and the encoder is read when the robot boots. * **Less than one encoder turn of travel.** The travel between the hard stops must be less than one rotation of the encoder. A 1:1 encoder on a mechanism that turns all the way round, or more, cannot meet this. * **The discontinuity point outside the travel.** On a 1:1 encoder, [`withExternalEncoderDiscontinuityPoint(Rotations.of(0.5))`](#withexternalencoderdiscontinuitypoint) should be sufficient. On a geared encoder, also install it so that the encoder never reaches its discontinuity point anywhere between the hard stops, with some margin at both ends. Move the mechanism from one hard stop to the other by hand and watch the white lines to check. {% hint style="success" %} **Without gearing, a discontinuity point of 0.5 rotations should be sufficient.** With [`withExternalEncoderDiscontinuityPoint(Rotations.of(1))`](#withexternalencoderdiscontinuitypoint) the reading goes from 0 to 360° and wraps at the line on the casing. With `Rotations.of(0.5)` it goes from -180° to 180° and wraps 180° from the line. The line on the casing does not move, only the discontinuity point does. With a [zero offset](#zero-offsets-and-the-discontinuity-point) set at the mechanism's zero, the discontinuity point is 180° from the mechanism's zero, so a 1:1 mechanism that stays within 180° of its zero never reaches it. {% endhint %} [Gearing the encoder](#withexternalencodergearing) is where this needs real care, because the encoder then turns further than the mechanism and the discontinuity point setting alone is no longer enough. [That section](#only-gear-an-absolute-encoder-if-it-cannot-wrap) has its own animation. **Supported on every motor controller.** Every controller accepts an external encoder, but only ones it can read itself. An encoder from another vendor cannot be used. | TalonFX | TalonFXS | SPARK MAX / Flex | Thrifty Nova | | --------------------- | --------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- | | ✅ `CANcoder`, `CANdi` | ✅ `CANcoder`, `CANdi` | ✅ its own absolute, alternate or external encoder | ✅ data port absolute or quadrature encoder, Thrifty CAN encoder | ## `withExternalEncoderGearing` The reduction between the mechanism and the external encoder, for an encoder that is not mounted 1:1 on the mechanism's output. The default is 1:1. ```java .withExternalEncoderGearing(new MechanismGearing(GearBox.fromStages("1:2"))) .withExternalEncoderGearing(0.5) ``` The number is how many times the encoder turns for one turn of the mechanism: `2` means the encoder turns twice as far as the mechanism. It appears on the right of the diagram at the top of this page. It throws a `SmartMotorControllerConfigurationException` if no external encoder is configured. ### Only gear an absolute encoder if it cannot wrap Gearing an absolute encoder up gives finer resolution, but it also uses up the encoder's one turn faster, so it reaches its [discontinuity point](#keep-the-discontinuity-point-outside-the-travel) sooner. Encoder gearing can and should be used on an absolute encoder **only** when careful installation guarantees that it never wraps anywhere in the range of motion. The [three conditions for every absolute encoder](#keep-the-discontinuity-point-outside-the-travel) still apply, and the second one gets stricter: the travel between the hard stops, **multiplied by the gearing**, must be less than one rotation. In the animation, 120° x 2 = 240° fits and 120° x 4 = 480° does not. If you cannot guarantee that, mount the encoder 1:1 on the mechanism's output, where a discontinuity point of 0.5 rotations should be sufficient. {% hint style="warning" %} YAMS reports a warning when the gearing makes the encoder turn further than the mechanism. It is safe to ignore **only** when all three conditions are met. {% endhint %} **Supported on:** every supported motor controller. ## `withExternalEncoderZeroOffset` Moves an absolute encoder's zero to the mechanism's zero. ```java .withExternalEncoderZeroOffset(Degrees.of(37)) ``` A negative offset is wrapped into the positive range for you. The distance version needs a [circumference](/documentation/understanding/editor/config/gearing-and-units.md#withmechanismcircumference). **Not supported everywhere.** On a quadrature encoder it throws a `SmartMotorControllerConfigurationException`. | TalonFX | TalonFXS | SPARK MAX / Flex | Thrifty Nova | | ------- | -------- | ------------------------- | --------------------------------- | | ✅ | ✅ | ⚠️ absolute encoders only | ⚠️ absolute and CAN encoders only | ### Zero offsets and the discontinuity point The zero offset and the discontinuity point work together, and the order matters: **the offset is applied first, and the range is applied to the result**. So the discontinuity point is measured from the encoder's zero, not from the line on the casing. | Zero offset | Discontinuity point of 1 rotation | Discontinuity point of 0.5 rotations | | --------------------------- | ----------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- | | None | Wraps where the white lines line up | Wraps 180° from where the white lines line up | | Set at the mechanism's zero | Wraps at the mechanism's zero | Wraps 180° from the mechanism's zero | What this means in practice: * **The white lines tell you where the wrap is only when there is no zero offset.** Once an offset is set, work from the mechanism's zero instead. * **Set the zero offset first, then choose the discontinuity point.** With the offset at the mechanism's zero and a discontinuity point of 0.5 rotations, a 1:1 encoder wraps as far from zero as it can, however it was installed. * **A geared encoder is still limited to one turn.** The same rule applies to the encoder's own shaft: 180° of the encoder is `180° / gearing` of the mechanism. See [Only gear an absolute encoder if it cannot wrap](#only-gear-an-absolute-encoder-if-it-cannot-wrap). #### Where each motor controller applies them The discontinuity point only moves with the zero offset because the offset is applied first. That is the case on every encoder YAMS supports: | Encoder | Zero offset applied | Discontinuity point applied | | ---------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- | | `CANcoder`, `CANdi` (TalonFX, TalonFXS) | On the encoder | On the encoder, after the offset | | SPARK absolute encoder, REV CAN encoder | On the SPARK or the encoder | On the SPARK or the encoder, after the offset | | Nova data port absolute encoder, Thrifty CAN encoder | On the Nova or the encoder | By YAMS, on the reading the device has already offset | YAMS has a unit test for this, `ZeroOffsetDiscontinuityPointTest`. With a zero offset of 90° it checks, for every one of these encoders in simulation, that 120° reads 120° with a discontinuity point of 0.5 rotations and that 300° reads 300° with 1 rotation. Neither would hold if the discontinuity point had stayed where it was. {% hint style="warning" %} **Gearing does not move the discontinuity point.** The zero offset is given in mechanism angle and converted for you, but the discontinuity point is always 0.5 or 1 rotation of the **encoder's own shaft**. On a geared encoder that is `180° / gearing` or `360° / gearing` of the mechanism from zero, not 180° or 360°. A SPARK raises an alert when gearing and a discontinuity point are set together, to say that the discontinuity point is not moved by the gearing and the wrapping will not be uniform. Take that alert seriously: see [Only gear an absolute encoder if it cannot wrap](#only-gear-an-absolute-encoder-if-it-cannot-wrap). {% endhint %} {% hint style="info" %} An offset you apply yourself is different. If you leave the encoder's zero offset unset and subtract an angle from the reading in your own code, the encoder's range has already been applied, so the discontinuity point stays where it was and only the numbers shift. {% endhint %} The order comes from the vendors' own documentation: * **CTRE** ([`MagnetSensorConfigs`](https://api.ctr-electronics.com/phoenix6/stable/java/com/ctre/phoenix6/configs/MagnetSensorConfigs.html)): the magnet offset "is added to the reported position", and the discontinuity point "determines the point at which the absolute sensor wraps around, keeping the absolute position (after offset) in the range \[x-1, x)". * **REV** ([`AbsoluteEncoderConfig`](https://codedocs.revrobotics.com/java/com/revrobotics/spark/config/absoluteencoderconfig)): the zero offset is "the position that is reported as zero", and with zero centering "the position will be reported in the range (-0.5, 0.5], instead of the default range \[0, 1)". REV does not spell out the order, but a range centered on the reported zero means the wrap is half a turn from the offset zero. REVLib deprecates zero centering in 2027 in favor of `rangeOffset`, which is what YAMS gives a SPARK's absolute encoder: "Set the offset of the range about zero of the absolute encoder." ## `withExternalEncoderDiscontinuityPoint` Chooses where an absolute encoder's reading wraps. ```java .withExternalEncoderDiscontinuityPoint(Rotations.of(0.5)) // reads -180° to 180° .withExternalEncoderDiscontinuityPoint(Rotations.of(1)) // reads 0° to 360° ``` Only `0.5` and `1` rotations are accepted. Like the zero offset, it is for absolute encoders only. **Not supported everywhere.** On a quadrature encoder it throws a `SmartMotorControllerConfigurationException`. | TalonFX | TalonFXS | SPARK MAX / Flex | Thrifty Nova | | ------- | -------- | ------------------------- | --------------------------------- | | ✅ | ✅ | ⚠️ absolute encoders only | ⚠️ absolute and CAN encoders only | ## `withUseExternalFeedbackEncoder` Chooses which encoder the closed loop controller follows. The default is `true`: the external encoder, when there is one. ```java .withUseExternalFeedbackEncoder(false) ``` ## `withFeedbackSynchronizationThreshold` When the loop follows the built in encoder, re-seeds it from the external encoder whenever the two disagree by more than this. ```java .withUseExternalFeedbackEncoder(false) .withFeedbackSynchronizationThreshold(Degrees.of(2)) ``` It is not available for distance mechanisms: it throws a `SmartMotorControllerConfigurationException` if a circumference is set. **Not supported everywhere.** Where it is not supported it throws an `IllegalArgumentException` on a TalonFX or TalonFXS, and a `SmartMotorControllerConfigurationException` on a SPARK. | TalonFX | TalonFXS | SPARK MAX / Flex | Thrifty Nova | | ------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------- | | ❌ | ❌ | ⚠️ only with an exponential profile or an [LQR controller](/documentation/understanding/editor/lqr-controllers.md) | ⚠️ only in closed loop mode | ## Code reference * [`SmartMotorControllerConfig`](https://yet-another-software-suite.github.io/YAMS/javadocs/yams/motorcontrollers/SmartMotorControllerConfig.html)

pages.title: Simulation
pages.content: # Simulation These options only change what happens in simulation. The real robot ignores them. Every option on this page is supported on every supported motor controller. ## `withSimClosedLoopController` and `withSimFeedforward` A second set of gains used only in simulation. They take the same arguments, including [slots](/documentation/understanding/editor/config/closed-loop-control.md#slots), as [`withClosedLoopController`](/documentation/understanding/editor/config/closed-loop-control.md#withclosedloopcontroller) and [`withFeedforward`](/documentation/understanding/editor/config/feedforward.md#withfeedforward). ```java .withClosedLoopController(4, 0, 0.2) .withSimClosedLoopController(12, 0, 0) .withFeedforward(new ArmFeedforward(0.15, 0.35, 1.2)) .withSimFeedforward(new ArmFeedforward(0, 0.3, 1.2)) ``` [Simulation-only PID + feedforward](/documentation/understanding/editor/simulation-only-pid-+-feedforward.md) explains why the two usually differ. ## `withSimStartingPosition` Where the simulated mechanism starts, when that should differ from the real [starting position](/documentation/understanding/editor/config/encoders.md#withstartingposition). ```java .withSimStartingPosition(Degrees.of(45)) ``` It is most useful with an absolute encoder: the real robot reads its position from the encoder, and simulation needs to be told one. ## `withMomentOfInertia` How hard the simulated load is to spin up. It is only needed when a `SmartMotorController` is simulated on its own. A mechanism class works it out from the mechanism's length and mass. ```java .withMomentOfInertia(KilogramSquareMeters.of(0.02)) .withMomentOfInertia(Inches.of(4), Pounds.of(1)) // a rod of this length and weight ``` ## `withSimulationPeriod` How often the simulated physics are stepped. The default is 20 ms, and it is independent of [`withClosedLoopControlPeriod`](/documentation/understanding/editor/config/closed-loop-control.md#withclosedloopcontrolperiod). ```java .withSimulationPeriod(Milliseconds.of(5)) ``` Each `simIterate()` call steps the physics by exactly this period, so it must match how often `simIterate()` is called. To step every 1 ms, as fast as a closed loop on the motor controller runs, call it from a `Notifier`: see [How do I run a high fidelity simulation?](/documentation/how-to-simulation-and-logging/how-do-i-run-a-high-fidelity-simulation.md) ## Running the simulation A mechanism class steps its motor's simulation for you. A `SmartMotorController` used without one needs `simIterate()` called from `simulationPeriodic()`: see [simulation without a mechanism](/documentation/understanding/editor.md#simulation-without-a-mechanism). Every simulated motor also draws from the shared [battery simulation](/documentation/understanding/battery-simulation.md). ## Code reference * [`SmartMotorControllerConfig`](https://yet-another-software-suite.github.io/YAMS/javadocs/yams/motorcontrollers/SmartMotorControllerConfig.html)

pages.title: Simulation-only PID + feedforward
pages.content:
# Simulation-only PID + feedforward

Simulation is not exactly 1:1 to the real robot, no matter how much we wish it was. Therefore it is useful to setup a sim-only PID and FF value that will mimic the robot fairly well.

## Configure this in YAMS

```java
SmartMotorControllerConfig smcConfig = new SmartMotorControllerConfig(this)
  .withControlMode(ControlMode.CLOSED_LOOP)
  // Feedback Constants (PID Constants)
  .withClosedLoopController(50, 0, 0)
  .withSimClosedLoopController(50, 0, 0)
  // Feedforward Constants
  .withFeedforward(new ArmFeedforward(0, 0, 0))
  .withSimFeedforward(new ArmFeedforward(0, 0, 0))
```

pages.title: Limiting power consumption
pages.content: # Limiting power consumption ## Current limits There are two types of currents involved in a `SmartMotorController`, the **Supply** current and the **Stator** current. * The current input of the motor controller is the **Supply** current. * The current output of the motor controller is the **Stator** current. {% hint style="danger" %} Some motor controllers, like SparkMax and SparkFlex, only support a stator current limit. `SparkWrapper` throws a `SmartMotorControllerConfigurationException` if you set a supply current limit. {% endhint %} CTRE has excellent documentation explaining the relationship between the supply and stator currents. {% embed url="" %} If your mechanism interacts with a game element or has a chance of getting stuck a current limit **WILL** cause the mechanism to stutter until the current is back below the limit. This can cause strains on the mechanism as it constantly starts then stops but it could save your motor controller and prevent brownouts because your mechanism will not be able to pull more power than necessary. ### Setting current limits in YAMS ```java SmartMotorControllerConfig motorConfig = new SmartMotorControllerConfig(this) .withStatorCurrentLimit(Amps.of(200)) // Current to the motor .withSupplyCurrentLimit(Amps.of(40)) // Current to the motor controller ``` ## Ramp rates Ramp rates is the minimum time it takes for a motor to go from 0% to 100% power to the motor. {% hint style="info" %} A ramp rate is the last thing to reach for. It delays everything the motor does, which makes the robot seem "slow" or "delayed". A mechanism that takes too much power when it starts moving is better fixed, in this order, with a [motion profile](/documentation/understanding/editor/config/motion-profiles.md) if one suits it, then a supply current limit where the motor controller has one, then a stator current limit where it does not. Use a ramp rate only if none of those is enough. {% endhint %} There are two ramp rates defined in motor controllers. * Closed loop ramp rate * Open loop ramp rate These ramp rates are applied whenever the motor controller is in the appropriate mode. So the **closed loop ramp rate** is used when the motor controller **PID** is used. The **open loop ramp rate** is used when the dutycycle or voltage control is used. {% hint style="warning" %} The Thrifty Nova has a single ramp rate for open and closed loop control. `NovaWrapper` throws a `SmartMotorControllerConfigurationException` if the two ramp rates differ, so set only one of them, or both to the same value. {% endhint %} ### Setting ramp rates in YAMS ```java SmartMotorControllerConfig motorConfig = new SmartMotorControllerConfig(this) .withClosedLoopRampRate(Seconds.of(0.25)) // 0.25 seconds minimum .withOpenLoopRampRate(Seconds.of(0.25)) // 0.25 seconds minimum ``` ## Testing brownout scenarios in simulation YAMS combines the current draw of every simulated mechanism into one shared battery model, so simulated voltage sag reflects the *whole* robot pulling power at once, not just one mechanism in isolation. That makes simulation the place to choose your limits: run the busiest moment of your match, watch the battery voltage, and lower the limits on the biggest loads until the dip is acceptable. {% stepper %} {% step %} #### Find the worst moment In simulation, do the things that happen together in a match: accelerate the drive, spin up the shooter, raise the elevator. Graph the battery voltage and each motor's `current/supply`. {% endstep %} {% step %} #### Start with the biggest load The drive is usually the largest draw, so limiting it does the most. Then the next largest. {% endstep %} {% step %} #### Limit each load in this order Stop at the first thing that brings the dip under control: 1. A [motion profile](/documentation/understanding/editor/config/motion-profiles.md), if one suits the mechanism, so it asks for less current in the first place. 2. A supply current limit, where the motor controller has one. 3. A stator current limit, where it does not. SPARK MAX and SPARK Flex have no supply limit. 4. A ramp rate, only if nothing else works. It slows everything the motor does. {% endstep %} {% step %} #### Tune the limits live At `TelemetryVerbosity.HIGH`, `current/limit/supply` and `current/limit/stator` are tunable under `NT:/Tuning/`. Change them while the simulation runs and watch the dip shrink. See [Live tuning](/documentation/understanding/live-tuning.md). {% endstep %} {% step %} #### Check the mechanism still does its job A limit that is too low makes the mechanism slow or stalls it. Lower it until the voltage is acceptable, not further. {% endstep %} {% endstepper %} See [Battery Simulation](/documentation/understanding/battery-simulation.md) for how each mechanism loads the battery, and how to enable realistic discharge over a match to reproduce brownout-prone scenarios before they happen on the field.

pages.title: Exponential profiles
pages.content: # Exponential profiles ## What is a motion profile? A motion profile is a trajectory that defines how a mechanism should move from one position to another over time. Instead of commanding a mechanism to instantly jump to a target position (which would require infinite acceleration), motion profiles generate a smooth path that respects the physical limitations of your system. Motion profiles output a series of intermediate setpoints (position and velocity) that your closed-loop controller tracks. This results in: * **Predictable motion** - You know exactly how long a movement will take * **Smooth transitions** - No jerky movements that stress mechanical components * **Controlled acceleration** - Prevents excessive current draw and brownouts ## Trapezoidal vs exponential profiles ### Trapezoidal profiles Trapezoidal profiles are the most common type. The name comes from the trapezoidal shape of the velocity-time graph. **Key characteristics:** * Constant acceleration until max velocity is reached * Cruise at max velocity (if distance is long enough) * Constant deceleration to stop at target * Assumes unlimited torque during acceleration phases **When trapezoidal profiles struggle:** * When a disturbance knocks the mechanism off the profile * When the motor cannot actually provide the commanded acceleration * When current limiting reduces available torque ### Exponential profiles Exponential profiles model how DC motors actually behave. Instead of assuming constant acceleration, they account for the motor's torque-speed curve and the system's physical dynamics. **Key characteristics:** * Acceleration naturally decreases as velocity increases (following motor physics) * Models the mechanism with a kV (velocity constant) and a kA (acceleration constant) * More accurately represents what the motor can actually achieve * Better disturbance rejection {% hint style="info" %} Exponential profiles are named for the exponential approach to maximum velocity, which mirrors the natural response of a first-order system like a DC motor. {% endhint %} ## The physics behind exponential profiles DC motors produce torque proportional to current. However, as the motor spins faster, back-EMF reduces the effective voltage across the windings, which reduces current and therefore torque. The relationship is: $$V = kS + kV \cdot \omega + kA \cdot \alpha$$ Where: * **V** = Applied voltage * **kS** = Static friction voltage (voltage to overcome stiction) * **kV** = Velocity constant (volts per unit velocity) * **kA** = Acceleration constant (volts per unit acceleration) * **ω** = Angular velocity * **α** = Angular acceleration Rearranging for acceleration: $$\alpha = \frac{V - kS - kV \cdot \omega}{kA}$$ This shows that as velocity (ω) increases, the available acceleration (α) decreases. This is the fundamental insight that exponential profiles capture. ## When to use each profile type | Situation | Recommended Profile | Why | | --------------------------------------- | ------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Motor is always current-limited | Trapezoidal | Current limiting makes torque roughly constant regardless of speed | | Motor is never current-limited | Exponential | Motor follows natural torque-speed curve | | Sometimes current-limited | Hybrid (not yet in YAMS) | See [this whitepaper](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/whitepaper-trapezoidal-exponential-motion-profiling/443468/12?u=nstrike) | | Heavy mechanism with adequate motor | Exponential | Gravity/friction dominate, exponential handles disturbances better | | Lightweight mechanism | Either | Both work well when inertia is low | | Mechanism with significant disturbances | Exponential | Better recovery when knocked off profile | | Precise timing required | Trapezoidal | Deterministic duration calculation | {% hint style="success" %} **Rule of thumb**: If your mechanism works well with trapezoidal profiles, keep using them. Switch to exponential profiles when you encounter disturbance rejection issues or when you want the profile to better match your motor's capabilities. {% endhint %} ## Exponential profiles in YAMS YAMS provides `ExponentialProfilePIDController` (`yams.core.math.ExponentialProfilePIDController`), which combines an exponential motion profile with a PID controller and has factory methods for the profile's constraints. In a `SmartMotorControllerConfig` you set the PID gains with `withClosedLoopController(kP, kI, kD)` and the profile with `withExponentialProfile(constraints)`, instead of a trapezoidal profile (`withTrapezoidalProfile`) or no profile at all. Exponential profiles in YAMS follow the same idea as CTRE's Motion Magic Expo, on every supported motor controller. CTRE's documentation is a good companion to this page: {% embed url="" %} ### What you set An exponential profile is defined by a kV and a kA, and those are what you tune, exactly as CTRE's documentation describes. What YAMS adds is a way to get **starting values** for them without measuring anything: you give the **maximum voltage** and one of two descriptions of the mechanism, and YAMS works out a kV and a kA to start from: | You give | YAMS works out the starting kV and kA from | | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Maximum voltage, the motor, and the mechanism's moment of inertia (or its mass and drum radius) | The motor and the load it has to move | | Maximum voltage, a maximum velocity and a maximum acceleration | `kV = maximum voltage / maximum velocity` and `kA = maximum voltage / maximum acceleration` | The second row is the same relationship [CTRE's Motion Magic Expo documentation](https://v6.docs.ctr-electronics.com/en/latest/docs/api-reference/device-specific/talonfx/motion-magic.html#motion-magic-expo) gives: dividing the voltage by kV gives the maximum velocity of the profile, and dividing it by kA gives its maximum acceleration from a standstill. CTRE's page is the best description of exponential profiles there is, and this page is meant to agree with it. If the two ever differ, CTRE's is right. From there you adjust kV and kA directly, either [live](#refining-the-profile-live) or by passing your own with `ExponentialProfile.Constraints.fromCharacteristics(maxVoltage, kV, kA)`. `SmartMotorControllerConfig` takes all of these directly: ```java .withExponentialProfile(Volts.of(10), DCMotor.getKrakenX60(1), KilogramSquareMeters.of(0.5)) // arm or flywheel .withExponentialProfile(Volts.of(10), DCMotor.getKrakenX60(2), Kilograms.of(8), Inches.of(1)) // elevator .withExponentialProfile(Volts.of(10), RotationsPerSecond.of(2), RotationsPerSecondPerSecond.of(8)) ``` ### Creating constraints YAMS provides factory methods to create exponential profile constraints for common mechanism types: #### For elevators ```java ExponentialProfile.Constraints constraints = ExponentialProfilePIDController.createElevatorConstraints( Volts.of(12), // Maximum voltage during profile DCMotor.getNEO(2), // Motor type and quantity Pounds.of(15), // Carriage mass Inches.of(1), // Drum radius (or sprocket pitch radius) gearing // MechanismGearing object ); ``` #### For arms ```java ExponentialProfile.Constraints constraints = ExponentialProfilePIDController.createArmConstraints( Volts.of(12), // Maximum voltage during profile DCMotor.getKrakenX60(1), // Motor type and quantity Pounds.of(8), // Arm mass (at center of mass) Inches.of(18), // Arm length (to center of mass) gearing // MechanismGearing object ); ``` #### For flywheels ```java ExponentialProfile.Constraints constraints = ExponentialProfilePIDController.createFlywheelConstraints( Volts.of(12), // Maximum voltage during profile DCMotor.getFalcon500(1), // Motor type and quantity Pounds.of(2), // Flywheel mass Inches.of(2), // Flywheel radius gearing // MechanismGearing object ); ``` #### Custom constraints If the factory methods don't fit your use case, you can create constraints directly: ```java ExponentialProfile.Constraints constraints = ExponentialProfilePIDController.createConstraints( Volts.of(12), // Maximum voltage RotationsPerSecond.of(100), // Maximum velocity (kV derived) RotationsPerSecondPerSecond.of(200) // Maximum acceleration (kA derived) ); ``` ### Using with SmartMotorControllerConfig ```java SmartMotorControllerConfig config = new SmartMotorControllerConfig(this) .withControlMode(ControlMode.CLOSED_LOOP) .withClosedLoopController(30, 0, 0) // kP, kI, kD .withExponentialProfile(ExponentialProfilePIDController.createElevatorConstraints( Volts.of(12), DCMotor.getNEO(2), Pounds.of(15), Inches.of(1), gearing )) .withGearing(gearing) .withFeedforward(new ElevatorFeedforward(0, 0.5, 0, 0)) .withTelemetry("Elevator", TelemetryVerbosity.HIGH); ``` ## Tuning exponential profiles ### Step 1: Get a starting kV and kA Start with the maximum voltage and a description of the mechanism, and let YAMS work out a kV and a kA to begin with. Then tune them directly in [Refining the profile live](#refining-the-profile-live): | Option | How | Good for | | ----------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- | | The mechanism | The motor, with the moment of inertia or the mass and drum radius | A first version, and simulation | | A maximum velocity and acceleration | The fastest you want the profile to go, and the hardest you want it to accelerate | Real mechanisms: both numbers are easy to see on a graph and to adjust | | kV and kA, measured | One constant voltage test, see [Measuring kV and kA](#measuring-kv-and-ka-optional) | Starting closer to the real mechanism, so there is less to tune | {% hint style="info" %} **Start slower than you think the mechanism can go.** CTRE's advice for Motion Magic Expo is that it is safer to start from a higher kV and kA than ideal, which is a profile with a lower maximum velocity and acceleration. So if the starting values are in doubt, raise kV and kA, or start from a lower maximum velocity and acceleration, and bring them down once the mechanism follows the profile well. {% endhint %} {% hint style="warning" %} A description from the motor and the mass is theoretical. Real mechanisms have friction, cable drag and other losses, so expect to slow the profile down a little from what the numbers say. {% endhint %} ### Measuring kV and kA (optional) This is another way to get starting values, from the real mechanism instead of from a calculation. It needs only a button binding and a graph, and it gives you both from one run. {% stepper %} {% step %} #### Find kS Raise the voltage slowly from zero until the mechanism just starts to move. That voltage is kS. {% endstep %} {% step %} #### Apply a constant voltage Bind a button to a fixed voltage, well below 12 V so the mechanism does not hit a hard stop before it reaches a steady speed: ```java driver.a().whileTrue(flywheel.setVoltage(Volts.of(6))); ``` Graph `NT:/Mechanisms///mechanism/velocity` in AdvantageScope while you hold the button. Leave it in rotations per second: the profile's kV and kA are per rotation of the mechanism. {% endstep %} {% step %} #### Read the steady speed: that gives kV Once the line goes flat, read the speed. `kV = (voltage - kS) / steady speed` {% endstep %} {% step %} #### Read the time to 63%: that gives kA Find the moment the velocity reached 63% of the steady speed, and how long after the voltage was applied that was. `kA = kV x that time` {% endstep %} {% step %} #### Put them in the config ```java .withExponentialProfile(ExponentialProfile.Constraints.fromCharacteristics( 10.0, // maximum voltage the profile may ask for 2.0, // kV, volts per rotation per second 0.30 // kA, volts per rotation per second squared )) ``` {% endstep %} {% endstepper %} {% hint style="info" %} **Gravity gets in the way of this test.** On an elevator, subtract kG as well: `kV = (voltage - kS - kG) / steady speed`. On an arm the pull of gravity changes with the angle, so the speed never settles: start from `createArmConstraints(...)` and refine it live instead. {% endhint %} ### Refining the profile live This is where the profile is actually tuned, by changing kV and kA directly. However you got the starting values, YAMS stores the profile as a maximum voltage, a kV and a kA, and all three can be changed while the robot is running. {% stepper %} {% step %} #### Turn on live tuning Give the motor `TelemetryVerbosity.HIGH` and start the `Live Tuning` command. [Live tuning](/documentation/understanding/live-tuning.md) covers both. {% endstep %} {% step %} #### Graph the profile against the mechanism In AdvantageScope, put these two on one graph: * `NT:/Mechanisms///closedloop/setpoint/velocity`: what the profile asks for. * `NT:/Mechanisms///mechanism/velocity`: what the mechanism does. {% endstep %} {% step %} #### Run a move Command a move long enough for the mechanism to reach its top speed, and watch how closely the second line follows the first. {% endstep %} {% step %} #### Tune `kA` on the way up Look at the start of the move, while the mechanism is speeding up. If it falls behind the profile, raise `NT:/Tuning///closedloop/motionprofile/kA`. A higher `kA` lowers the profile's acceleration. Run the move again and repeat until it keeps up. {% endstep %} {% step %} #### Tune `kV` at top speed Look at the fastest part of the move. If the mechanism falls behind there, or never reaches the profile's top speed, raise `NT:/Tuning///closedloop/motionprofile/kV`. A higher `kV` lowers the profile's top speed. {% endstep %} {% step %} #### Speed it up if there is room If the mechanism follows the whole move easily with voltage to spare on `NT:/Mechanisms///motor/outputVoltage`, lower `kV` and `kA` a little at a time, or raise `NT:/Tuning///closedloop/motionprofile/maxInput`. Stop as soon as it starts to fall behind again, and go back one step. {% endstep %} {% step %} #### Put the tuned values in the config Live values are lost when the robot code restarts, so copy them into the config: ```java .withExponentialProfile(ExponentialProfile.Constraints.fromCharacteristics( 10.0, // maxInput: maximum voltage the profile may ask for 2.2, // kV, tuned 0.35 // kA, tuned )) ``` {% endstep %} {% endstepper %} ### Step 2: Set maximum voltage The maximum voltage determines how aggressively the profile will command the mechanism. Consider: * **12V** - Full battery voltage, most aggressive * **10V** - Leaves headroom for PID corrections * **8V** - Conservative, good for testing ### Step 3: Tune PID gains With a good feedforward ([Step 4](#step-4-add-feedforward)), the feedforward does most of the work. The PID handles: * **kP** - Corrects position error. Start low (1-5) and increase until responsive * **kI** - Usually not needed with good feedforward. Use only if steady-state error persists * **kD** - Dampens oscillations. Add if mechanism oscillates around target ### Step 4: Add feedforward The profile only plans the move. It does not drive the motor: the voltage that follows the plan comes from the feedforward and the PID. So an exponential profile still needs a full feedforward: * **kS** for friction. * **kG** for gravity, on arms and elevators. The profile does not know about gravity. * **kV and kA** for the speed and acceleration the profile asks for. ```java // For an arm .withFeedforward(new ArmFeedforward( 0.1, // kS - voltage to overcome friction 0.3, // kG - voltage to hold horizontal 1.2, // kV - voltage per unit of speed 0.05 // kA - voltage per unit of acceleration )) // For an elevator .withFeedforward(new ElevatorFeedforward( 0.1, // kS - voltage to overcome friction 0.2, // kG - voltage to counteract gravity 3.0, // kV - voltage per unit of speed 0.1 // kA - voltage per unit of acceleration )) ``` {% hint style="info" %} **The profile's kV and kA are not the feedforward's kV and kA.** The profile's pair only shape the plan. The feedforward's pair turn that plan into voltage. CTRE's Motion Magic Expo example sets both, the gain slot's `kV` and `kA` and the profile's `MotionMagicExpo_kV` and `MotionMagicExpo_kA`, and YAMS keeps them separate in the same way. [Feedforward](/documentation/understanding/editor/config/feedforward.md) covers finding the feedforward's values. {% endhint %} ## Motor controller support | Motor Controller | Trapezoidal Profile | Exponential Profile | Notes | | ------------------------ | ------------------------ | ----------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- | | TalonFX (Kraken, Falcon) | On-device (Motion Magic) | On-device (Motion Magic Expo) | Best performance | | TalonFXS | On-device (Motion Magic) | On-device (Motion Magic Expo) | Best performance | | SparkMax/SparkFlex | On-device (MAXMotion) | SystemCore | Exponential runs on the SystemCore | | Thrifty Nova | SystemCore | SystemCore | All closed loop control runs on the SystemCore | {% hint style="info" %} When exponential profiles run on the SystemCore, there's slightly more latency compared to on-device execution. However, the profile calculation is still very fast and suitable for most mechanisms. {% endhint %} ## Common issues and solutions ### Profile is too slow * Increase maximum voltage * Check that your mechanism parameters (mass, length, gearing) are accurate * Verify motor type matches actual hardware ### Profile overshoots target * Decrease kP * Add kD for damping * Slow the profile down: a profile that asks for more than the mechanism can do overshoots ### Mechanism can't keep up with profile * Your motor may be undersized for the mechanism * Reduce maximum voltage * Check for mechanical binding or excessive friction ### Profile works in sim but not on real robot * Slow the profile down: lower the maximum velocity and acceleration, or see [Refining the profile live](#refining-the-profile-live) * Account for friction with kS in feedforward * Check current limits aren't restricting torque ## Example: Complete Elevator with exponential profile ```java public class ElevatorSubsystem extends SubsystemBase { private final Distance chainPitch = Inches.of(0.25); private final int toothCount = 22; private final Mass carriageMass = Pounds.of(15); private final DCMotor motors = DCMotor.getNEO(2); private final MechanismGearing gearing = new MechanismGearing(GearBox.fromReductionStages(5, 4)); private final SmartMotorControllerConfig motorConfig = new SmartMotorControllerConfig(this) .withControlMode(ControlMode.CLOSED_LOOP) .withDrumRadius(chainPitch, toothCount) .withClosedLoopController(15, 0, 0) .withExponentialProfile(ExponentialProfilePIDController.createElevatorConstraints( Volts.of(10), // Conservative voltage for testing motors, carriageMass, chainPitch.times(toothCount).div(2 * Math.PI), gearing )) .withSimClosedLoopController(15, 0, 0) .withFeedforward(new ElevatorFeedforward(0.1, 0.25, 0, 0)) .withSimFeedforward(new ElevatorFeedforward(0, 0.2, 0, 0)) .withGearing(gearing) .withZeroPower(MotorMode.BRAKE) .withStatorCurrentLimit(Amps.of(40)) .withSoftLimits(Meters.of(0), Meters.of(1.2)) .withStartingPosition(Meters.of(0)) .withTelemetry("ElevatorMotor", TelemetryVerbosity.HIGH); private final SparkMax leftSpark = new SparkMax(CANPorts.fromBusId(1), 1, MotorType.kBrushless); private final SparkMax rightSpark = new SparkMax(CANPorts.fromBusId(1), 2, MotorType.kBrushless); private final SmartMotorController motor = new SparkWrapper( leftSpark, motors, motorConfig.withFollowers(Pair.of(rightSpark, true)) ); private final Elevator elevator = new Elevator( new ElevatorConfig() .withHardLimits(Meters.of(-0.05), Meters.of(1.3)) .withCarriageWeight(carriageMass) .withTelemetry("Elevator", TelemetryVerbosity.HIGH), motor ); public Command goToHeight(Distance height) { return elevator.setHeight(height); } @Override public void periodic() { elevator.updateTelemetry(); } @Override public void simulationPeriodic() { elevator.simIterate(); } } ``` ## Further reading * [CTRE Motion Magic Expo Documentation](https://v6.docs.ctr-electronics.com/en/latest/docs/api-reference/device-specific/talonfx/motion-magic.html#motion-magic-expo) - CTRE's explanation of exponential profiles * [How do I use Exponential Profiles?](/documentation/how-to-motor-controllers-and-sensors/how-do-i-use-exponential-profiles.md) - Quick how-to guide * [Trapezoidal/Exponential Motion Profiling Whitepaper](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/whitepaper-trapezoidal-exponential-motion-profiling/443468/12?u=nstrike) - Advanced hybrid profiling techniques * [WPILib Tuning Guide](https://docs.wpilib.org/en/stable/docs/software/advanced-controls/introduction/tuning-turret.html) - General PID and feedforward tuning
