pages.title: Swerve Input Stream
pages.content: # Swerve Input Stream `SwerveInputStream` bridges raw joystick axes (each in the range `[-1, 1]`) and the field-relative `ChassisVelocities` (WPILib 2027's name for `ChassisSpeeds`) that [`SwerveDrive.setFieldRelativeChassisSpeeds(...)`](/documentation/understanding/swerve-drive.md) expects. It implements `Supplier`, so once built it is read with `get()` every loop by the command that drives the robot. Import it from the package that matches your vendordep: `yams.commands2.swerve.SwerveInputStream` (Commands v2) or `yams.commands3.swerve.SwerveInputStream` (Commands v3). The API is the same in both. In C++ it is `yams::mechanisms::swerve::utility::SwerveInputStream` from `yams/mechanisms/swerve/utility/SwerveInputStream.hpp`, with the same methods in PascalCase (`Of`, `WithDeadband`, `Get`, ...). {% hint style="warning" %} The output is **field relative**, even with `withRobotRelative()`. Drive with it through `setFieldRelativeChassisSpeeds(...)`, not `SwerveDrive.drive(...)`, which expects robot-relative speeds. If you do want `drive(...)`, convert it first: `drive.drive(() -> input.get().toRobotRelative(drive.getGyroRotation3d().toRotation2d()))`. {% endhint %} ## Building a stream `SwerveInputStream.of(drive, x, y)` is the base factory, translation axes only. `SwerveInputStream.of(drive, x, y, rot)` (or the matching constructor) adds an angular velocity axis, and the `new SwerveInputStream(drive, x, y, headingX, headingY)` constructor adds heading axes for point-and-hold control instead. `drive` is your YAMS `SwerveDrive`. From there, `with*()` methods layer on deadbanding, scaling, non-linear response, and alliance-relative flipping: {% tabs %} {% tab title="Commands v2" %} ```java NiDsXboxController driver = new NiDsXboxController(0); SwerveInputStream input = SwerveInputStream.of(drive, () -> -driver.getLeftY(), () -> -driver.getLeftX()) .withControllerRotationAxis(() -> -driver.getRightX()) .withDeadband(0.05) .withScaleTranslation(0.8) .withScaleRotation(0.6) .withMaximumLinearVelocity(MetersPerSecond.of(4.5)) .withMaximumAngularVelocity(DegreesPerSecond.of(360)) .withCubeTranslationControllerAxis() .withAllianceRelativeControl(); // SwerveInputStream output is field relative. setDefaultCommand(run(() -> drive.setFieldRelativeChassisSpeeds(input.get()))); ``` {% endtab %} {% tab title="Commands v3" %} ```java // In a teleop opmode. robot.drive is the swerve Mechanism; getSwerveDrive() returns its YAMS SwerveDrive. var controller = robot.xboxController; robot.drive.setInputStream(SwerveInputStream.of( robot.drive.getSwerveDrive(), () -> -controller.getLeftY(), () -> -controller.getLeftX(), () -> -controller.getRightX()) .withDeadband(0.05) .withCubeTranslationControllerAxis() .withAllianceRelativeControl()); robot.drive.setDefaultCommand(robot.drive.driveInputStream()); ``` The Mechanism's drive command reads the active stream every loop: ```java public Command driveInputStream() { return run(coroutine -> { while (true) { drive.setFieldRelativeChassisSpeeds(inputStream.get()); coroutine.yield(); } }).named("Swerve Drive Input Stream"); } ``` {% endtab %} {% tab title="C++" %} ```cpp #include "yams/mechanisms/swerve/utility/SwerveInputStream.hpp" using namespace yams::mechanisms::swerve::utility; // Member of your subsystem. SwerveInputStream<4> m_driveStream = SwerveInputStream<4>::Of(m_drive, [this]{ return -m_driverController.GetLeftY(); }, [this]{ return -m_driverController.GetLeftX(); }) .WithControllerRotationAxis([this]{ return -m_driverController.GetRightX(); }) .WithDeadband(0.05) .WithScaleTranslation(0.8); // In Periodic(). SwerveInputStream output is field relative. void Periodic() override { m_drive.SetFieldRelativeChassisSpeeds(m_driveStream.Get()); } ``` C++ has `Of(drive, x, y)` plus constructors taking a rotation axis or two heading axes. {% endtab %} {% endtabs %} ## Mutations apply immediately Every `with*()` method mutates the stream in place and returns `this`; none of them return a new copy. That matters because a `SwerveInputStream` is usually stored once and read by a long-lived drive command. Calling a mutator on that same reference later, from anywhere else in your code, changes what the already-running default command does on its very next loop; you never need to rebuild the stream or call `setDefaultCommand(...)` again. For example, auto-aim can be retargeted on the fly from a completely separate button binding, without touching the drive command at all: ```java input.withAim(() -> FieldConstants.SPEAKER_POSE, driver::getRightBumperButton); setDefaultCommand(run(() -> drive.setFieldRelativeChassisSpeeds(input.get()))); new Trigger(driver::getLeftBumperButton).onTrue(Commands.runOnce(() -> input.withAim(() -> FieldConstants.AMP_POSE, driver::getRightBumperButton))); ``` Pressing the left bumper swaps the aim target from the speaker to the amp. The default command keeps reading the exact same `input` instance; it just starts computing `ChassisVelocities` toward a different pose the moment the mutation happens. {% hint style="info" %} `clone()` is the one method here that doesn't mutate: it returns an independent copy, useful for deriving a second variant of a stream from a shared base configuration without one affecting the other. See [Copying a Stream](#copying-a-stream) below. {% endhint %} ## From stick to velocity Every loop, `get()` runs the stick values through the same steps, in this order: | Step | Method | What it does | | ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Deadband | `withDeadband(...)` | Ignores small values near the center, then rescales the rest to the full range. | | Scale | `withScaleTranslation(...)`, `withScaleRotation(...)` | Multiplies by a constant. | | Cube | `withCubeTranslationControllerAxis()`, `withCubeRotationControllerAxis()` | Raises to the third power for finer control near the center. | | Alliance flip | `withAllianceRelativeControl()` | Turns translation 180 degrees on the red alliance. | | Maximum velocity | `withMaximumLinearVelocity(...)`, `withMaximumAngularVelocity(...)` | Turns the result into meters per second and radians per second. | {% hint style="warning" %} The scale is applied **before** the cube. With `withScaleTranslation(0.8)` and the cube enabled, a full stick gives `0.8³ = 0.512` of the maximum velocity, not `0.8`. {% endhint %} ## Velocity limits The maximum velocities are what a fully pushed stick produces. ### `withMaximumLinearVelocity` `withMaximumLinearVelocity(LinearVelocity)` sets the top driving speed. ```java input.withMaximumLinearVelocity(MetersPerSecond.of(4.5)); ``` ### `withMaximumAngularVelocity` `withMaximumAngularVelocity(AngularVelocity)` sets the top turn rate. ```java input.withMaximumAngularVelocity(DegreesPerSecond.of(360)); ``` {% hint style="info" %} A stream copies `SwerveDriveConfig.withMaximumChassisSpeed(...)`'s value (if set) into its own maximum fields once, at construction time; if the drive has no maximum configured, the stream starts from its own defaults (4 m/s, 1 rotation/s) instead. Calling `withMaximumLinearVelocity(...)`/`withMaximumAngularVelocity(...)` afterward overrides that starting value for this stream only and takes effect immediately; the drive's config is never re-checked after construction, so the override sticks. {% endhint %} ## Controller axes Both methods set or replace a rotation source after construction. That is useful when a stream starts out with `SwerveInputStream.of(drive, x, y)` (no rotation source at all) and gains one later. ### `withControllerRotationAxis` `withControllerRotationAxis(DoubleSupplier)` sets the axis that says how fast the robot turns. ```java input.withControllerRotationAxis(() -> -driver.getRightX()); ``` ### `withControllerHeadingAxis` `withControllerHeadingAxis(DoubleSupplier, DoubleSupplier)` sets the pair of axes whose direction becomes a target heading. It does nothing on its own: the heading is used by [`withHeadingControl`](#withheadingcontrol) in `HEADING` mode. The heading axes only replace rotation. The left stick keeps driving the robot, so it can move one way while facing another: ```java input.withControllerHeadingAxis(() -> -driver.getRightX(), () -> -driver.getRightY()); ``` ## Deadband `withDeadband(double)` (an alias for `deadband(double)`) applies the same deadband to every axis before any scaling or cubing happens. `0` clears it. ```java input.withDeadband(0.05); ``` ## Axis scaling The scale methods multiply the stick output by a constant in `(0, 1]`, useful for a "slow mode" that doesn't require re-mapping the physical stick range. ### `withScaleTranslation` `withScaleTranslation(double)` scales the driving speed. ```java input.withScaleTranslation(0.5); // e.g. bound to a "slow mode" trigger ``` ### `withScaleRotation` `withScaleRotation(double)` scales the turn rate. ```java input.withScaleRotation(0.5); ``` ## Non-linear (cubic) response Cubing gives finer control near the center of the stick without sacrificing full speed at the edges. Each method also has a `BooleanSupplier` overload to toggle the effect live. ### `withCubeTranslationControllerAxis` `withCubeTranslationControllerAxis()` cubes the translation magnitude. ```java input.withCubeTranslationControllerAxis(); ``` ### `withCubeRotationControllerAxis` `withCubeRotationControllerAxis()` cubes the rotation axis. ```java input.withCubeRotationControllerAxis(driver::getBButton); // only while B is held ``` ## Modes are chosen automatically A stream is always in exactly one of four internal modes: `ANGULAR_VELOCITY` (the default), `TRANSLATION_ONLY`, `HEADING`, or `AIM`. You never select a mode directly. `get()` re-derives it on every call from which optional pieces are configured and whether the relevant `BooleanSupplier` trigger currently reports true, then transitions cleanly (resetting the relevant PID controllers) if the mode changed since the last call. Mode priority, highest to lowest: `TRANSLATION_ONLY` > `AIM` > `HEADING` > `ANGULAR_VELOCITY`. `getCurrentModeName()` returns the mode the last `get()` used. `HEADING`, `AIM` and `TRANSLATION_ONLY` turn the robot with the rotation controller from `SwerveDriveConfig.withRotationController(...)`, so configure one before using them. {% hint style="info" %} `SwerveInputStream` used to have a `DRIVE_TO_POSE` mode and a matching `atTargetPose(...)` method; both have been removed. Use [`SwerveDrive.driveToPose(...)`](/documentation/understanding/swerve-drive.md#auto-align) for auto-align instead. {% endhint %} ### Heading-snap control #### `withHeadingControl` `withHeadingControl(trigger)` enables `HEADING` while `trigger` reports true, snapping to a heading derived from [`withControllerHeadingAxis(x, y)`](#withcontrollerheadingaxis) instead of rotating at a velocity. The robot stops turning while the heading stick is inside the deadband. ```java SwerveInputStream headingStream = input.clone() .withControllerHeadingAxis(() -> -driver.getRightX(), () -> -driver.getRightY()) .withHeadingControl(driver::getAButton); ``` #### `withHeading` `withHeading(Supplier)` faces a field-relative heading from code instead of a stick, and replaces any controller heading axes. ```java input.withHeading(() -> Degrees.of(90)) .withHeadingControl(driver::getAButton); ``` ### Aim at a target `withAim(Supplier targetPose, BooleanSupplier trigger)` enables `AIM` while `trigger` reports true, rotating to face `targetPose` while translation keeps working normally. See [Mutations Apply Immediately](#mutations-apply-immediately) above for an example that retargets it live. ```java input.withAim(() -> FieldConstants.SPEAKER_POSE, driver::getRightBumperButton); ``` `withAim` points the front of the robot at the pose it is given. The options below refine that. They are the same in Commands v2 and Commands v3, and C++ has each one in PascalCase. {% hint style="info" %} Aiming at a target is not the same as shooting on the move. The stream turns the robot, and it knows nothing about your shooter or how long a shot is in the air. [How do I shoot on the move?](/documentation/how-to-mechanisms/how-do-i-shoot-on-the-move.md) explains what these options cover and what you still have to work out yourself. {% endhint %} #### Aim lookahead `withAimLookahead(Time)` aims from where the robot will be after a delay, instead of where it is now. The pose is moved along the robot's field relative velocity by that time before the direction to the target is worked out. A game piece leaves the robot a moment after the aim was calculated: the camera, the loop, the motors and the feed all take time, and the robot keeps moving through all of it. Add those delays together for a starting value, then tune it. It is often 100 to 200 milliseconds. ```java input.withAimLookahead(Milliseconds.of(150)); ``` The lookahead assumes the robot keeps its current velocity, so it works best while driving in a straight line. #### Aim feedforward `withAimFeedforward(SimpleMotorFeedforward)` adds a feedforward to the aim rotation. The rotation controller only reacts to heading error, so while the robot drives past a target it trails a little behind. The feedforward is calculated from the robot's current angular velocity to the angular velocity the controller asks for, and its result is added to that angular velocity. ```java input.withAimFeedforward(new SimpleMotorFeedforward(0, 0.1)); ``` **How to use it:** hold the aim button and drive sideways past the target while you watch the heading, or [`aimLock`](#aim-lock). If the robot trails the target, start with a small `kV` and raise it until it keeps up. Too much makes the heading overshoot and wobble. `kS` and `kA` can usually stay at 0. The feedforward does not remove the lag completely, and it is no substitute for a rotation controller that is tuned well. Tune the controller in [`SwerveDriveConfig`](/documentation/understanding/swerve-drive/swerve-drive-config.md) first. #### Aim heading offset `withAimHeadingOffset(Rotation2d)` rotates the aim heading, for a shooter that does not point out of the front of the robot. The offset is counter-clockwise positive. `withAimHeadingOffset(Rotation2d, BooleanSupplier)` only applies it while the supplier is true. ```java // The shooter points out of the back of the robot. input.withAimHeadingOffset(Rotation2d.fromDegrees(180)); ``` **How to use it:** the offset is the angle from the front of the robot to the direction the shooter points, counter-clockwise positive. A shooter out of the back is 180 degrees, out of the left side is 90 degrees, and out of the right side is -90 degrees. A small offset, such as 2 degrees, also works as a trim for a shooter that throws slightly to one side. The version with a `BooleanSupplier` lets one stream serve two mechanisms: aim the front at a target for an intake, and turn the offset on while a shooter on the back is in use. #### Aim lock `aimLock(Angle)` returns a `Trigger` that is true while the robot is aiming and its heading is within the tolerance of the aim heading. `isAimLocked(Angle)` gives the same answer as a plain `boolean`. Use them to decide when to feed a game piece. ```java Trigger aimed = input.aimLock(Degrees.of(2)); ``` The lock only updates while the stream is being read, and it is false whenever aiming is not enabled. C++ has `IsAimLocked(tolerance)` and no trigger version. #### Building your own aim Two methods expose the pieces the aim mode is made of: | Method | Returns | | --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `getTargetVector(Pose2d)` | The field relative vector from the robot to a target, from the looked ahead position if a lookahead is set. | | `calculateAngularVelocity(Angle)` | The angular velocity that turns the robot to a heading, from the rotation controller and the aim feedforward. | ### Translation only `withTranslationOnly(trigger)` enables `TRANSLATION_ONLY` while `trigger` reports true, locking the current heading and suppressing rotation entirely: ```java input.withTranslationOnly(driver::getStartButton); ``` ## Robot-relative control By default the translation axes are field relative. `withRobotRelative()` treats them as robot relative instead, so pushing the stick forward drives toward the robot's front. The stream still outputs **field-relative** `ChassisVelocities` (it converts using the current heading), so the drive command does not change. The `withRobotRelative(BooleanSupplier)` overload toggles it live, e.g. while a button is held. ```java input.withRobotRelative(driver::getXButton); // robot-relative while X is held ``` ## Alliance-relative control `withAllianceRelativeControl()` flips the field-relative translation 180 degrees on the Red alliance, so "forward" always means away from your own driver station regardless of which side you're on. `withAllianceRelativeControl(BooleanSupplier)` toggles it live. ```java input.withAllianceRelativeControl(); ``` {% hint style="info" %} `withAllianceRelativeControl()` and `withRobotRelative()` can both be set. While robot-relative control is active, alliance flipping is skipped. {% endhint %} ## Translation heading offset `withTranslationHeadingOffset(Rotation2d)` rotates the translation direction by a fixed angle before it's output, useful when a secondary driver's "forward" should map to something other than the robot's own forward. `withTranslationHeadingOffset(Rotation2d, BooleanSupplier)` only applies it while the supplier is true. ```java input.withTranslationHeadingOffset(Rotation2d.fromDegrees(90)); ``` ## Center of rotation The stream outputs a rotation rate, and the drive decides which point the robot rotates around. That point is not part of the stream: it is `SwerveDriveConfig.withCenterOfRotation(...)`. The default is the center of the robot. ```java // 0, 0 is the center of the robot. X is forward and Y is left. SwerveDriveConfig config = new SwerveDriveConfig(this, fl, fr, bl, br) .withCenterOfRotation(Meters.of(0.3), Meters.of(0.3)); // the front left corner ``` Like the stream, the config is mutable, and the drive reads the center of rotation every loop. Changing it on the running drive's config takes effect on the next loop, for example to pivot around a corner while a button is held: ```java new Trigger(driver::getLeftBumperButton) .onTrue(Commands.runOnce(() -> drive.getConfig().withCenterOfRotation(Meters.of(0.3), Meters.of(0.3)))) .onFalse(Commands.runOnce(() -> drive.getConfig().withCenterOfRotation(Meters.of(0), Meters.of(0)))); ``` ## Copying a stream `clone()` is the only method on this page that doesn't mutate the original; it returns an independent copy that shares the base stream's configuration at the moment it was called. Changing the copy afterward, or changing the original, doesn't affect the other. A clone has no [telemetry](#telemetry-and-live-tuning); call `withTelemetry` on it if it needs its own. ```java SwerveInputStream headingStream = input.clone(); ``` ## Telemetry and live tuning Telemetry is off until you call `withTelemetry(name, verbosity)` on a stream. It publishes every time the stream is read with `get()`, so there is nothing to call each loop. `getTelemetry()` returns the stream's `SwerveInputStreamTelemetry` as an `Optional`. | Verbosity | Publishes | | --------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `LOW` | The current drive mode | | `MID` | Also the stream's configuration, read-only | | `HIGH` | Also editable copies of the configuration, and a `Live Tuning` command on the dashboard | Call `withTelemetry` last, after the rest of the configuration, so the dashboard starts with the configured values. Calling it again replaces the stream's telemetry, and `getTelemetry().get().close()` stops publishing it, e.g. when replacing a stream with another of the same name. {% tabs %} {% tab title="Commands v2" %} ```java SwerveInputStream driveStream = SwerveInputStream.of(drive, () -> -controller.getLeftY(), () -> -controller.getLeftX()) .withControllerRotationAxis(() -> -controller.getRightX()) .withDeadband(0.05) .withScaleTranslation(0.8) .withTelemetry("Driver", TelemetryVerbosity.HIGH); // SwerveInputStream output is field relative. swerve.setDefaultCommand(swerve.run(() -> drive.setFieldRelativeChassisSpeeds(driveStream.get()))); ``` The `Live Tuning` command is a Commands v2 `Command`. {% endtab %} {% tab title="Commands v3" %} ```java // In a teleop opmode. robot.drive.setInputStream(SwerveInputStream.of(robot.drive.getSwerveDrive(), () -> -controller.getLeftY(), () -> -controller.getLeftX(), () -> -controller.getRightX()) .withDeadband(0.05) .withScaleTranslation(0.8) .withTelemetry("Driver", TelemetryVerbosity.HIGH)); robot.drive.setDefaultCommand(robot.drive.driveInputStream()); ``` The `Live Tuning` command is a Commands v3 `Command`, published through `CommandTunable`. When an opmode replaces the active stream, close the old stream's telemetry first: ```java public void setInputStream(SwerveInputStream inputStream) { if (this.inputStream != null) { this.inputStream.getTelemetry().ifPresent(SwerveInputStreamTelemetry::close); } this.inputStream = inputStream; } ``` {% endtab %} {% tab title="C++" %} ```cpp SwerveInputStream<4> m_driveStream = SwerveInputStream<4>::Of(m_drive, [this]{ return -m_driverController.GetLeftY(); }, [this]{ return -m_driverController.GetLeftX(); }) .WithControllerRotationAxis([this]{ return -m_driverController.GetRightX(); }) .WithDeadband(0.05) .WithScaleTranslation(0.8) .WithTelemetry("Driver", SwerveDriveConfig::TelemetryVerbosity::HIGH); ``` C++ has the same API: `WithTelemetry(name, verbosity)` and `GetTelemetry()`, which returns a `std::optional>>`. The verbosities are `SwerveDriveConfig::TelemetryVerbosity`: `LOW`, `MEDIUM` (Java's `MID`) and `HIGH`, and `NONE` turns telemetry off. The `Live Tuning` command is a Commands v2 `Command`, from `GetLiveTuningCommand()`. The stream is a value type, so ownership works differently from Java: * `WithTelemetry` stores the name and verbosity. The telemetry is created when the stream is first read with `Get()` or `GetTelemetry()` is called, so the copies made while building a stream do not publish. * The stream owns its telemetry and stops publishing when it is destroyed. * A copy of a stream keeps the telemetry settings and publishes under the same name once it is read. `Clone()` returns a copy without telemetry. * Moving a stream moves the settings; the moved-from stream stops publishing. {% endtab %} {% endtabs %} Neither framework's `Live Tuning` command requires a subsystem or mechanism, so running it does not interrupt the command driving with the stream. ### Live tuning At `HIGH`, values edited on the dashboard are applied to the stream every loop while the `Live Tuning` command runs. Start and stop it from the dashboard, or bind `getTelemetry().get().getLiveTuningCommand()` to a button. Tunable values stay in sync both ways while it runs: a change made in code, such as a slow mode binding calling `withScaleTranslation`, or a `BooleanSupplier` passed to `withAllianceRelativeControl` changing, is published to the dashboard and is not overridden. Dashboard values outside the allowed range are replaced with the stream's current value. ### NetworkTables topics `mode` (the current drive mode: `ANGULAR_VELOCITY`, `HEADING`, `AIM` or `TRANSLATION_ONLY`) is published to `/SwerveInputStream//` at every verbosity. At `MID` (`MEDIUM` in C++) and `HIGH`, the values below are also published there read-only. At `HIGH` they are published as tunable values under `/Tuning/SwerveInputStream//`, with the command at `/Tuning/SwerveInputStream//Live Tuning`. | Topic | Type | Range | Description | | -------------------- | ------- | ------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `deadband` | double | \[0, 1) | Controller axis deadband | | `translationScale` | double | (0, 1] | Translation axis scaling factor | | `rotationScale` | double | (0, 1] | Rotation axis scaling factor | | `maxLinearVelocity` | double | > 0 | Maximum chassis linear velocity (m/s). Starts at the drive config's maximum and overrides it | | `maxAngularVelocity` | double | > 0 | Maximum chassis angular velocity (rad/s). Starts at the drive config's maximum and overrides it | | `translationCube` | boolean | - | Enable cubic translation response curve | | `rotationCube` | boolean | - | Enable cubic rotation response curve | | `allianceRelative` | boolean | - | Enable alliance-relative translation flip | | `robotRelative` | boolean | - | Enable robot-relative control | The output velocities are not published: reading them would call `get()` a second time each loop, which runs the heading controller twice. Log the speeds you send to the drive instead. {% hint style="success" %} Once the values feel right, copy them from NetworkTables back into the stream's `with*()` calls in code. Values edited live are not persisted. For competition, use `TelemetryVerbosity.LOW`; in Java `getTelemetry().get().close()` stops publishing, and in C++ `WithTelemetry(name, TelemetryVerbosity::NONE)` does. {% endhint %} | Issue | Solution | | ---------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | | Telemetry not appearing | Check the stream was given `withTelemetry` and is read with `get()` every loop | | Changes don't apply | Start the `Live Tuning` command; it only exists at `TelemetryVerbosity.HIGH` | | A dashboard value snaps back | The value is outside the allowed range in the table above | ## Code reference {% @github-files/github-code-block url="" %}

pages.title: Telemetry
pages.content:
# Telemetry ## The basics of telemetry | Destination | On by default? | Turn it on or off with | Use it for | | ------------------- | -------------- | ------------------------------------- | ---------------------------- | | NetworkTables (NT4) | Yes | `withoutNetworkTables()` turns it off | Watching and tuning live | | DataLog file | No | `withDataLogName(name)` turns it on | Reviewing a match afterwards | Both are set on `SmartMotorControllerTelemetryConfig`. `MechanismTelemetry` does the work: every mechanism, and every `SwerveModule`, owns one, and it sends the same values to both destinations. {% hint style="success" %} Set a DataLog name for competition matches. It is one line, and it means you can see what actually happened on the field. {% endhint %} {% hint style="info" %} A DataLog uses storage on the SystemCore, and logging everything fills it quickly. Log only what you need. See the [WPILib DataLog docs](https://docs.wpilib.org/en/stable/docs/software/telemetry/datalog.html#custom-data-logging-using-datalog). {% endhint %} **Going further** * [DataLog Best Practices](/documentation/understanding/datalog-best-practices.md): choosing what to log, and how it works for `SwerveDrive`. * [How do I view my DataLog in AdvantageScope?](/documentation/how-to-simulation-and-logging/how-do-i-view-my-datalog-in-advantagescope.md): a step by step walkthrough. ## NetworkTables YAMS publishes under two tables. Nothing goes under `NT:/SmartDashboard`. | Table | Holds | Path | | ---------------- | --------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ | | `NT:/Mechanisms` | What the mechanism is doing. Read-only. | `NT:/Mechanisms///` | | `NT:/Mechanisms` | The mechanism's `Mechanism2d` | `NT:/Mechanisms//mechanism` | | `NT:/Tuning` | Values you can edit | `NT:/Tuning///` | | `NT:/Tuning` | The `Live Tuning` command | `NT:/Tuning//Live Tuning` | `` and `` are the telemetry names given to `withTelemetry(...)` on the mechanism config and on the `SmartMotorControllerConfig`. See [Live tuning](/documentation/understanding/live-tuning.md) for how to use the tunable side. ## Simulation vs reality The simulation view of each mechanism is done with `Mechanism2d`'s. These windows could be outputted while on the actual robot but that is not necessary as all of the data from the `Mechanism2d` is in the Telemetry fields and accessible to the user. {% embed url="" %} ## Mechanism telemetry A mechanism's table is a folder: it holds the `Mechanism2d` and one table for each `SmartMotorController` in the mechanism, so the values are easy to find. ## Smart motor controller telemetry There are two ways to choose what a motor publishes: pick a verbosity level, or pick the fields yourself. ### Verbosity levels `withTelemetry(name, TelemetryVerbosity)` is the quick way. Each level includes the one before it. | Level | Adds | Good for | | ------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- | | `LOW` | Positions, velocities and accelerations (`mechanism/*`, `measurement/*`, `rotor/*`, and `externalencoder/*` when there is an external encoder), the setpoints (`closedloop/setpoint/*`) and the active slot | Competition, where you only need to see what happened | | `MID` | `motor/outputVoltage`, `current/stator`, `current/supply` | Checking power draw | | `HIGH` | Every tunable value, `motor/temperature`, `closedloop/period`, the status booleans, and the `Live Tuning` command | Tuning and development | ### Choosing fields yourself Build a `SmartMotorControllerTelemetryConfig` and enable only what you want: ```java SmartMotorControllerTelemetryConfig motorTelemetryConfig = new SmartMotorControllerTelemetryConfig() .withMechanismPosition() .withRotorPosition() .withMechanismLowerLimit() .withMechanismUpperLimit(); SmartMotorControllerConfig motorConfig = new SmartMotorControllerConfig(this) .withClosedLoopController(4, 0, 0) .withTrapezoidalProfile(DegreesPerSecond.of(180), DegreesPerSecondPerSecond.of(90)) .withSoftLimits(Degrees.of(-30), Degrees.of(100)) .withGearing(new MechanismGearing(GearBox.fromReductionStages(3, 4))) .withZeroPower(MotorMode.BRAKE) .withTelemetry("ElevatorMotor", motorTelemetryConfig); ``` `withCustom(...)` covers everything else. Use it for a field with no `with*()` method of its own, or to switch several fields in one call. It takes a `BooleanTelemetryField` or `DoubleTelemetryField`, or an array of either, and a boolean: ```java SmartMotorControllerTelemetryConfig motorTelemetryConfig = new SmartMotorControllerTelemetryConfig() .withTelemetryVerbosity(TelemetryVerbosity.LOW) .withCustom(SmartMotorControllerTelemetry.DoubleTelemetryField.SupplyCurrent, true) .withCustom(new SmartMotorControllerTelemetry.BooleanTelemetryField[]{ SmartMotorControllerTelemetry.BooleanTelemetryField.MotorInversion, SmartMotorControllerTelemetry.BooleanTelemetryField.EncoderInversion }, false); ``` | | Java | C++ | | -------------- | ---------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- | | Switch a field | `withCustom(field, enabled)` | `WithCustom(field, enabled)` | | Switch several | `withCustom(fields[], enabled)` | `WithCustom(std::vector, enabled)` | | Package | `yams.core.telemetry` | | | Verbosity enum | `yams.core.telemetry.enums.TelemetryVerbosity` | | See the `SmartMotorControllerTelemetryConfig` API reference page for the full method list. ## Swerve drive telemetry A swerve drive publishes poses, chassis velocities and module states. Those are not single numbers, so they are published as NT4 structs that AdvantageScope understands directly. ### Setting it up `SwerveDrive` and `SwerveModule` have their own telemetry configs. They work the same way as a motor's: every field is off until a verbosity level or a `with*()` method turns it on. | Config | Passed to | Notable fields | | ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | | `SwerveDriveTelemetryConfig` | `SwerveDriveConfig.withTelemetry(name, config)` | `withPose()`, `withGyro()`, `withCurrentModuleStates()`, `withDesiredModuleStates()` | | `SwerveModuleTelemetryConfig` | `SwerveModuleConfig.withTelemetry(name, config)` | `withAbsoluteEncoder()`, `withState()` | ```java SwerveDriveTelemetryConfig driveTelemetryConfig = new SwerveDriveTelemetryConfig() .withTelemetryVerbosity(TelemetryVerbosity.HIGH) .withPose() .withGyro() .withCurrentRobotRelativeChassisSpeeds() .withFieldRelativeChassisSpeeds() .withDesiredRobotRelativeChassisSpeeds() .withDesiredModuleStates() .withCurrentModuleStates() .withDataLogName("swerve"); SwerveDriveConfig driveConfig = new SwerveDriveConfig(this, frontLeft, frontRight, backLeft, backRight) .withGyro(gyro::getRotation3d) .withTelemetry("swerve", driveTelemetryConfig); ``` `new SwerveDriveTelemetryConfig(TelemetryVerbosity.HIGH)` is shorthand for `new SwerveDriveTelemetryConfig().withTelemetryVerbosity(TelemetryVerbosity.HIGH)`. `SwerveModuleTelemetryConfig` has the same shorthand. ### Things that differ from a motor * **The name is required.** `SwerveDriveConfig.withTelemetry(...)` always takes the name first: `withTelemetry(name, TelemetryVerbosity)` or `withTelemetry(name, SwerveDriveTelemetryConfig)`. There is no `withTelemetryName(...)`. * **DataLog is set on the telemetry config.** `SwerveDriveConfig` and `SwerveModuleConfig` have no `withDataLogName(...)`. Use `SwerveDriveTelemetryConfig.withDataLogName(...)` and `SwerveModuleTelemetryConfig.withDataLogName(...)`. * **A module's state is `HIGH` only.** At `LOW` and `MID` a module publishes only its absolute encoder angle. * **The motors are configured separately.** Neither swerve config reaches the drive and azimuth motors inside a module. Give each motor's `SmartMotorControllerConfig` its own `.withTelemetry(name, SmartMotorControllerTelemetryConfig)`, as for any other motor. See [DataLog Best Practices](/documentation/understanding/datalog-best-practices.md). * **`withCustom(...)` works here too.** It takes a `DoubleTelemetryField`, `StructTelemetryField`, `StructArrayTelemetryField` or `BooleanTelemetryField`, or an array of one, and a boolean. {% hint style="info" %} WPILib 2027 renamed `ChassisSpeeds` to `ChassisVelocities` and `SwerveModuleState` to `SwerveModuleVelocity`. The YAMS method and telemetry field names (`withDesiredModuleStates()`, `setSwerveModuleStates(...)`, `withFieldRelativeChassisSpeeds()`) kept their old spelling. {% endhint %}
How struct telemetry works: StructTelemetry and StructArrayTelemetry `SmartMotorControllerTelemetry` publishes plain numbers and booleans with `DoubleTelemetry` and `BooleanTelemetry`. Swerve telemetry is built on two generic counterparts: | Class | Publishes | Used for | | ------------------------- | ------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- | | `StructTelemetry` | One struct value | `Pose2d`, `ChassisVelocities`, one `SwerveModuleVelocity` | | `StructArrayTelemetry` | An array of struct values | The four module `SwerveModuleVelocity[]` fields | Both behave like `DoubleTelemetry`: they can be enabled per field, sent to NetworkTables and to a DataLog, and, for fields marked tunable, read back a value edited on the dashboard. You do not normally construct them yourself. The swerve telemetry configs create and manage them.
### Live tuning At `HIGH` verbosity `SwerveDriveTelemetryConfig` also publishes tunable keys for auto-align and for the drive and azimuth motors under `NT:/Tuning//`. See [Live tuning: Swerve drive](/documentation/understanding/live-tuning.md#swerve-drive) for the keys and how to use them. ## Colors You may notice there are different colors in the Mechanism windows displayed for simulation. These are there to provide you with reference points of your Soft and Hard Limits. * Green is the upper hard limit * Red is the lower hard limit * Pink is the upper soft limit * Yellow is the lower soft limit These are provided to you so you can identify relative motion easily between the simulation and reality. ## Telemetry units All telemetry values in YAMS are logged with specific units. Understanding these units helps you interpret data correctly and configure your visualization tools. ### Standard telemetry units | NetworkTables key | Unit | Description | | ------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `mechanism/position` | Rotations (rot) | Position of the mechanism output shaft | | `mechanism/velocity` | Rotations per second (rot/s) | Velocity of the mechanism output shaft | | `rotor/position` | Rotations (rot) | Position of the motor rotor, before gearing | | `rotor/velocity` | Rotations per second (rot/s) | Velocity of the motor rotor | | `closedloop/setpoint/position` | Rotations, or meters for linear mechanisms | Closed loop position target | | `closedloop/setpoint/velocity` | rot/s, or m/s | Closed loop velocity target | | `mechanism/limit/lower`, `mechanism/limit/upper` | Degrees (deg) | Soft limits | | `motor/outputVoltage` | Volts (V) | Voltage being applied to the motor | | `closedloop/period` | Seconds (s) | How often the closed loop runs: 1 ms on the motor controller, or the closed loop control period on the SystemCore | | `current/supply` | Amps (A) | Current drawn from the battery | | `current/stator` | Amps (A) | Current through the motor windings | | `motor/temperature` | Fahrenheit (°F) | Motor temperature | ### LQR units A motor controller configured with an [LQR](/documentation/understanding/editor/lqr-controllers.md) publishes its values at `HIGH`, in place of kP, kI and kD, and only the ones its type uses. They use the same units as the tunable setpoints. | NetworkTables key | Unit | Description | | ---------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- | | `closedloop/lqr/qelms/position` | Degrees, or meters for an elevator | Position error tolerance. Arm and elevator only | | `closedloop/lqr/qelms/velocity` | RPM, or m/s for an elevator | Velocity error tolerance | | `closedloop/lqr/relms` | Volts (V) | Control effort tolerance | | `closedloop/lqr/model/position`, `closedloop/lqr/model/velocity` | Degrees and RPM, or meters and m/s for an elevator | Model standard deviations. Position: arm and elevator only | | `closedloop/lqr/encoder/position` | Degrees, or meters for an elevator | Encoder standard deviation. Arm and elevator only | | `closedloop/lqr/encoder/velocity` | RPM | Encoder standard deviation. Flywheel only | | `closedloop/lqr/maxVoltage` | Volts (V) | Most voltage the LQR outputs | ### Linear mechanism units When a mechanism has a circumference (from `.withMechanismCircumference()`, or one of the `.withWheelDiameter()`, `.withWheelRadius()` or `.withDrumRadius()` helpers), the linear keys are published too: | NetworkTables key | Unit | Description | | ---------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------- | -------------------------------- | | `measurement/position` | Meters (m) | Linear position of the mechanism | | `measurement/velocity` | Meters per second (m/s) | Linear velocity of the mechanism | | `measurement/limit/lower`, `measurement/limit/upper` | Meters (m) | Soft limits in linear units | {% hint style="info" %} YAMS logs rotational units by default. Linear units are calculated from rotational units using your configured circumference: `linear = rotational × circumference` {% endhint %} ## Using AdvantageScope for unit conversion AdvantageScope provides powerful unit conversion capabilities that let you view telemetry data in whatever units make sense for your analysis, without changing your robot code. ### Changing display units To change how a value is displayed in AdvantageScope: 1. Add the telemetry field to a graph (Line Graph, Discrete, etc.) 2. Right-click on the field in the legend 3. Select **"Convert Units..."** 4. Choose your desired output unit from the list For example, you can convert: * Rotations → Degrees, Radians, or custom mechanism units * Rotations per Second → RPM, Degrees per Second, Radians per Second * Meters → Inches, Feet, Centimeters * Meters per Second → Feet per Second, Inches per Second ### Multiple units on the same axis AdvantageScope allows you to plot values with **different units on the same axis**, which is incredibly useful for comparing related measurements: **Example: Comparing Position and Velocity** You can plot both `mechanism/position` (in degrees) and `mechanism/velocity` (in degrees/second) on the same graph to see how velocity changes relative to position during a motion profile. **Example: Comparing Setpoint vs Actual** Plot `closedloop/setpoint/position` and `mechanism/position` with the same unit conversion to directly compare your target trajectory against actual mechanism movement. **Example: Analyzing Current Draw** Plot `current/supply` and `current/stator` together to understand the relationship between battery load and motor torque output. ### Setting up unit conversion in AdvantageScope 1. **Open Line Graph**: Drag fields from the sidebar to a Line Graph tab 2. **Access Unit Settings**: Right-click on any field in the graph legend 3. **Select Convert Units**: Choose the conversion you want 4. **Apply to Multiple Fields**: Each field can have its own conversion, allowing mixed-unit comparisons {% hint style="success" %} **Pro Tip**: When tuning a mechanism, convert position to your natural units (degrees for arms, inches for elevators) and plot alongside velocity. This helps you visualize how your motion profile executes and identify where the mechanism accelerates, cruises, and decelerates. {% endhint %} ### Common unit conversions for FRC | Original Unit | Useful Conversions | Use Case | | ------------- | ------------------- | ------------------------------------ | | Rotations | Degrees, Radians | Arm angles, turret position | | Rotations | Inches, Centimeters | Elevator height (with circumference) | | rot/s | RPM | Flywheel speed | | rot/s | deg/s, rad/s | Arm angular velocity | | Meters | Inches, Feet | Elevator/linear mechanism position | | m/s | ft/s, in/s | Linear mechanism velocity | ### Exporting data with units When exporting data from AdvantageScope, the exported values use the **converted units** you have selected in the display. This makes it easy to: * Share data with team members in familiar units * Import into spreadsheets for further analysis * Create documentation with consistent unit conventions

pages.title: DataLog best practices
pages.content:
# DataLog best practices

{% hint style="info" %}
Using DataLog will increase your storage usage on the SystemCore and could have negative consequences if left unmanaged. Review [WPILib's DataLog documentation](https://docs.wpilib.org/en/stable/docs/software/telemetry/datalog.html#custom-data-logging-using-datalog) for more information.
{% endhint %}

Every YAMS telemetry field is published to NetworkTables by default. Separately, you can opt any field into a WPILib `DataLog`, the same file format read by AdvantageScope offline, and the one WPILib's `DataLogManager` automatically saves to a USB drive or the SystemCore's local storage during a match. This page covers how to control both destinations independently, and calls out the one place, `SwerveDrive`, where the rules are different.

## The two knobs: NetworkTables and DataLog

For any single-motor mechanism (`Arm`, `Elevator`, `Pivot`, `FlyWheel`, `DifferentialMechanism`, `DoubleJointedArm`) telemetry is controlled per motor controller with `SmartMotorControllerTelemetryConfig`:

```java
SmartMotorControllerTelemetryConfig telemetryConfig = new SmartMotorControllerTelemetryConfig()
    .withTelemetryVerbosity(TelemetryVerbosity.LOW)
    .withStatorCurrent()
    .withTemperature()
    .withDataLogName("motors/shooter")   // log the fields above to DataLog...
    .withoutNetworkTables();             // ...and don't publish them to NT4

SmartMotorControllerConfig motorConfig = new SmartMotorControllerConfig(this)
    .withClosedLoopController(4, 0, 0)
    .withGearing(new MechanismGearing(GearBox.fromReductionStages(3, 4)))
    .withTelemetry("ShooterMotor", telemetryConfig);
```

* `withDataLogName(name)` turns on DataLog for every field enabled on that config, under the given prefix.
* `withoutNetworkTables()` (or `withNetworkTables(false)`) stops those fields from being published to NT4 at all. You can freely enable DataLog, NetworkTables, both, or neither, they're independent toggles.
* Which fields get logged is controlled the same way for both destinations, there's only one set of enabled fields, per `withTelemetryVerbosity()` and the individual `with*()` methods described in [Telemetry](/documentation/understanding/telemetry.md).

{% hint style="success" %}
Set a DataLogName for competition matches. It costs almost nothing to add and gives you a full record to review between matches, often the difference between guessing why a mechanism stalled and knowing exactly why.
{% endhint %}

## Choosing what to log

Every field is disabled by default. `withTelemetryVerbosity()` gives you a cumulative preset (`LOW` → `MID` → `HIGH`, each including everything below it) so you don't have to enable dozens of fields by hand, then layer on or remove individual fields as needed.

A few guidelines:

* **Don't just reach for `HIGH` everywhere.** `HIGH` includes PID gains, feedforward gains, current limits, and every boolean status flag, useful while tuning, but mostly redundant once a mechanism is dialed in. Prefer `LOW` or `MID` plus the handful of fields you actually watch (current, temperature, setpoint error) for a competition build.
* **Prune before you log, not after.** DataLog files only grow, there's no way to selectively remove a field after the fact without re-recording. Decide what you need before the match, not while reviewing the log afterward.
* **DataLog is not a substitute for NetworkTables during development.** Live tools (Elastic, Shuffleboard, AdvantageScope in live mode) read NT4, not DataLog. Keep NetworkTables on while you're actively tuning, and consider disabling it only for fields you truly don't need live, once you're locking in a competition build.

Need to flip a field that doesn't have its own `with*()` method, or toggle several fields at once? `withCustom(field, value)` takes any `BooleanTelemetryField`/`DoubleTelemetryField` (or an array of either) plus a boolean, and enables or disables them accordingly:

```java
SmartMotorControllerTelemetryConfig telemetryConfig = new SmartMotorControllerTelemetryConfig()
    .withTelemetryVerbosity(TelemetryVerbosity.LOW)
    .withCustom(new SmartMotorControllerTelemetry.DoubleTelemetryField[]{
        SmartMotorControllerTelemetry.DoubleTelemetryField.SupplyCurrent,
        SmartMotorControllerTelemetry.DoubleTelemetryField.StatorCurrentLimit
    }, true);
```

## Enabling/disabling NetworkTables conditionally

Because `withNetworkTables(boolean)` just takes a boolean, you can drive it from anything, including whether you're at an event:

```java
SmartMotorControllerTelemetryConfig telemetryConfig = new SmartMotorControllerTelemetryConfig()
    .withTelemetryVerbosity(TelemetryVerbosity.LOW)
    .withDataLogName("motors/shooter")
    .withNetworkTables(!RobotState.isFMSAttached()); // org.wpilib.driverstation.RobotState
```

This keeps full NT4 telemetry for pit testing and practice, then automatically drops NT4 traffic (while still writing to DataLog) once you're on the field at an event.

## Swerve drive is different

{% hint style="warning" %}
`SwerveDriveConfig`/`SwerveModuleConfig` do **not** use `SmartMotorControllerTelemetryConfig`, they have their own `SwerveDriveTelemetryConfig`/`SwerveModuleTelemetryConfig`. The shape is the same (verbosity preset plus individual `with*()` fields, `withoutNetworkTables()`, `withDataLogName(...)`), but the DataLog name for both the drive-level fields (pose, gyro, chassis speeds, module states) and a module's absolute encoder angle has to go through the telemetry config, neither `SwerveDriveConfig` nor `SwerveModuleConfig` has a `withDataLogName(...)` of its own.
{% endhint %}

`SwerveDriveConfig.withTelemetry(name, TelemetryVerbosity)` and `SwerveModuleConfig.withTelemetry(name, TelemetryVerbosity)` pick a verbosity preset the same way a single-motor mechanism does, both always take the telemetry name as the first argument, there's no name-less overload. For anything more, hand `withTelemetry(name, ...)` a `SwerveDriveTelemetryConfig`/`SwerveModuleTelemetryConfig` instead of a bare `TelemetryVerbosity`, that's what lets you enable individual fields, disable NetworkTables, or set a DataLog name for the drive-level and per-module fields (pose, gyro, chassis speeds, module states, absolute encoder angle).

You can still send this to DataLog:

```java
SwerveDriveConfig driveConfig = new SwerveDriveConfig(this, frontLeft, frontRight, backLeft, backRight)
    .withGyro(gyro::getRotation3d)
    .withTelemetry("swerve", new SwerveDriveTelemetryConfig(TelemetryVerbosity.HIGH)
        .withDataLogName("swerve"));                 // logs pose, gyro, chassis speeds, module states

SwerveModuleConfig frontLeftConfig = new SwerveModuleConfig(driveMotorFL, azimuthMotorFL)
    .withWheelRadius(Meters.of(0.0508))
    .withLocation(new Translation2d(0.381, 0.381))
    .withTelemetry("FrontLeft", new SwerveModuleTelemetryConfig(TelemetryVerbosity.HIGH)
        .withDataLogName("swerve/frontLeft"));       // logs this module's absolute encoder angle (+ state at HIGH)
```

`new SwerveDriveTelemetryConfig(TelemetryVerbosity.HIGH)`/`new SwerveModuleTelemetryConfig(TelemetryVerbosity.HIGH)` are shorthand constructors for `new SwerveDriveTelemetryConfig().withTelemetryVerbosity(TelemetryVerbosity.HIGH)` and the module equivalent. Each module's DataLog name is independent of the drive's `SwerveDriveTelemetryConfig.withDataLogName(...)` above, set it separately per module if you want per-module DataLog prefixes.

{% hint style="info" %}
Neither the drive's nor a module's DataLog name cascades to the drive/azimuth motors that make up that module. Setting one does not log the other, and neither logs the motors.
{% endhint %}

### Getting granular fields out of a swerve module's motors

The drive and azimuth motors of a `SwerveModule` are still ordinary `SmartMotorController`s under the hood. If you want field-level control (or a DataLog name) on just the drive motor or just the azimuth motor, set it on that motor's own `SmartMotorControllerConfig`, before you build the `SwerveModule`, exactly as you would for a standalone motor:

```java
SmartMotorControllerTelemetryConfig driveTelemetry = new SmartMotorControllerTelemetryConfig()
    .withStatorCurrent()
    .withTemperature()
    .withDataLogName("swerve/frontLeft/drive");

SmartMotorControllerConfig driveMotorConfig = new SmartMotorControllerConfig(this)
    .withClosedLoopController(0.1, 0.0, 0.0)
    .withGearing(new MechanismGearing(GearBox.fromReductionStages(6.75)))
    .withTelemetry("driveMotor", driveTelemetry);

SmartMotorController driveMotorFL = new TalonFXWrapper(new TalonFX(10, new CANBus(CANPort.CAN_S0)), DCMotor.getKrakenX60(1), driveMotorConfig);
```

This gives you the same fine-grained control (and independent DataLog name) on that one motor that you'd get on any other mechanism's motor, it's only the swerve-level pose/gyro/chassis-speed/encoder fields that are all-or-nothing per verbosity level.

## Related pages

* [Telemetry](/documentation/understanding/telemetry.md)
* [Swerve Drive](/documentation/tutorials/swerve-drive.md)
* [How do I view my DataLog in AdvantageScope?](/documentation/how-to-simulation-and-logging/how-do-i-view-my-datalog-in-advantagescope.md)

pages.title: Live tuning
pages.content:
# Live tuning Live tuning lets you change gains, motion profiles and limits from a dashboard while the robot is enabled, and see the result straight away. It works over NetworkTables with AdvantageScope or Elastic. ## Turn it on Give the motor's telemetry `TelemetryVerbosity.HIGH`. That is all most robots need. 
SmartMotorControllerConfig lowerFlyWheelConfig = new SmartMotorControllerConfig(this)
      .withControlMode(ControlMode.CLOSED_LOOP)
      .withZeroPower(MotorMode.COAST)
      .withGearing(new MechanismGearing(GearBox.fromReductionStages(3, 4)))
      .withMomentOfInertia(Inches.of(4), Pounds.of(2))
      .withClosedLoopController(1,
                                0,
                                0) // You generally do not want a profile because its not a position controlled loop.
      .withFeedforward(new SimpleMotorFeedforward(0, 0, 0)) // Helps track changing RPM goals
      .withMotorInverted(false)
      .withTelemetry("LowerFlyWheel", TelemetryVerbosity.HIGH) // yams.core.telemetry.enums.TelemetryVerbosity
| How the motor's telemetry is set up | Live Tuning command | | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- | | `withTelemetry(name, TelemetryVerbosity.HIGH)` | Registered for you | | `withTelemetry(name, telemetryConfig)` with a `SmartMotorControllerTelemetryConfig` | Registered for you | | A mechanism, such as an `Arm`, `Elevator`, `Pivot` or `FlyWheel`, with `withTelemetry(...)` on its own config too | Registered for you, for the mechanism's motor controllers | | You call `setupTelemetry(NetworkTable, NetworkTable)` yourself (Java) | Call `setupLiveTuning()` afterwards, see below | | C++ with `TelemetryVerbosity::HIGH` and a subsystem on the config | Registered for you when `SetupTelemetry()` runs | YAMS registers **one** `Live Tuning` command per subsystem (Commands v2) or mechanism (Commands v3). Every motor controller in that subsystem or mechanism joins the same command.
Setting up live tuning explicitly If you set up telemetry yourself, the `Live Tuning` command is not registered for you. Call `setupLiveTuning()` on the config after the telemetry is set up: ```java SmartMotorControllerConfig motorConfig = new SmartMotorControllerConfig(this) .withTelemetry("ArmMotor", TelemetryVerbosity.HIGH); SmartMotorController motor = new TalonFXWrapper(armMotor, DCMotor.getKrakenX60(1), motorConfig); motor.setupTelemetry(telemetryTable, tuningTable); motorConfig.setupLiveTuning(); ``` `setupLiveTuning()` does nothing when: * the `SmartMotorController` has not set up its telemetry yet (that is what attaches the controller to the config), or * the config has no subsystem (Commands v2) or mechanism (Commands v3). Registering two different subsystem or mechanism instances with the same name throws an `IllegalStateException`. Give each one a unique name, for example `LeftTurret` and `RightTurret`. In C++ there is no explicit call.
{% hint style="info" %} Tuning an elevator, arm, pivot or flywheel? The [YAMS Live Tuner](/documentation/understanding/live-tuning/live-tuner.md) walks you through checking the mechanism, then sends setpoints and gains while you watch a graph. {% endhint %} {% hint style="info" %} Using CTRE TalonFX or TalonFXS motors? Phoenix Tuner X can connect to your simulation too. See [TunerX in simulation](/documentation/understanding/live-tuning/tunerx-in-simulation.md). {% endhint %} ## Use it {% hint style="danger" %} Like all tuning, live tuning can be **dangerous**. It's best to practice in simulation before the real robot. {% endhint %} {% stepper %} {% step %} #### Try it in simulation Run the robot code in simulation and go through the steps below there first. {% endstep %} {% step %} #### Enable the robot Dashboard edits are only applied while the robot is enabled and the `Live Tuning` command is running. {% endstep %} {% step %} #### Start the `Live Tuning` command It is published at `NT:/Tuning/SUBSYSTEM_NAME/Live Tuning`, where `SUBSYSTEM_NAME` is the name of the subsystem (Commands v2) or mechanism (Commands v3) given to the `SmartMotorControllerConfig`. {% tabs %} {% tab title="Commands v2" %} In Elastic, drag the `Live Tuning` command from `NT:/Tuning/SUBSYSTEM_NAME/Live Tuning` onto your dashboard and press its button. It is a regular WPILib Commands v2 `Command` that requires the subsystem. {% endtab %} {% tab title="Commands v3" %} Commands v3 commands are not dashboard widgets themselves, so YAMS publishes the command through `yams.commands3.telemetry.CommandTunable`. It shows up with a single `running` boolean at `NT:/Tuning/MECHANISM_NAME/Live Tuning/running`: * Set `running` to `true` to schedule the command on the default `Scheduler`. * Set `running` to `false` to cancel it. * `running` reads back whether the command is currently running. The command requires the mechanism and runs a `while (true)` loop that applies the dashboard values and calls `coroutine.yield()` each loop. {% endtab %} {% endtabs %} The command takes over from the default command. If that default command coasts the motor with a duty cycle or voltage, it stopped a closed loop that runs on the SystemCore, such as an LQR or an exponential profile. The `Live Tuning` command starts it again, holding the setpoint the motor controller had. {% endstep %} {% step %} #### Change a value The tunable values are published under `NT:/Tuning/`. Edit one, and it is applied on the next loop. {% tabs %} {% tab title="AdvantageScope" %} AdvantageScope only reads NetworkTables until you turn on **tuning mode**. Click the tuning mode button, the sliders icon beside the search box at the top of the sidebar. It is only shown while AdvantageScope is connected to a live robot or simulation. With tuning mode on, the fields under `NT:/Tuning` can be edited in the sidebar. If typing a value does nothing, check this button first. {% endtab %} {% tab title="Elastic" %} Drag a field from `NT:/Tuning/` onto the dashboard as a text or number widget and type the new value. Elastic can always write to NetworkTables, so there is nothing to turn on. {% endtab %} {% endtabs %} {% endstep %} {% step %} #### Watch what happens Graph the matching read-only fields under `NT:/Mechanisms/`. [NetworkTables keys](#networktables-keys) shows where they are, and [What to tune and what to watch](#what-to-tune-and-what-to-watch) lists which key to watch for each value. {% endstep %} {% endstepper %} {% hint style="warning" %} The `Live Tuning` command requires the subsystem or mechanism, so the controller, a default command, or any other trigger for that subsystem or mechanism can interrupt it. Dashboard edits stop being applied when it is interrupted. {% endhint %} ## NetworkTables keys Everything on this page is named by its NetworkTables key, which is what you see in AdvantageScope and Elastic. | What | Where it is published | | ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ | | Values you type | `NT:/Tuning///` | | Values you watch | `NT:/Mechanisms///` | | The `Live Tuning` command | `NT:/Tuning//Live Tuning` | `` and `` are the names given to `withTelemetry(...)` on the mechanism config and on the `SmartMotorControllerConfig`. A motor controller used without a mechanism class has no `` level. For example, an arm named `Arm` with a motor named `ArmMotor`: * You type kP into `NT:/Tuning/Arm/ArmMotor/closedloop/feedback/kP`. * You watch the arm at `NT:/Mechanisms/Arm/ArmMotor/mechanism/position`. {% hint style="info" %} Some keys exist in both tables. `closedloop/setpoint/position` under `NT:/Tuning` is the setpoint you type. Under `NT:/Mechanisms` it is the setpoint the controller is using right now. {% endhint %} ### The position and velocity to watch Which keys hold the position and velocity depends on the mechanism. | Mechanism | Position | Velocity | Units | | -------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------- | ---------------------- | ---------------- | | Rotational: arms, pivots, turrets, flywheels | `mechanism/position` | `mechanism/velocity` | Rotations, rot/s | | Linear: elevators, and anything with a mechanism circumference | `measurement/position` | `measurement/velocity` | Meters, m/s | The tables below write `mechanism/position` and `mechanism/velocity`. On a linear mechanism, read them as `measurement/position` and `measurement/velocity`. ## Units: what you type and what you read Tunable fields and read-only fields do not use the same units. | Quantity | You type (tunable fields) | You read (read-only fields) | | -------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------- | ----------------------------- | | Angular position | **Degrees** | **Rotations** | | Angular velocity | **RPM** | **Rotations per second** | | Angular acceleration | **RPM per second** | **Rotations per second²** | | Linear position, velocity, acceleration (linear closed loop control) | **Meters**, **m/s**, **m/s²** | **Meters**, **m/s**, **m/s²** | | Voltage, current | **Volts**, **Amps** | **Volts**, **Amps** | | Temperature | Not tunable | **Fahrenheit** | ### See both in the same units with AdvantageScope AdvantageScope can convert any read-only field for display, without changing the data or your robot code. 1. Drag the telemetry field, for example `NT:/Mechanisms/Arm/ArmMotor/mechanism/position`, into a Line Graph. 2. Right-click the field in the graph legend and choose **Convert Units…** 3.
