## Drive a motor at a voltage Sometimes you want no closed loop at all, just a voltage: to find the voltage that just starts a mechanism moving, to check that a positive voltage moves it the way you expect, or to see how fast it goes at 3 V. Every motor controller with `TelemetryVerbosity.HIGH` has two keys for this under `NT:/Tuning///`: | You type | Units | What it is | | ------------------ | ------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `voltage/enabled` | Boolean | Drive the motor at `voltage/setpoint` while `true`. | | `voltage/setpoint` | Volts | The voltage. Set back to `0` when `voltage/enabled` turns on, and sent to the motor and its loosely coupled followers every loop while `voltage/enabled` is `true`, even when it has not changed. It is not applied while `voltage/enabled` is `false`. | {% stepper %} {% step %} #### Start the `Live Tuning` command As in [Use it](#use-it). The voltage is only applied while the command runs. {% endstep %} {% step %} #### Turn it on, then type a voltage Set `voltage/enabled` to `true`. YAMS stops the closed loop and starts the motor at 0 V, with `voltage/setpoint` set back to `0`, so nothing moves until you type a voltage. A closed loop that runs on the SystemCore, on a Nova or with an LQR or exponential profile, would replace the voltage on its next loop, which is why it is stopped. Now type a small voltage, such as `1`, into `voltage/setpoint`. It is sent every loop, so the motor keeps outputting it until you change it. {% endstep %} {% step %} #### Watch it move Graph `mechanism/velocity` (or `measurement/velocity`), `motor/outputVoltage` and `current/stator`. Raise or lower `voltage/setpoint` a little at a time. {% endstep %} {% step %} #### Turn it off Set `voltage/enabled` to `false`. The voltage goes to 0, the closed loop starts again, and the setpoint it held before is sent again, so the mechanism goes back to it. {% endstep %} {% endstepper %} **Setpoints typed while the voltage is on are skipped.** A value typed into `closedloop/setpoint/position` or `closedloop/setpoint/velocity` then is not saved for later. Type it again once the voltage is off. Gains, limits and the other tunable values are applied as soon as you type them, even while the voltage is on. **Loosely coupled followers** are driven at the same voltage. A follower is normally sent its leader's setpoints and runs its own closed loop, so it is not sent a voltage the leader is driven at. With `voltage/enabled` on, YAMS stops the followers' closed loops with the leader's and sends each follower the voltage itself. Each follower's own inversion still applies. Turning the voltage off starts the followers' closed loops again and sends them the setpoint with the leader's. **When the `Live Tuning` command ends**, because you stopped it or another command for the subsystem or mechanism interrupted it, the voltage stops too. YAMS turns the voltage off, sets `voltage/enabled` back to `false` so the voltage is not applied again as soon as the command starts again, and the closed loop holds the setpoint. {% hint style="warning" %} A voltage has no speed limit and no motion profile. Start low, keep the mechanism away from its hard stops, and keep a hand on disable. On an arm or elevator, a voltage too small to hold it up lets it fall. {% endhint %} {% hint style="info" %} Live tuning needs `ControlMode.CLOSED_LOOP`. The voltage keys are published at `TelemetryVerbosity.HIGH`, or with `withCustom(DoubleTelemetryField.TunableVoltage, true)` and `withCustom(BooleanTelemetryField.TunableVoltageEnabled, true)` on a `SmartMotorControllerTelemetryConfig`. {% endhint %} ## Tuning order Tune the feedforward first, then the feedback, then the motion profile last, one value at a time. {% hint style="success" %} **New to tuning?** The WPILib docs explain what each gain does and have interactive simulations to practice on. Read the one for your mechanism before tuning the real thing: * [Introduction to PID](https://docs.wpilib.org/en/stable/docs/software/advanced-controls/introduction/introduction-to-pid.html) and [introduction to feedforward](https://docs.wpilib.org/en/stable/docs/software/advanced-controls/introduction/introduction-to-feedforward.html) * [Tuning a flywheel velocity controller](https://docs.wpilib.org/en/stable/docs/software/advanced-controls/introduction/tuning-flywheel.html) * [Tuning a turret position controller](https://docs.wpilib.org/en/stable/docs/software/advanced-controls/introduction/tuning-turret.html) * [Tuning a vertical arm position controller](https://docs.wpilib.org/en/stable/docs/software/advanced-controls/introduction/tuning-vertical-arm.html) * [Tuning a vertical elevator](https://docs.wpilib.org/en/stable/docs/software/advanced-controls/introduction/tuning-elevator.html) {% endhint %} {% tabs %} {% tab title="Flywheel" %} With `SimpleMotorFeedforward`: 1. **kS**: raise slowly until the wheel just starts to move. 2. **kV**: set a target speed with kP = 0, then adjust kV until the steady speed matches. 3. **kP**: raise to remove the leftover error and speed up the response. 4. **kD**: only if it oscillates, add a little to damp it. 5. **kA** (optional): for faster spin up. {% hint style="success" %} **Units example:** a kV of 0.12 V/(rot/s) means 0.12 volts for every rotation per second. At 100 rot/s (6000 RPM) the feedforward contributes 12 V. {% endhint %} {% endtab %} {% tab title="Arm" %} With `ArmFeedforward`. The motion profile comes last: 1. **kG**: with kP, kI, kD and the other feedforward gains at 0, hold the arm level (0° from horizontal) and raise kG until it stays there. 2. **kS**: raise until the arm is just about to move, then back off a little. 3. **kP, then kD**: command small moves of a few degrees. Raise kP until the arm reaches them quickly without oscillating, then add kD if it overshoots. Without a profile a setpoint is a sudden jump, so keep the moves small. 4. **Motion profile**: now type a `closedloop/motionprofile/maxVelocity` (RPM) and `maxAcceleration` (RPM/s), for example 15 RPM (90°/s) and 30 RPM/s, and raise them a step at a time. Stop when `mechanism/velocity` starts falling behind the setpoint or `current/stator` spikes. 5. **kV**: kV only acts while the setpoint is moving, so tune it with the profile. Raise it until `mechanism/velocity` tracks `closedloop/setpoint/velocity` during a long move. Leave kA at 0 unless the arm lags while accelerating. {% hint style="info" %} `kG * cos(angle)` is applied, so there is no gravity compensation when the arm is vertical (±90° from horizontal) and full kG when it is level. {% endhint %} {% endtab %} {% tab title="Elevator" %} With `ElevatorFeedforward`. An elevator is a linear mechanism, so you type meters and watch the `measurement/` keys. The motion profile comes last: 1. **kG**: with kP, kI, kD and kS at 0, raise kG until the carriage holds its height without drifting down. It is the same at every height. 2. **kS**: raise until the carriage is just about to move, then back off a little. 3. **kP, then kD**: command small moves of a few centimeters. Raise kP until `measurement/position` reaches them quickly without oscillating, then add kD if it still rings. Without a profile a setpoint is a sudden jump, so keep the moves small. 4. **Motion profile**: now type a `closedloop/motionprofile/maxVelocity` (m/s) and `maxAcceleration` (m/s²), for example 0.5 m/s and 1 m/s², and raise them a step at a time. Stop when `measurement/velocity` starts falling behind the setpoint or `current/stator` spikes. 5. **kV**: kV only acts while the setpoint is moving, so tune it with the profile. Raise it until `measurement/velocity` tracks `closedloop/setpoint/velocity` during a long move. Leave kA at 0 unless the carriage lags while accelerating. {% hint style="info" %} Tune in the middle of the travel, away from the hard stops, and keep the soft limits (`measurement/limit/lower`, `measurement/limit/upper`) set while you do. {% endhint %} {% endtab %} {% endtabs %} {% hint style="info" %} **With an LQR**, tune the feedforward the same way, then the `closedloop/lqr/` fields where these steps say kP and kD. See [Tune it live](/documentation/understanding/editor/lqr-controllers.md#tune-it-live). {% endhint %} ### Motion profiles on arms and elevators Arms and elevators should end up moving on a motion profile, added once the gains hold the mechanism and reach small setpoints cleanly. Without one, a new setpoint is a sudden jump and the mechanism slams toward it. With one, the setpoint slides there at a speed and acceleration you choose. | You type (`NT:/Tuning/.../closedloop/motionprofile/`) | Arm | Elevator | Raise it when | Lower it when | | ----------------------------------------------------- | ----- | -------- | ---------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `maxVelocity` | RPM | m/s | The move is slow and the motor has voltage to spare. | The velocity never reaches the flat top of the profile. | | `maxAcceleration` | RPM/s | m/s² | The mechanism takes too long to get up to speed. | `current/stator` spikes, the belt or chain skips, or the mechanism lags on the ramps. | Watch `closedloop/setpoint/velocity` against `mechanism/velocity` (arm) or `measurement/velocity` (elevator). The setpoint is the profile, and the measured line should sit on top of it. {% hint style="info" %} The profile only exists if the config has one, for example `withTrapezoidalProfile(MetersPerSecond.of(0.5), MetersPerSecondPerSecond.of(1))` on an elevator. For an exponential profile, tune `kV`, `kA` and `maxInput` under the same `closedloop/motionprofile/` keys instead. See [Exponential profiles](/documentation/understanding/editor/exponential-profiles.md). {% endhint %} ### Elevators with a constant force spring A constant force spring pulls the carriage up with about the same force at every height. It does part of the motor's job, which changes what kG should be. Do not copy kG from a calculation or from the robot before the springs went on. Measure it. The steps below type the voltages into `closedloop/feedforward/kG`; you can type them into [`voltage/setpoint`](#drive-a-motor-at-a-voltage) with `voltage/enabled` on instead, which takes the closed loop out of the way without zeroing any gains: {% stepper %} {% step %} #### Find the voltage that just moves it up Put the carriage in the middle of the travel and start the `Live Tuning` command. Set kP, kI, kD and `closedloop/feedforward/kS` to 0. Now `closedloop/feedforward/kG` is the only voltage reaching the motor. Raise it slowly until the carriage just creeps upward, and write the value down. {% endstep %} {% step %} #### Find the voltage that just moves it down Lower `closedloop/feedforward/kG` slowly until the carriage just creeps downward. This number is often negative on a sprung elevator. Write it down. {% endstep %} {% step %} #### Work out kG and kS `kG = (up + down) / 2` and `kS = (up - down) / 2`. Type them into `closedloop/feedforward/kG` and `closedloop/feedforward/kS`. {% endstep %} {% step %} #### Check it at the bottom, middle and top With only the feedforward, the carriage should stay where you leave it at every height. "Constant force" springs are not perfectly constant, and each stage of a multi stage elevator can have its own springs. If the carriage drifts at one end, use the kG that holds best in the range you care about most and let kP hold the rest. {% endstep %} {% step %} #### Tune kV, kP and kD as usual Follow the elevator steps in [Tuning order](#tuning-order). The spring does not change them. {% endstep %} {% endstepper %} | With a spring, expect | Why | | ----------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | kG near zero, or negative | The spring carries the weight. If it is stronger than the carriage, the motor has to pull down. | | A larger kS | The spring and its spool add friction. | | Different effort up and down | Check `motor/outputVoltage` in both directions. Size the motion profile's `maxAcceleration` for the direction that needs more. | | A drift when the load changes | A spring sized for the empty carriage is too weak with a game piece, and the other way round. Tune for the load you hold longest. | {% hint style="warning" %} The simulation does not know about the spring: it models the full carriage weight from `ElevatorConfig.withCarriageWeight(...)`. Keep a separate kG for simulation with `withSimFeedforward(...)`, so a sprung robot's small kG does not make the simulated elevator sag. {% endhint %} ## When tuning does not help Some mechanisms cannot be tuned, because the motor does not have enough torque for the job. No gain fixes that, and it is worth recognizing early so you stop chasing numbers. {% tabs %} {% tab title="Elevator" %} Raising kP does nothing, because the motor was already at full voltage with the smaller gain. {% endtab %} {% tab title="Arm" %} An arm needs the most torque when it is level and almost none when it is upright. An underpowered arm therefore looks fine at some setpoints and hopeless at others. If it only misbehaves near level, suspect torque before you suspect the gains. {% endtab %} {% tab title="Flywheel" %} A flywheel has a top speed set by the motor, the gearing and the battery voltage. Below it everything works, and the closer the setpoint gets to it the longer the spin up takes. Above it, no gain will ever get there. Remember that the battery sags under load, so the top speed in a match is lower than on a fresh battery on the bench. {% endtab %} {% endtabs %} ### It works at low setpoints This is what makes an underpowered mechanism hard to spot. It tunes well on the easy moves, and then the same gains fail on the hard ones: | Mechanism | Works | Fails | | --------- | --------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- | | Elevator | Short moves, slow profiles, an empty carriage | Long fast moves, or carrying a game piece | | Arm | Setpoints near upright | Setpoints near level, where gravity pulls hardest | | Flywheel | Low speeds | Speeds near the motor's top speed, and recovery between shots | When that happens, do not retune for the hard case. Look at `motor/outputVoltage` during the move that fails. If it is at the maximum, the gains are not the problem. ### It gets slower every time An overworked motor heats up, and a hot motor is weaker. The first few moves look fine, then each one takes a little longer, until the mechanism stops reaching its setpoint at all. | Watch (`NT:/Mechanisms`) | What you see | | ---------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `current/stator` | Higher on every repeat of the same move, until it sits on the limit. | | `motor/temperature` | Climbing steadily and not coming back down between moves. | | `mechanism/velocity` or `measurement/velocity` | The peak speed of the same move dropping over time. | | `mechanism/position` or `measurement/position` | Arriving later each time, then stopping short. | {% hint style="danger" %} If the gains that worked ten minutes ago no longer work, check `motor/temperature` before you touch them. Retuning to a hot motor gives you gains that are wrong once it cools, and running it harder is how motors burn out. Stop, let it cool, and fix the load. {% endhint %} **How to recognize it** | Watch (`NT:/Mechanisms`) | What you see | | ---------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `motor/outputVoltage` | Pinned at the maximum for most of the move, not just at the start. | | `current/stator` | Sitting on the stator current limit. | | `mechanism/position` or `measurement/position` | The same slow curve whatever you set kP to, and it may stop short of the setpoint. | | `mechanism/velocity` or `measurement/velocity` | Far below the profile's `closedloop/setpoint/velocity`, however the profile is set. | | `motor/temperature` | Climbing quickly while the mechanism holds a position. | **What to do about it** The fix is mechanical or electrical, not a gain: * **More gear reduction.** The most common fix. It trades top speed, which you are not reaching anyway, for torque. * **More motors**, or a stronger motor. * **Take load off the motor**: a lighter mechanism, a counterweight, or a [constant force spring](#elevators-with-a-constant-force-spring) on an elevator. * **Check the current limit.** A stator limit set too low makes a capable motor look underpowered. Raise `current/limit/stator` and see whether the move changes. See [Limiting power consumption](/documentation/understanding/editor/limiting-power-consumption.md). * **Check for binding.** Disable the robot and move the mechanism by hand through its whole travel. * **Ask for less.** Lower the motion profile's `maxVelocity` and `maxAcceleration` to what the motor can deliver. {% hint style="info" %} Check this in simulation first. With the real motor, gearing and mass in the config, an underpowered mechanism shows the same pinned voltage in simulation, before anything is built. {% endhint %} ## Swerve drive `SwerveDrive` has its own tuning command and its own keys. It can tune three things, one at a time: | Mode | Turn it on with | What it does | | --------------------- | ------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Module azimuth motors | `modules/azimuth/enabled` | Turns every module to an angle you type. | | Module drive motors | `modules/drive/enabled` | Runs every module's drive motor at a velocity you type. | | Auto-align | `autoalign/enabled` | Drives the robot to a pose you type, using the translation and rotation PID gains. | | What | Where it is published | | ----------------------- | ------------------------------ | | Values you type | `NT:/Tuning//` | | The tuning command | `NT:/Mechanisms//tuning` | | The robot pose to watch | `NT:/Mechanisms//pose` | `` is the name given to `SwerveDriveConfig.withTelemetry(name, ...)`. The keys are published at `TelemetryVerbosity.HIGH`. Only one mode drives the robot at a time. Auto-align outranks drive tuning, and drive tuning outranks azimuth tuning: turning on a mode turns the ones below it back off, in NetworkTables too, so the dashboard shows what is actually running. {% hint style="warning" %} The tuning command is only published when both a translation and a rotation controller are set with `withTranslationController(...)` and `withRotationController(...)`. Nothing you type is applied unless the command is running. {% endhint %} ### Start the tuning command {% tabs %} {% tab title="Commands v2" %} Drag `NT:/Mechanisms//tuning` onto your Elastic dashboard and press its button, or bind it to a controller button. {% endtab %} {% tab title="Commands v3" %} The command is published through `CommandTunable`. Set `NT:/Mechanisms//tuning/running` to `true` to start it and `false` to stop it. {% endtab %} {% endtabs %} Starting the command resets the translation and rotation PID controllers. Stopping it turns every mode off and holds the wheels where they are. ### Tune the swerve modules Tune the modules before auto-align: auto-align can only be as good as the modules under it. Do the azimuth motors first, so the wheels point where they are told while you tune the drive motors. The module keys are shared. One value is applied to all four modules, which is what you want when the modules are built the same. | What | Where it is published | | ------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Values you type | `NT:/Tuning//modules/azimuth/...` and `NT:/Tuning//modules/drive/...` | | One motor's telemetry | `NT:/Mechanisms//modules///...` | | All four modules at once | `NT:/Mechanisms//states/desired` and `states/current` | `` and `` are the names given to the module's and the motor's `withTelemetry(...)`. In AdvantageScope, drag `states/desired` and `states/current` onto a **Swerve** tab to see every module's target and actual state together. {% hint style="warning" %} Always start on the real robot with it lifted on blocks, and every wheel clear of the blocks and of the ground, for the azimuth and drive steps. {% endhint %} {% hint style="info" %} **Simulation is practice, not tuning.** Going through these steps in simulation first is a great way to learn them and to catch config mistakes, but gains found in simulation cannot be relied on for the first run of the real modules. Even if you tuned in simulation, tune again on the lifted robot before the wheels touch the ground. {% endhint %} #### Azimuth motors | You type (`NT:/Tuning//`) | Units | What it is | | ----------------------------------------- | ----------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `modules/azimuth/enabled` | Boolean | Hold the angle while `true`. | | `modules/azimuth/angle` | Degrees | Target angle for every module. | | `modules/azimuth/feedback/p`, `i`, `d` | PID gains | Azimuth motor feedback gains. | | `modules/azimuth/feedforward/s`, `v`, `a` | Feedforward gains | Azimuth motor kS, kV, kA. | | `modules/azimuth/voltage/enabled` | Boolean | Turn the azimuth motors at `voltage/setpoint` instead of holding the angle. See [Characterize the modules](#characterize-the-modules). | | `modules/azimuth/voltage/setpoint` | Volts | Voltage for every azimuth motor. | Watch one azimuth motor's `mechanism/position` against its `closedloop/setpoint/position`, or the module arrows on the Swerve tab. {% stepper %} {% step %} #### Start the tuning command and turn the mode on Start `NT:/Mechanisms//tuning`, type `0` into `modules/azimuth/angle`, then set `modules/azimuth/enabled` to `true`. The drive motors are held at 0, so the wheels only turn in place. {% endstep %} {% step %} #### Step the angle Type `90` into `NT:/Tuning//modules/azimuth/angle`, then `0`, and keep switching. That key is the setpoint angle for every azimuth motor, in degrees. Each change is a step you can judge the gains by. {% endstep %} {% step %} #### Raise `feedback/p` Raise it until the modules snap to the angle quickly. If they stop short or turn lazily, it is too low. If they overshoot and shake, it is too high: back it off. {% endstep %} {% step %} #### Add `feedback/d` if it still overshoots A small amount takes out the last of the overshoot. Leave `feedback/i` at 0. {% endstep %} {% step %} #### Add `feedforward/s` if the modules stop just short If they settle a degree or two away from the angle, a little kS overcomes the friction. {% endstep %} {% step %} #### Save the gains and turn the mode off Copy the gains into the azimuth motor's `withClosedLoopController(...)` and `withFeedforward(...)`. Values typed on the dashboard are lost when the robot code restarts. Set `modules/azimuth/enabled` to `false`. The modules stay at the last angle; they do not return to 0°. {% endstep %} {% endstepper %} #### Drive motors | You type (`NT:/Tuning//`) | Units | What it is | | --------------------------------------- | ----------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `modules/drive/enabled` | Boolean | Run the drive motors while `true`. | | `modules/drive/velocity` | Meters per second | Wheel speed for every module. | | `modules/drive/inplace` | Boolean | `false`: every module points at 0° and the robot drives straight. `true`: the modules point tangent to the robot center and the robot spins in place. | | `modules/drive/feedback/p`, `i`, `d` | PID gains | Drive motor feedback gains. | | `modules/drive/feedforward/s`, `v`, `a` | Feedforward gains | Drive motor kS, kV, kA. | | `modules/drive/voltage/enabled` | Boolean | Drive the drive motors at `voltage/setpoint` instead of the velocity. See [Characterize the modules](#characterize-the-modules). | | `modules/drive/voltage/setpoint` | Volts | Voltage for every drive motor. | Watch one drive motor's `measurement/velocity` against its `closedloop/setpoint/velocity`. The gains start at the first module's configured values. {% stepper %} {% step %} #### Start the tuning command and turn the mode on Start `NT:/Mechanisms//tuning`, type `0` into `modules/drive/velocity`, then set `modules/drive/enabled` to `true`. {% endstep %} {% step %} #### Zero the feedback Set `modules/drive/feedback/p`, `i` and `d` to 0 so you can see what the feedforward does on its own. {% endstep %} {% step %} #### Find `feedforward/s` Type a very small velocity, such as `0.1`, into `NT:/Tuning//modules/drive/velocity`. That key is the setpoint velocity for every drive motor, in meters per second. Raise `modules/drive/feedforward/s` until the wheels just start to turn, then back it off slightly. {% endstep %} {% step %} #### Find `feedforward/v` Type a normal driving speed, such as `2`, into `NT:/Tuning//modules/drive/velocity`. Raise `modules/drive/feedforward/v` until the motor's `measurement/velocity` settles on its `closedloop/setpoint/velocity`. Check a second speed, such as `1` or `3`, in the same key: it should match there too. {% endstep %} {% step %} #### Add `feedback/p` Raise `modules/drive/feedback/p` until the speed reaches the setpoint quickly and holds when the wheels are loaded. If the speed starts to buzz or oscillate, it is too high. `feedback/d` is rarely needed on a drive motor. {% endstep %} {% step %} #### Check it on the ground with `inplace` Take the robot off the blocks and set `modules/drive/inplace` to `true`. The modules point tangent to the robot center, so the robot spins in place instead of crossing the field. A positive `modules/drive/velocity` spins it counter-clockwise. {% endstep %} {% step %} #### Save the gains and turn the mode off Copy the gains into the drive motor's `withClosedLoopController(...)` and `withFeedforward(...)`, then set `modules/drive/enabled` to `false`. The drive motors are commanded to 0 m/s once it is off. {% endstep %} {% endstepper %} ### Characterize the modules Instead of tuning by hand, the modules can be driven at a voltage and the gains worked out from how they move, the way WPILib's SysId does. While drive or azimuth tuning is on, set its `voltage/enabled` to `true` and type a voltage into `voltage/setpoint`: * **Drive:** every drive motor runs at the voltage, without its closed loop. The wheels point forward, or around the robot with `modules/drive/inplace`, and are not optimized, so they always drive the same way. * **Azimuth:** every azimuth motor turns at the voltage, without its closed loop, and the drive motors are held still. A closed loop that runs on the SystemCore, on a Nova or with an LQR or exponential profile, would replace the voltage on its next loop, so YAMS stops it while the voltage is on and starts it again when the voltage turns off. The setpoint you typed is sent again then, or the wheels are held where they are if no mode is on. {% hint style="info" %} The YAGSL config generator's [Quick Start Guide](https://config.yagsl.com/guide) uses these keys in its Live mode: **Auto**, next to the gain fields, runs a slow ramp and a quick step each way, fits the feedforward, works out the feedback with an LQR, and fills in all six gains. The feedback depends on how often the closed loop runs, which each motor controller publishes as `closedloop/period` at `TelemetryVerbosity.HIGH`. {% endhint %} {% hint style="warning" %} A voltage has no speed limit. On a real robot, do this on blocks with every wheel clear, and keep the voltage low. {% endhint %} ### Tune auto-align | You type (`NT:/Tuning//`) | Units | What it is | | ---------------------------------------------- | -------------- | ------------------------------- | | `autoalign/enabled` | Boolean | Drive to the pose while `true`. | | `autoalign/setpoint/x`, `autoalign/setpoint/y` | Meters | Field relative target position. | | `autoalign/setpoint/rot` | Degrees | Field relative target heading. | | `autoalign/translation/p`, `i`, `d` | PID on meters | Translation gains. | | `autoalign/rotation/p`, `i`, `d` | PID on radians | Rotation gains. | The gains start at the values given to `withTranslationController(...)` and `withRotationController(...)`, not `0`. 1. Start the tuning command. 2. Type the target into `autoalign/setpoint/x`, `autoalign/setpoint/y` and `autoalign/setpoint/rot`. 3. Set `autoalign/enabled` to `true`. The robot drives to the pose with the current gains. 4. Change a gain and watch `NT:/Mechanisms//pose` on a 2D field. Changing a gain only resets that controller when the value actually changed. 5. Copy the gains you like into `withTranslationController(...)` and `withRotationController(...)`. Values typed on the dashboard are lost when the robot code restarts. 6. Set `autoalign/enabled` back to `false` before handing control back to the driver. ### Good to know * **One mode at a time.** If more than one `enabled` key is `true`, YAMS keeps one and sets the others back to `false`. Auto-align wins over drive tuning, and drive tuning wins over azimuth tuning. * **Every module shares the values.** The `modules/drive/*` and `modules/azimuth/*` keys apply to all modules at once. There are no per-module keys. * **Module optimization still applies.** Both module modes go through `SwerveDrive.setSwerveModuleStates(...)`, so `withOptimization(true)` behaves the same as it does while driving. * **No gyro needed in simulation.** The simulated drive tracks its own heading, so you can practice tuning the drive and azimuth motors before writing any gyro code. On a real robot, `SwerveDrive` throws an `IllegalStateException` if `withGyro(...)` was never called.

pages.title: TunerX in simulation
pages.content:
# TunerX in simulation

For TalonFX and TalonFXS motors, YAMS feeds its physics simulation results back through CTRE's vendorsim layer via Phoenix's `getSimState()` API. This means Phoenix Tuner X can connect to your simulation and display every motor signal, position, velocity, closed-loop error, applied voltage, current draw, exactly as it would on real hardware.

**To use TunerX in sim:**

1. In a terminal, run your robot code in simulation (for example, `./gradlew simulateJava`).
2. Open Phoenix Tuner X.
3. Connect to the simulation instance. It appears as a local device.
4. In the motor view, open the **Signal** tab. The physics simulation updates every signal in real time.

This is the same workflow as diagnosing real hardware. You can verify gain behavior, confirm soft/hard limit triggering, and plot signal graphs without ever touching a physical robot.

{% hint style="info" %}
TunerX vendorsim integration is specific to **CTRE TalonFX and TalonFXS** motors. REV Spark motors use WPILib's simulation framework and are visible through AdvantageScope or Elastic via NetworkTables instead.
{% endhint %}

TunerX shows the motor controller's own signals. To change YAMS gains, profiles and limits while the code runs, use [Live tuning](/documentation/understanding/live-tuning.md).

pages.title: AdvantageKit Integration
pages.content: # AdvantageKit Integration YAMS integrates seamlessly with [AdvantageKit](https://docs.advantagekit.org/), Team 6328's logging and replay framework. This guide shows how to use YAMS mechanisms with AdvantageKit's IO layer pattern for deterministic log replay. ## What is AdvantageKit? [AdvantageKit](https://docs.advantagekit.org/getting-started/what-is-advantagekit) is a logging framework that records **all inputs** to your robot code, enabling deterministic replay in simulation. Unlike traditional logging that captures specific values, AdvantageKit captures everything flowing into your code, allowing you to: * Replay matches exactly as they happened * Add new logged fields after the fact * Test code changes against real match data * Debug issues that only occurred on the real robot {% hint style="info" %} AdvantageKit is optional. YAMS works perfectly without it using its built-in telemetry system. Consider AdvantageKit if you want deterministic log replay capabilities. {% endhint %} ## Architecture overview AdvantageKit uses an [IO interface pattern](https://docs.advantagekit.org/data-flow/recording-inputs/io-interfaces) to separate hardware interaction from business logic. Traditionally, this requires separate IO implementations for real hardware and simulation: ## YAMS simplification: one IO class for real and sim **With YAMS, you don't need separate Real and Sim IO implementations.** Every `SmartMotorController` wrapper (TalonFXWrapper, SparkWrapper, etc.) and every Mechanism class (Arm, Elevator, FlyWheel, SwerveModule, SwerveDrive, etc.) includes **passive simulation** that runs automatically when `Robot.isSimulation()` returns true. The YAMS mechanism under the IO class picks real hardware or its own simulation by itself, based on `Robot.isSimulation()`. This means: * **One IO class** handles both real robot and simulation * **No duplicate code** - configuration is written once * **No SimWrapper needed** - real hardware wrappers simulate themselves * **Physics are automatic** - based on your DCMotor, gearing, and mass/MOI configuration {% hint style="success" %} **Key Insight**: When you create a `TalonFXWrapper`, `TalonFXSWrapper`, `SparkWrapper`, or any YAMS Mechanism, the simulation physics run automatically in sim mode. You write your IO class once using real hardware objects, and YAMS handles the rest. {% endhint %} ## Tutorial The tutorial builds an arm, an elevator and a shooter with the IO layer pattern, one step per page: | Page | What it covers | | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | [Step 1: Define the IO interface](/documentation/understanding/advantagekit-integration/io-interface.md) | The inputs each mechanism logs, and the AdvantageKit setup in `build.gradle`. | | [Step 2: Implement the IO class](/documentation/understanding/advantagekit-integration/io-implementation.md) | One IO class per mechanism that works on the real robot and in simulation. | | [Steps 3 and 4: The subsystem and RobotContainer](/documentation/understanding/advantagekit-integration/subsystem-and-robotcontainer.md) | The subsystem that uses the IO class, and wiring it up. | | [Log replay](/documentation/understanding/advantagekit-integration/log-replay.md) | Replaying a log, and the pattern in summary. | | [Swerve drive with AdvantageKit](/documentation/understanding/advantagekit-integration/swerve-drive.md) | The same pattern for a YAMS swerve drive. | | [Without an IO layer](/documentation/understanding/advantagekit-integration/direct-subsystem.md) | A simpler pattern that logs straight from the subsystem. | ## Benefits of YAMS + AdvantageKit | Feature | Benefit | | --------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- | | **No Duplicate IO Classes** | Single IO class works for real robot AND simulation | | **Deterministic Replay** | Debug issues from real matches using log replay | | **Automatic Physics** | YAMS uses DCMotor, gearing, and mass/MOI for accurate sim | | **Less Boilerplate** | 2 IO classes instead of 3 per mechanism | | **Consistent Behavior** | Same code paths execute in real and sim modes | | **Flexible Hardware** | Swap vendors by changing one IO class | ## Further reading * [AdvantageKit Documentation](https://docs.advantagekit.org/) * [What is AdvantageKit?](https://docs.advantagekit.org/getting-started/what-is-advantagekit) * [IO Interfaces](https://docs.advantagekit.org/data-flow/recording-inputs/io-interfaces) * [Template Projects](https://docs.advantagekit.org/getting-started/template-projects) * [YAMS AdvantageKit Example (Commands v2)](https://github.com/Yet-Another-Software-Suite/YAMS/tree/master/examples/commands2/advantage_kit) * [YAMS AdvantageKit Example (Commands v3)](https://github.com/Yet-Another-Software-Suite/YAMS/tree/master/examples/commands3/advantage_kit)

pages.title: Overview
pages.content:
# Overview

YAMS (Yet Another Mechanism Suite) is a WPILib vendordep library for FRC robots. It provides a unified motor controller abstraction over REV, CTRE, and Thrifty hardware, pre-built mechanism classes for common robot subsystems, and advanced control algorithms, all with simulation support and automatic NetworkTables telemetry. Both Java and C++ are supported with parallel APIs.

This documentation tracks YAMS for WPILib 2027 (`2027_alpha7`), where robot code runs on the SystemCore. Java command bindings ship for both WPILib Commands v2 (`yams.commands2`) and Commands v3 (`yams.commands3`); C++ supports Commands v2. See [Getting Started](/api-reference/getting-started.md) for installation.

## Features

* **Motor controller abstraction:** a single `SmartMotorController` interface over SPARK MAX, SPARK FLEX, TalonFX, TalonFXS, and Thrifty Nova
* **Mechanism classes:** `Arm`, `Elevator`, `Pivot`, `FlyWheel`, `DoubleJointedArm`, `DifferentialMechanism`, and `SwerveDrive` (`DoubleJointedArm` and `DifferentialMechanism` are Java only)
* **Advanced control:** LQR, exponential motion profiles, trapezoidal profiles, and a derivative-time filter
* **Extended units:** `YUnits` constants and `EasyCRT` multi-encoder absolute position solver
* **Simulation:** built-in sim support for all mechanism classes via WPILib's simulation framework, with one shared `BatterySim` across every motor controller
* **Commands v2 and v3:** the same mechanisms with `Command` and `Trigger` factories for either WPILib command framework (Java)

## Quick navigation

* [Java API](/api-reference/java-reference/java.md)
* [C++ API](/api-reference/c++-reference/cpp.md)
* [Guides](/api-reference/guides/guides.md)

## Supported hardware

| Device     | Vendor          | Interface |
| ---------- | --------------- | --------- |
| SPARK MAX  | REV Robotics    | CAN       |
| SPARK FLEX | REV Robotics    | CAN       |
| TalonFX    | CTR Electronics | CAN       |
| TalonFXS   | CTR Electronics | CAN       |
| Nova       | Thrifty Bot     | CAN       |

pages.title: Changelog
pages.content:
# Changelog

New updates and improvements

## Unreleased

These changes are on `master` and will ship in the next release.

### Added

* `getPose3d()` on every mechanism (C++ `GetPose3d()`): its `Pose3d` relative to the robot, to publish as a component of an AdvantageScope robot model. It is worked out from the motor's position, so it works on the robot as well as in simulation: an arm's or pivot's axis turned to its angle, an elevator's carriage at its height, or a flywheel's axle turned by its position. `DoubleJointedArm.getUpperPose3d()` gives the upper arm's. See [How do I show my mechanisms on a 3D robot model?](https://yams.yassrobotics.com/documentation/how-to-simulation-and-logging/how-do-i-show-my-mechanisms-on-a-3d-robot-model).
* `MechanismPositionConfig.withRelativePosition(Transform3d)`, which also sets how the mechanism is turned where it is mounted, and `withParent(Supplier<Pose3d>)`, which mounts it on another mechanism, such as an arm on `elevator::getPose3d`. `getMountPose()`, `getRotatedPose(Angle)` and `getTranslatedPose(Distance, Angle)` do the math for parts YAMS has no mechanism for.
* **C++:** `ArmConfig`, `ElevatorConfig`, `PivotConfig` and `FlyWheelConfig` take a `MechanismPositionConfig` with `WithMechanismPositionConfig(...)`.
* `ElevatorConfig.withStages(Distance... stageHeights)` (C++ `WithStages(0.6_m, 0.6_m, 0.5_m)`): how far each of the elevator's moving stages travels relative to the stage below it, one height for each stage, the carriage last. `Elevator.getCascadePose3d()` and `getContinuousPose3d(boolean carriageFirst)` (C++ `GetCascadePose3d()` and `GetContinuousPose3d(bool carriageFirst)`) then give each stage's pose, from the stage nearest the fixed stage to the carriage: a cascade elevator's stages all move at once, each by its share of the carriage's height, and a continuous elevator's stages move one at a time, the carriage first or last. Both need 2 or more stages. The stage heights must add up to the elevator's maximum height, or the `Elevator` throws an `ElevatorConfigurationException`, and without hard limits they give the elevator's height, from 0 to their total (`getStageHeightTotal()`). See [Elevator stages](https://yams.yassrobotics.com/documentation/how-to-simulation-and-logging/how-do-i-show-my-mechanisms-on-a-3d-robot-model#elevator-stages).
* `YMotors.getThriftyPulsar(int)`: a `DCMotor` of the Thrifty Pulsar 775 from Thrifty's specs, since WPILib has none. `TalonFXSWrapper` drives it as `NEO_JST`.
* Swerve live tuning can drive the modules at a voltage, without their closed loops, to characterize them: `modules/drive/voltage/enabled` and `modules/drive/voltage/setpoint` while drive tuning is on, and `modules/azimuth/voltage/enabled` and `modules/azimuth/voltage/setpoint` while azimuth tuning is on, under `Tuning/<name>/`. A closed loop that runs on the SystemCore is stopped while its voltage is on. The YAGSL config generator's Live mode uses these for its **Auto** gains. See [Characterize the modules](https://yams.yassrobotics.com/documentation/understanding/live-tuning#characterize-the-modules).
* `SmartMotorController.getClosedLoopControllerPeriod()` (C++ `GetClosedLoopControllerPeriod()`): how often the closed loop runs, 1 ms on the motor controller or the closed loop control period on the SystemCore. Published as `closedloop/period` at `HIGH`, or with `withClosedLoopPeriod()` (`WithClosedLoopPeriod()`).
* `SwerveModule.getCouplingVelocity()` (C++ `GetCouplingVelocity()`) is public, and the C++ `SwerveDrive` has `ApplyTuningValues()`, as Java does.
* SPARK and TalonFX feedback and feedforward gains are checked with the vendor's status code when they change, retrying for up to 15 ms, and raise an alert if they still aren't applied. Only the SPARK's closed loop or feedforward config, or the TalonFX's slot, is sent, to use less of the CAN bus.

### Changed

* **Breaking:** the mechanisms' `getRelativeMechanismPosition()` is replaced by `getPose3d()` (C++: `GetRelativeMechanismPosition()` by `GetPose3d()`). The old method was read from the simulation's `Mechanism2d`, threw a `NullPointerException` on the robot, gave degrees to `Rotation3d` as radians, and turned the wrong way. `SmartMotorController.getRelativeMechanismPosition()`, which reads the relative encoder, is unchanged.
* **Breaking (C++):** `MechanismPositionConfig` is now the class that places a mechanism in 3D, as in Java. It was a named setpoint class that was declared but never defined.
* A `Pivot`'s pose turns in its movement plane: XY, like a turret, unless it is given a `MechanismPositionConfig`, which is XZ unless set otherwise. The C++ `PivotConfig` defaults to XY too, as the Java one does.
* **Behavior change:** stopping a `SmartMotorController`'s closed loop, as a mechanism does before driving it at a duty cycle or voltage, also stops its loosely coupled followers' closed loops and sets them to a duty cycle of 0. Starting it starts theirs (Java and C++).
* `TalonFXSWrapper` drives a NEO Vortex as `VORTEX_JST` rather than `NEO_JST`, as the C++ wrapper and YAMG already did.
* **Behavior change:** swerve live tuning applies only the values that changed, and sends the setpoints again when a tuning mode turns on or off. A tuning mode that is on turns off the ones it outranks (auto-align, then drive tuning, then azimuth tuning). Ending the tuning command turns every mode off and holds the wheels where they are.
* **Breaking (C++):** the swerve tuning command is published at `Mechanisms/<name>/tuning`, as in Java, rather than `Mechanisms/<name>/tuning/driveToPose`.

### Removed

* **Breaking:** `SmartMechanism.getRelativeMechanismPosition()` (Java) and `GetRelativeMechanismPosition()` on the C++ `Arm`, `Elevator`, `Pivot` and `FlyWheel`. Use `getPose3d()`.

### Fixed

* A loosely coupled follower whose closed loop runs on the SystemCore (a Thrifty Nova, a SPARK with an exponential profile, or any motor controller with an LQR) kept driving to its last setpoint after its leader stopped, including after a duty cycle of 0: its closed loop set its output again on the next loop.
* Simulation: a `Pivot` stops at its hard stops. It kept its speed when put back on a stop, and flew past again on the next loop. A pivot that wraps continuously (`withContinuousWrapping`) has no hard stops, and turns on past where it wraps (Java and C++).
* Simulation: a `Pivot` starts at its starting position. Its simulation started at 0, away from its encoder, so it was stopped at hard stops it had not reached (Java and C++).
* Simulation: a TalonFX or TalonFXS keeps an encoder position it is set to. It set the position before moving its simulated rotor, so a Talon at 60 degrees set to 0 read -60 (Java).
* `TalonFXSWrapper` threw `IllegalArgumentException("Unknown motor for TalonFXS...")` for a Thrifty Pulsar.
* C++ `cpptest` example: `projectYear` is `2027_alpha7`, to match its GradleRIO.

## 2026.10.15

See [Updating from v2026.10.09 to v2026.10.15](https://github.com/Yet-Another-Software-Suite/YAMS/blob/master/MIGRATION.md#updating-from-v20261009-to-v20261015) in the migration guide.

### Added

* `SwerveInputStream` aim options, carried over from YAGSL 2026: `withAimLookahead(Time)`, `withAimFeedforward(SimpleMotorFeedforward)`, `withAimHeadingOffset(Rotation2d)`, `isAimLocked(Angle)` and the `aimLock(Angle)` Trigger, `getTargetVector(Pose2d)` and `calculateAngularVelocity(Angle)`. Aiming without them behaves as before.
* `SwerveDrive.setAzimuthAngles(Rotation2d)`: turns every module to one angle without driving it. Azimuth live tuning uses it, so it turns the modules again.
* **C++:** the swerve drive matches the Java one: the 3D gyro and gyro heading axis, anti-tipping, module speed desaturation, the coupling ratio, feedforward forces and the default velocity deadband.
* Commands v2 `SwerveDrive.driveToPose(Pose2d, Distance, Angle)`, which ends once the robot is within the tolerances, and `isNear(Pose2d, Distance, Angle)` and `stop()`. These were only on the Commands v3 `SwerveDrive`; `isNear` and `stop` now live on the shared `SwerveDrive`.
* `SmartMechanism.getMeasurementSetpoint()`: the mechanism's position setpoint as a `Distance`, converted with the mechanism circumference. It is empty when there is no position setpoint or no circumference is configured.
* `EasyCRT.solve(Angle, Angle)` / `EasyCRT::Solve(...)`: solve for travel centered on zero, with a `solve(a, b, minAngle, maxAngle)` overload for other travel.
* `EasyCRT.getUniqueRange()` / `EasyCRT::GetUniqueRange()`: how far the shared gear can turn before the two encoder readings repeat.
* A `Turret` that seeds its motor from `EasyCRT` at startup, with a unit test, in the `BroncBotz_2026` examples for Commands v2 and Commands v3.

### Changed

* **Behavior change:** an `ArmFeedforward`'s kV and kA are per rotation everywhere. The closed loop on the SystemCore (such as the Thrifty Nova's) read them per radian. If you tuned an arm's kV or kA on the SystemCore with 2026.10.9, multiply them by 2π to keep the same behavior.
* **Breaking:** `SwerveModule.lock(Rotation2d)` is now `setAzimuthAngle(Rotation2d)`. It turns the wheel without driving it.
* The external encoder telemetry is only published when there is an external encoder. `externalencoder/position` and `externalencoder/velocity` keep their names.
* The vendordep JSONs require the matching WPILib command library (`command2` or `command3`).
* **Behavior change:** the Commands v2 `SwerveDrive.driveToPose(Pose2d)` now stops the drive when it ends or is interrupted, as the Commands v3 one already did. It used to leave the last commanded speeds in place.
* **Behavior change:** `withTemperatureCutoff` now follows where the closed loop runs, because the cutoff is only checked by the closed loop on the SystemCore (Java and C++). On a SPARK MAX or SPARK Flex it needs an exponential profile or an LQR controller: a trapezoidal profile with a cutoff used to be accepted and silently ignored, and now throws at startup. On a TalonFX or TalonFXS it is now accepted with an LQR controller, where it used to always throw.
* **Breaking:** `EasyCRT` is now built from three tooth counts and solves from two readings (Java and C++). The match tolerance is derived from the tooth counts, and a reading pair that does not agree returns an empty result.
* **Breaking (Java):** `DifferentialMechanism.set(...)` now takes `(tilt, twist)` like every other method, and mixes them with the same signs as `setPosition` (left = tilt + twist, right = tilt - twist). It took `(twist, tilt)` and drove the twist the opposite way. Swap the arguments if you called it as `(twist, tilt)`.
* `EasyCRTConfigGuide.md` is replaced by `EasyCRTGuide.md`, which explains how to choose tooth counts, zero and invert the encoders, handle gear trains, and check your margin yourself.
* `MIGRATION.md` now covers the whole 2026 to 2027 upgrade.

### Removed

* **Breaking:** `EasyCRTConfig`, including its gearing helpers, offset and inversion setters, match tolerance, and gear recommender, and the `EasyCRT` status, error and iteration getters.

### Fixed

* Simulated SPARKs follow their profile and feedforward. REVLib's simulation does not run MAXMotion, and works out kCos from the setpoint instead of the position, so in simulation a SPARK with a trapezoidal profile runs the profile on the SystemCore. On the robot it still uses MAXMotion. See [wpilibsuite/SystemcoreTesting#425](https://github.com/wpilibsuite/SystemcoreTesting/issues/425).
* Simulated SPARKs start at their starting position, and report their real voltage. Both were off by the gear ratio.
* Every motor controller gives the same voltage for the same kP, kI, kD, kS, kV, kA and kG in YAMS units, from every closed loop slot. This fixed an elevator feedforward under velocity control on the SystemCore, which left out kV.
* **C++:** swerve fixes the Java swerve already had, and swerve azimuth live tuning.
* `ExponentialProfilePIDController.createConstraints(maxVolts, maxVelocity, maxAcceleration)` passed kV and kA as state space terms, which gave an unstable profile with a negative maximum velocity. It now builds the same constraints as `SmartMotorControllerConfig.withExponentialProfile(Voltage, AngularVelocity, AngularAcceleration)`.
* Simulation: `Arm`, `Elevator`, `Pivot`, `FlyWheel`, `DoubleJointedArm` and `DifferentialMechanism` no longer replace the shared `BatterySim` voltage with one computed from their own current draw alone. The simulated battery now sags from every mechanism's combined draw, and `enableDischarge(...)` is respected, no matter which mechanism iterates last (Java and C++).
* `simple_robot-2027` examples: the simulated gyro yaw was set in radians instead of degrees, and the elevators were missing the carriage weight and starting position that `Elevator` requires in simulation.
* C++ `cpptest` example: the field-relative `SwerveInputStream` output is converted to robot-relative before `SwerveDrive::Drive`.
* `GearBox` Javadoc: `fromTeeth(...)` is a train of meshing gears, so `fromTeeth(12, 60, 12, 60)` is 5:1, not 25:1.

Intended as a "known truth" source for simulated vision systems.

Use `getPose()`, `resetOdometry(Pose2d)`, and `addVisionMeasurement(...)` instead.

## 2026.8.20

### Added

* `BatterySim` (Java & C++) now models a single, shared robot battery in simulation. Every simulated `SmartMotorController` — via its `SimSupplier` (`ArmSimSupplier`, `ElevatorSimSupplier`, `DCMotorSimSupplier`) or hardware wrapper (`SparkWrapper`, `TalonFXWrapper`, `TalonFXSWrapper`) — reports its own current draw into one combined loaded-voltage calculation, instead of each mechanism computing `RoboRioSim` voltage sag from only its own current draw and overwriting the others.
* `BatterySim.enableDischarge(double, Voltage, Resistance)` (Java) / `BatterySim::EnableDischarge(double, units::volt_t, units::ohm_t)` (C++) — optional realistic battery discharge simulation. Current draw is integrated into amp-hours consumed over time, sagging the open-circuit voltage and raising internal resistance as the battery empties, following a typical FRC sealed lead-acid discharge curve. Also added `disableDischarge()`/`DisableDischarge()`, `resetDischarge()`/`ResetDischarge()`, and `getStateOfCharge()`/`GetStateOfCharge()`.
* `BatterySim.replaceSOCInterpolation(InterpolatingDoubleTreeMap)` (Java) / `BatterySim::ReplaceSOCInterpolation(const std::map<double, double>&)` (C++) — swap in a custom state-of-charge → voltage discharge curve, for modeling a well-used competition battery, a different chemistry, or a curve measured from a real battery on a load tester.

### Changed

* **C++:** `Arm`, `Elevator`, `Pivot`, and `FlyWheel` no longer call `RoboRioSim::SetVInVoltage(...)` directly from their own current draw. Voltage now comes from the shared `BatterySim`, so combined load across multiple mechanisms sags the simulated bus voltage realistically instead of only reflecting whichever mechanism updated last.

{% hint style="info" %}
Discharge simulation is off by default and only affects simulation — on a real robot, `RobotController.getBatteryVoltage()`/`frc::RobotController::GetBatteryVoltage()` always reflects actual hardware.
{% endhint %}

## 2026.1.2

* Added `SmartMotorControllerConfig().clone()` to allow for clonable configs.
* Added `MechanismConfig.withSmartMotorController()` for all mechanism and null param constructors
* Added `SensorData.set()` overloads
* 'Trapazoidal' Spelling Error Correction by [@akhaled247](https://github.com/akhaled247) in [#56](https://github.com/Yet-Another-Software-Suite/YAMS/pull/56)
* REV 2026 with Feedforwards and PIDs by [@thenetworkgrinch](https://github.com/thenetworkgrinch) in [#55](https://github.com/Yet-Another-Software-Suite/YAMS/pull/55)
* Added the option to loosely coupled followers. by [@thenetworkgrinch](https://github.com/thenetworkgrinch) in [#58](https://github.com/Yet-Another-Software-Suite/YAMS/pull/58)
* Allow for independently created config classes for constants files. by [@thenetworkgrinch](https://github.com/thenetworkgrinch) in [#59](https://github.com/Yet-Another-Software-Suite/YAMS/pull/59)
* Changed `SwerveInputStream.copy()` to `SwerveInputStream.clone()`
* Modified `SmartMotorControllerConfig` to allow for creation without a `Subsystem` but still require a subsystem eventually.
* Modified `SmartMotorController` telemetry to only create Live Tuning and other useful commands if tunable setpoints are not enabled.
* Added `MechanismGearing(double...)` overload
* Added DifferentialDrive example.

## 2025.12.22

* Added the ability to use multiple SMC's with Live Tuning in one subsystem
* Added AdvantageKit example
* Modified `SwerveDrive` to support AdvantageKit better.
* Updated Telemetry Setup for standalone SMC's to be automatic.
* Added Units to Telemetry Fields.
* Added DoubleFlyWheel example.
* Fixed ElevatorConfig comments saying "length" instead of "angle" [#54](https://github.com/Yet-Another-Software-Suite/YAMS/pull/54)
* Added support for user moment of inertia in ExponentialProfilePIDController [#50](https://github.com/Yet-Another-Software-Suite/YAMS/pull/50)
* Improved Exponential Elevator Examples [#46](https://github.com/Yet-Another-Software-Suite/YAMS/pull/46)
* Added ExponentialProfile.
* Add MapleSim Integration to SwerveDrive by [@konnorreynolds](https://github.com/konnorreynolds) in [#49](https://github.com/Yet-Another-Software-Suite/YAMS/pull/49)

## 2025.11.05

* Renamed `.withExternalGearing` to `.withExternalEncoderGearing`.
* Added several new easy commands, like "Up", "Down", and "ZeroEncoder".
* Moved commands to "SmartDashboard/Mechanisms/MECHNAME/MOTORNAME/Commands/".
* Fixed immutable SensorData fields.
* Fixed `SparkWrapper.setEncoderPosition` to set the sim position correctly.

## 2025.11.02

* Renamed `SmartMotorControllerConfig.withZeroOffset` to `SmartMotorControllerConfig.withExternalEncoderZeroOffset`

## 2025.10.31

* Updated `SwerveInputStream` to use `.with*` for shared styling.
* Added `swerve_drive` example.

## 2025.10.29

* Added setpoint visualization to Arm Mechanism2d
* Fixed ArmFeedforward calculation on Spark's, and Nova's. Changed velocity calculation from Rotations to Radians. Found by 8114 (The Rocketeers)

## 2025.10.27

* Renamed `Shooter` to `FlyWheel`
* Added Loop Time to each mechanism.

## 2025.10.14

* Added `YUnits` which allows you to include more exotic units in your code.
* Added `Sensor`s which allow you to seamlessly fetch automatically modified sensor data during sim and real data when running IRL.
